text_zh: 至聖命脈。列祖大機。換骨靈方。頤神妙術。其 惟雪竇禪師。具超宗越格正眼。提掇正令。不 露風規。秉烹佛煅祖鉗鎚。頌出衲僧向上巴 鼻。銀山鐵壁。孰敢鑽研。蚊咬鐵牛。難為下 口。不逢大匠。焉悉玄微。粵有佛果老人。住碧 巖日。學者迷而請益。老人愍以垂慈。剔抉淵 源。剖析底理。當陽直指。豈立見知。百則公 案。從頭一串穿來。一隊老漢。次第總將按過。 須知趙璧本無瑕纇。相如謾誑秦王。至道實 乎無言。宗師垂慈救弊。儻如是見。方知徹底 老婆。其或泥句沈言。未免滅佛種族。普照幸 親師席。得聞未聞。道友集成簡編。鄙拙敘其 本末。時建炎戊申。暮春晦日。參學嗣祖比丘 普照謹序。
text_en: was the master Xuedou who possessed the true eye that surpasses schools and transcends standards, who lifted up the correct command and did not reveal the customary style. Wielding the tongs and hammer that boil Buddhas and forge patriarchs, he cast verses that bring forth a patch-robed monk’s upward nose. A silver mountain, an iron wall—who would dare bore into it? A mosquito biting an iron ox—hard to even get one’s teeth into it. If one does not meet a great master-craftsman, how could one fathom its hidden subtlety? There was also the old man Foguo, who, while residing at Blue Cliff, was asked for guidance by students who were confused. The old man, moved with compassion, plucked out and brought forth the deep sources, dissected the underlying principles, and pointed straight ahead in the full light of day—how could this be mere quick cleverness? The hundred public cases, threaded together from the beginning like a single string; a whole squad of old fellows, examined one by one and all passed through. You must know that the Zhao jade originally has no flaw; Xiangru only hoodwinked the King of Qin. The ultimate Way truly lies beyond words. The lineage master let down compassion to rescue what was going astray; if one sees it like this, only then does one know the thoroughgoing old granny. But if one clings to phrases and sinks into words, one cannot avoid extinguishing the Buddha-seed. Fortunately, Universal Illumination by personally drawing close to the master’s seat, one gets to hear what one has never heard. Dharma friends gathered it into a brief compilation; with my crude incompetence I narrate its beginning and end. This was in the Jianyan era, wushen year, on the last day of late spring. A bhikshu in training, heir in the patriarchal line, respectfully writes this preface. Universal Illumination

text_en: the Sixth Patriarch transmitting the robe, only then did there begin to be phrases and sayings. “Originally there is not a single thing” became the Southern School. “Constantly, diligently wipe it clean” became the Northern School. Thus there came to be Chan verses on old cases circulating in the world. Their followers also had the method of overturning cases: scolding Buddha, cursing the patriarchs—nothing they would not do. Among them, there were some who deeply grasped the living method of our poets. Yet as for what is called the First Principle—what use has it for phrases? Xuedou and Yuanwu, with the urgent heart of an old granny; Dahui already burned it with a single torch. Zhang Wei Mingyuan of Yuzhong rekindled dead ashes and printed it anew—this too is what one might call the urgent heart of an old granny, is it not? In the fourth year of Dade, gengzi, on the eighth day of the fourth month, guichou, Fang Hui Wanli of Ziyang Mountain wrote this preface.

text_zh: 碧巖集者。圜悟大師之所述也。其大弟子大 慧禪師。乃焚棄其書。世間種種法皆忌執著。 釋子所歸敬莫如佛。猶有時而罵之。蓋有我 而無彼。由我而不由彼也。舍己徇物。必至於 失己。夫心與道一。道與萬物一。充滿太虛。何 適而非道。第常人觀之。能見其所見。而不 見其所不見。求之於人。而人語之。如東坡日 喻之說。往復推測。愈遠愈失。自吾夫子體道。 猶欲無言。而況佛氏為出世間法。而可文字 言語而求之哉。雖然亦有不可廢者。智者少 而愚者多。已學者少未學者多。大藏經五千 餘卷。盡為未來世設。苟可以忘言。釋迦老 子便當閉口。何至如是叨叨。天下之理。固有 不離尋常之中。而超出於尋常之表。雖若易 知。而實未易知者。不求之於人。則終身不可 得。古者名世之人。非千人之英。則萬人之傑 也。太阿之劍。天下之利劍也。登山則戮虎 豹。入水則剸蛟龍。人之知之。盡於是已。然古 人有善用之者。乘城而戰。順風而揮之。三軍 為之大敗。流血赭乎千里。是豈可以一己之 所能。而盡疑之哉。自吾聞有是書。求之甚至。 嵎中張氏。始更刻木。來謀於予。遂贊而成之。 且為題其首。大德九年歲乙巳。三月吉日。玉 岑休休居士。聊城周馳。書於錢唐觀橋寓舍。
text_en: then burned and discarded the book. The various dharmas of the world all dread attachment. For a son of Śākya, nothing is more worthy of reverence than the Buddha; yet there are times when he is even cursed. This is because there is “me” and no “other”—it proceeds from me, not from the other. If one abandons oneself and chases after things, one will inevitably come to lose oneself. The mind is one with the Way; the Way is one with all things. It fills the great void—where could one go that is not the Way? But ordinary people, looking at it, can see what they see, and yet do not see what they do not see. They seek it from others, and others speak of it—like Dongpo’s explanation by metaphor: conjecturing back and forth, the farther one goes, the more one misses. Even our Master, embodying the Way, still wished to be without words—how much more for the Buddha’s teaching, as a supramundane dharma: how could it be sought through letters, through language? Even so, there are also things that cannot be dispensed with. The wise are few and the foolish are many; those who have learned are few and those who have not learned are many. The Great Canon’s more than five thousand volumes were all set up for future ages. If one could truly forget words, old Śākyamuni should have kept his mouth shut—why all this endless chatter? The principles under heaven indeed include what does not depart from the ordinary, yet transcends the surface of the ordinary. Though it may seem easy to know, in truth it is not easy to know. If one does not seek it from others, then for one’s whole life one cannot obtain it. In ancient times, people renowned in the world were either the best among a thousand, or outstanding among ten thousand. The Tai’a sword is the sharp sword under heaven: climb a mountain and it slays tigers and leopards; enter the water and it cuts down flood-dragons. People’s knowledge of it ends there. Yet the ancients had those who were skilled in using it: fighting from the city walls, they swung it with the wind at their back, and the three armies suffered great defeat, blood flowing red for a thousand li. How could one, with only one’s own limited capacity, exhaust all its possibilities with doubt? Since I heard there was such a book, I sought it with utmost urgency. The Zhang family of Yuzhong began anew to carve the woodblocks and came to consult me; I then assisted and brought it to completion. I also inscribed its opening. In the ninth year of Dade, yisi year, on an auspicious day in the third month, Yu Cen Xiuxiu, layman; Zhou Chi of Liaocheng, wrote this at a lodging by Guan Bridge in Qiantang.

text_zh: 或問。碧巖集之成毀孰是乎。曰皆是也。齴齲 來東單傳心印。不立文字固也。而血脈歸空 諸論。果誰為之哉。古謂不在文字不離文字 者。真知言。已使人人於卷簾聞板竪指觸脚 之際。了却大事。文字何有哉。拈花微笑以來。 門竿倒却之後。才涉言句。非文字無以傳。是 又不可廢者也。甞謂祖教之書。謂之公案者。 倡於唐而盛於宋。其來尚矣。二字乃世間法 中吏牘語。其用有三。面壁功成。行脚事了。定 槃之星難明。野狐之趣易墮。具眼為之勘辨。 一呵一喝。要見實詣。如老吏據獄讞罪。底裏 悉見。情欵不遺一也。其次則嶺南初來。西江 未吸。亡羊之岐易泣。指海之針必南。悲心 為之接引。一棒一痕要令證悟。如廷尉執法 平反。出人於死二也。又其次則犯稼憂深。繫 驢事重。學弈之志須專。染絲之色易悲。大善 知識為之付囑。俾之心死蒲團。一動一參。如 官府頒示條令。令人讀律知法。惡念才生。旋 即寢滅三也。具方冊。作案底。陳機境。為格 令。與世間所謂金科玉條清明對越諸書。初 何以異。祖師所以立為公案。留示叢林者。意 或取此。柰何末法以來。求妙心於瘡紙。付正 法於口談。點盡鬼神。猶不離簿。傍人門戶。任 喚作郎。劍去矣而舟猶刻。兔逸矣而株不移。 滿肚葛藤。能問千轉。其於生死大事。初無干 涉。鐘鳴漏盡。將焉用之。烏乎。羚羊掛角。未 可以形迹求。而善學下慧者。豈步亦步。趨亦 趨哉。知此則二老之心皆是矣。圜悟顧子念 孫之心多。故重拈雪竇頌。大慧救焚拯溺之 心多。故立毀碧巖集。釋氏說一大藏經。末後 乃謂。不曾說一字。豈欺我哉圜悟之心。釋氏 說經之心也。大慧之心。釋氏諱說之心也。禹 稷顏子易地皆然。推之輓之。主於車行而已。 爾來二百餘年。嵎中張明遠。復鏤梓。以壽其 傳。豈祖教回春乎。抑世故有數乎。然是書之 行。所關甚重。若見水即海。認指作月。不特大 慧憂之。而圜悟又將為之去粘解縛矣。昔人 寫照之詩曰。分明紙上張公子。盡力高聲喚 不譍。欲觀此書。先參此語。大德甲辰四月望。 三教老人書。
text_en: came from the West and transmitted the seal of mind directly, without establishing letters—this is surely so. Yet as for discussions of bloodline and returning to emptiness, who, in fact, made them? The ancients said, “Not in words, not apart from words”— these are truly knowing words. If it already enables everyone, at the moment of raising a curtain, hearing a board, holding up a finger, or stubbing a toe, to settle the great matter—what place have words? Since the “flower held up and a faint smile,” after the gate-pole fell, the moment one touches phrases, without words there is no way to transmit. This too is something that cannot be abandoned. It has been said that the books of the ancestral teaching, those called public cases, began in the Tang and flourished in the Song; their origins go back far. The two characters are originally a worldly term from clerical documents in secular law. Their uses are three. First: when wall-gazing practice is fulfilled and roaming on foot is finished, the star of nirvana is hard to discern, and one easily falls into the ways of the wild fox; those with eyes examine and distinguish it. With one scolding and one shout, it must reveal actual attainment—like an old clerk judging guilt from the case records, seeing the inside all at once, leaving out not a single confession. Second: when one has just come from Lingnan and has not yet swallowed the waters of the West River, the byways where sheep are lost easily bring tears; the needle that points to the sea must face south. With compassionate heart, one guides and receives them; one blow, one mark—making them realize and awaken—like the chief judge enforcing the law, overturning a wrongful verdict and pulling people out of death. Third: when one’s transgressions in the fields are deep and the matter of tethering the donkey is weighty, one’s resolve in learning the game of go must be single, and the color that dyes silk easily grieves. A great good spiritual friend entrusts and charges them, making their mind die on the meditation cushion; with each movement, with each inquiry— like an office issuing posted regulations, making people read the statutes and know the law. As soon as an evil thought arises, it is immediately put to sleep and extinguished—this is the third. It provides registers, makes case files, sets out the mechanisms and situations, and serves as regulations, so how is it different, at first, from the world’s so-called golden rules, jade statutes, and other clear, reverent manuals? Why did the patriarchs establish them as public cases and leave them to the monasteries? Their intent may have taken up something like this. But since the latter days of the Dharma, people seek the wondrous mind in scraps of wound-paper, and hand over the true Dharma to mouth-talk; even if they exhaust the ghosts and spirits, they still cannot leave the ledger. Clinging to others’ doorways, they let themselves be called “sir.” The sword is gone but the boat is still notched; the rabbit has fled but the stump will not move. Their belly is full of tangled vines; they can ask a thousand turns. Yet with the great matter of life and death, it has no connection at all. When the bell rings and the water-clock runs out, what use will it be? Alas—an antelope hangs its horns; it cannot be sought by forms and traces. And those who study well, though of lesser faculties—how could they merely follow step for step, hurry whenever the other hurries? Knowing this, the hearts of both old men are right. Yuanwu’s heart, looking after children and grandchildren, was strong; therefore he again lifted up Xuedou’s verses. Dahui’s heart, saving from burning and rescuing from drowning, was strong; therefore he established the destruction of the Blue Cliff Collection. The Śākya teaching speaks a whole Great Canon, yet in the end it says, “I have not spoken a single word.” How could it be deceiving me? Yuanwu’s heart is the heart of the Śākya teaching when it speaks sutras; Dahui’s heart is the heart of the Śākya teaching that forbids speaking. Yu, Ji, and Yanzi would all be the same if placed in the other’s position. Pushing it or pulling it, the point is simply to get the cart to move. After more than two hundred years, Zhang Mingyuan of Yuzhong again carved the blocks, to prolong its transmission. Is this the ancestral teaching returning to spring, or do worldly circumstances have their fixed number? Yet the circulation of this book bears very great consequence. If one sees water and takes it for the sea, or recognizes the pointing finger as the moon, it is not only Dahui who would worry; Yuanwu too would then remove the sticking and loosen the bonds. Someone of old wrote a poem on a portrait, saying: plainly, on the paper, Master Zhang; with all one’s strength one calls out in a loud voice, yet he does not answer. If you wish to look into this book, first take up this saying. In the Dade era, jiachen, on the full moon of the fourth month. Written by the Old Man of the Three Teachings.

But when it comes to cutting off all streams, surging in the east and sinking in the west, going against or along, roaming freely, giving and taking at will—right at such a time, tell me: whose place of conduct and practice is this? Zhigong said, “Does Your Majesty recognize this man?” The emperor said, “I do not.” Zhigong said, This wild-fox demon cannot avoid a bout of muddle, going from west to east, from east to west. A poor child remembering old debts; bystanders have eyes. Along with the Venerable Zhigong, drive him out of the country, that will do. Give him thirty blows. Bodhidharma is here! Fine too, drive him out of the country all at once. he still would not return.” Venerable Zhigong also deserves thirty blows. He does not know that beneath his heels great light is released.

text_zh: 達磨遙觀此土有大乘根器。遂泛海得得而 來。單傳心印。開示迷塗。不立文字。直指人 心。見性成佛。若恁麼見得。便有自由分。不隨 一切語言轉。脫體現成。便能於後頭。與武帝 對譚。并二祖安心處。自然見得。無計較情塵。 一刀截斷。洒洒落落。何必更分是分非。辨得 辨失。雖然恁麼。能有幾人。武帝甞披袈裟。自 講放光般若經。感得天花亂墜地變黃金。辨 道奉佛。誥詔天下。起寺度僧。依教修行。人謂 之佛心天子。達磨初見武帝。帝問。朕起寺度 僧。有何功德。磨云。無功德。早是惡水驀頭 澆。若透得這箇無功德話。許爾親見達磨。且 道。起寺度僧。為什麼都無功德。此意在什麼 處。帝與婁約法師傅大士昭明太子。持論真 俗二諦。據教中說。真諦以明非有。俗諦以明 非無。真俗不二。即是聖諦第一義。此是教 家極妙窮玄處。帝便拈此極則處。問達磨。如 何是聖諦第一義。磨云。廓然無聖。天下衲僧 跳不出。達磨與他一刀截斷。如今人多少錯 會。却去弄精魂。瞠眼睛云。廓然無聖。且喜沒 交涉。五祖先師甞說。只這廓然無聖。若人透 得。歸家穩坐。一等是打葛藤。不妨與他打破 漆桶。達磨就中奇特。所以道。參得一句透。千 句萬句一時透。自然坐得斷把得定。古人道。 粉骨碎身未足酬。一句了然超百億。達磨劈 頭與他一拶。多少漏逗了也。帝不省。却以 人我見故。再問對朕者誰。達磨慈悲忒殺。又 向道不識。直得武帝眼目定動不知落處。是 何言說。到這裏有事無事。拈來即不堪。端和 尚有頌云。一箭尋常落一鵰。更加一箭已相 饒。直歸少室峯前坐。梁主休言更去招。復云。 誰欲招。帝不契。遂潛出國。這老漢只得懡㦬。 渡江至魏。時魏孝明帝當位。乃此北人種 族姓拓跋氏。後來方名中國。達磨至彼。亦不 出見。直過少林。面壁九年。接得二祖。彼方號 為壁觀婆羅門。梁武帝後問志公。公云。陛下 還識此人否。帝曰。不識。且道與達磨道底。是 同是別。似則也似。是則不是。人多錯會道。前 來達磨是答他禪。後來武帝是對他志公。乃 相識之識。且得沒交涉。當時志公恁麼問。且 道作麼生祇對。何不一棒打殺。免見搽胡。 武帝却供他欵道不識。志公見機而作。便云。 此是觀音大士。傳佛心印。帝悔遂遣使去取。 好不唧𠺕。當時等他道此是觀音大士傳佛 心印。亦好擯他出國。猶較些子。人傳。志公天 鑒十三年化去。達磨普通元年方來。自隔 七年。何故却道同時相見。此必是謬傳。據 傳中所載。如今不論這事。只要知他大綱。且 道達磨是觀音。志公是觀音。阿那箇是端的 底觀音。既是觀音。為什麼却有兩箇。何止兩 箇。成群作隊。時後魏光統律師。菩提流支三 藏。與師論議。師斥相指心。而褊局之量。自 不堪任。競起害心。數加毒藥。至第六度。化緣 已畢。傳法得人。遂不復救。端居而逝。葬於熊 耳山定林寺。後魏宋雲奉使。於葱嶺遇師手 携隻履而往。武帝追憶。自撰碑文云。嗟夫。見 之不見。逢之不逢。遇之不遇。今之古之。怨 之恨之。復讚云。心有也。曠劫而滯凡夫。心 無也。剎那而登妙覺。且道。達磨即今在什 麼處。蹉過也不知。
text_en: arrived. He transmitted only the mind-seal, opened and revealed the deluded path, established no words and letters, and pointed directly to the human mind: see your nature and become Buddha. If you see it like this, you have a share of freedom and do not follow any language’s turns. Fully embodied and already complete, then later you can face Emperor Wu in dialogue, and also see where the Second Patriarch settled the mind. Naturally you will see it—without calculating emotional dust. Cut it off with a single stroke—clean and unbound. Why divide into right and wrong again, and argue over what is gained or lost? Even so, how many can do it? Emperor Wu once donned the robe himself and personally lectured on the Radiant Prajñā scripture, moving heaven to rain down flowers and making the ground turn to gold. He distinguished the Way and served the Buddha, issued proclamations to the realm, built temples, ordained monks, and practiced according to the teachings. People called him the “Son of Heaven with the Buddha-mind.” When Bodhidharma first met Emperor Wu, the emperor asked, “I have built temples and ordained monks—what merit is there?” Bodhidharma said, “No merit.” Right away it was like foul water poured over his head. If you penetrate this “no merit” word, I’ll allow you to personally meet Bodhidharma. But tell me— building temples and ordaining monks—why is there no merit at all? Where does this meaning lie? The emperor, along with Dharma Master Louyue, Great Master Fu, and Crown Prince Zhaoming, upheld discussions of the true and the conventional two truths. According to the teachings, the ultimate truth clarifies “not being,” and the conventional truth clarifies “not non-being.” Ultimate and conventional are not two—this is the first meaning of the noble truth. This is the teaching school’s most subtle and most profound point. The emperor picked up this utmost principle and asked Bodhidharma, “What is the first meaning of the noble truth?” Bodhidharma said, “Vast and open—no holiness.” All patch-robed monks under heaven cannot jump out of it. Bodhidharma cut him off with one stroke. Nowadays how many people misunderstand it, then go on playing with “spirit and soul,” bulging their eyes and saying, “Vast and open—no holiness.” They’re pleased there’s no involvement. The former master, the Fifth Patriarch, once said: if someone penetrates just this “vast and open—no holiness,” they return home and sit steady. If they are the kind who just tangle up vines, there’s no harm in smashing their lacquer bucket. Bodhidharma was extraordinary in this, so it is said: penetrate one phrase, and a thousand phrases, ten thousand phrases are penetrated all at once. Naturally you can sit through it and hold it firm. The ancients said, “Grinding bones to powder and shattering the body still would not repay it; one clear phrase surpasses a hundred billion.” Bodhidharma split his head open and gave him a squeeze—yet how much still leaked out. The emperor did not awaken, and instead, with views of self and other, asked again, “Who is it that stands before me?” Bodhidharma was compassionate to an extreme, and again said, “I do not know.” It left Emperor Wu’s eyes and mind fixed, moving yet not knowing where to land. What words could speak here? At this point, whether there is something or nothing, if you pick it up it cannot be borne. Master Duan had a verse: “One arrow, as usual, brings down a falcon; add another arrow and you’ve already been too generous. He returns directly to sit before Mount Shaoshi; let the ruler of Liang not speak of inviting him again.” It goes on: “Who would want to invite him?” The emperor did not accord with it, so Bodhidharma quietly left the country. The old fellow could only feel dispirited. He crossed the river to Wei. At that time Emperor Xiaoming of Wei was on the throne, of this northern people’s Tuoba clan; only later was it called “China.” When Bodhidharma arrived there, he also did not go out to meet anyone. He went straight past to Shaolin, faced the wall for nine years, and received the Second Patriarch. There they called him the “Brahman of wall-gazing.” Later, Emperor Wu of Liang asked Zhigong. Zhigong said, “Does Your Majesty recognize this man?” The emperor said, “I do not.” Tell me—what was said to Bodhidharma: was it the same or different? It seems alike, yet it seems not; it is, yet it is not. Many people misunderstand and say: earlier Bodhidharma was answering him with Chan; later Emperor Wu was replying to Zhigong. Thus it is “recognizing” recognition—so it has no involvement. Back then, when Zhigong asked like this, tell me how should one respond? Why not kill him with a single blow, to avoid seeing all this muddling? Emperor Wu instead honestly admitted, “I do not.” Zhigong, seeing the moment, acted and said, “This is the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, transmitting the Buddha’s mind-seal.” The emperor regretted it and then sent envoys to fetch him. How fitting—and how not. If at the time, once he said, “This is the Great Being Avalokiteśvara transmitting the Buddha’s mind-seal,” it would also have been fine to banish him from the country—still a bit better. People say Zhigong, in the thirteenth year of Tianjian, passed away. Bodhidharma only came in the first year of Putong. They are separated by seven years—so why say they met at the same time? This must be a mistaken tradition. According to what is recorded in the tradition, we will not debate this now. We only need to know the main outline. Tell me: Bodhidharma is Avalokiteśvara; Zhigong is Avalokiteśvara—then which one is the true Avalokiteśvara? If it is Avalokiteśvara, why are there two? Not only two— they form groups and squads. Later, in Northern Wei, Vinaya Master Guangtong and Tripiṭaka Bodhiruci debated with the master. The master rebuked them for clinging to characteristics and pointing at mind, and for their narrow, cramped measure. They themselves could not bear it, and competed in raising harmful intent, repeatedly administering poison. By the sixth time, his karmic ties of teaching were complete and he had found a person to transmit the Dharma to, so he no longer tried to save himself. He sat upright and passed away. He was buried at Dinglin Monastery on Bear Ear Mountain. Later, Song Yun of Northern Wei, on an embassy, met the master in the Congling Mountains, carrying a single sandal in his hand as he went. Emperor Wu, recalling him, composed an inscription himself, saying: “Alas! To see and not see; to meet and not meet; to encounter and not encounter—now and ancient alike. I resent it, I hate it.” And he further praised: “When mind exists, through vast kalpas one remains stuck as an ordinary man. When mind does not exist, in an instant one ascends wondrous awakening.” Tell me—where is Bodhidharma right now? You’ve already missed him and don’t even know it.
The noble truth is vast and open—how could one ever discern it? Who is it that stands before me? An arrow flies past Silla. Hm? It has passed. What is hard to discern?

text_zh: 聖諦廓然箭過新羅。咦何當辨的過也。有什麼難辨對朕者 誰再來不直半文錢。又恁麼去也還云不識三个四个中也。咄因茲 暗渡江穿人鼻孔不得。却被別人穿。蒼天蒼天。好不大丈夫豈免生荊 棘脚跟下已深數丈闔國人追不再來兩重公案。用追作麼。在什麼處。 大丈夫志氣何在千古萬古空相憶換手槌胸。望空啟告休相憶 道什麼。向鬼窟裏作活計清風匝地有何極果然。大小雪竇向草裏輥 師顧視左右云。這裏還有祖師麼爾待番欵那。猶作 這去就。自云有塌薩阿勞喚來與老僧洗脚更與三十棒趕出。也未 為分外。作這去就。猶較些子。
text_en: Who again says, “I do not know”? Because of this, Come again and it is not worth half a coin. Off he goes like that again. Among three or four. Bah! he secretly crossed the river—how could thorns and brambles not grow? Unable to pierce others' nostrils, yet pierced by others. Blue heaven, blue heaven! What a sorry excuse for a man. The whole nation pursued him, but he did not return; through a thousand ages, ten thousand ages, they vainly remember—do not remember, do not remember. Beneath the heels it is already several zhang deep. A twofold koan. What use is it to chase after it? Where is it? Where is a great man's resolve? Switching hands, he pounds his chest and makes an announcement to empty space. A clear wind circles the earth—what limit could it have? What is he saying? Doing business in a ghost cave. Sure enough. Big and small, Xuedou rolls into the grass. The master looked around to left and right and said, “Is there still a Patriarch here?” Then he said himself, “There is—call him here to wash this old monk’s feet.” You wait for that fellow, still doing this coming and going, muddled and confused. Give him thirty more blows and drive him out; even that is not excessive. Doing this coming and going, he is still a bit closer.
Now, judging by Xuedou’s verse on this case, it is like someone skilled at dancing with the Tai’a sword.

text_zh: 且據雪竇頌此公案。一似善舞太阿劍相似。 向虛空中盤礴。自然不犯鋒鋩。若是無這般 手段。纔拈著便見傷鋒犯手。若是具眼者。看 他一拈一掇。一褒一貶。只用四句。揩定一則 公案。大凡頌古只是繞路說禪。拈古大綱據 欵結案而已。雪竇與他一拶。劈頭便道。聖 諦廓然。何當辨的。雪竇於他初句下。著這一 句。不妨奇特。且道。畢竟作麼生辨的。直饒鐵 眼銅睛。也摸索不著。到這裏。以情識卜度得 麼。所以雲門道。如擊石火。似閃電光。這箇些 子。不落心機意識情想。等爾開口。堪作什麼。 計較生時。鷂子過新羅。雪竇道。爾天下衲僧。 何當辨的。對朕者誰。著箇還云不識。此是雪 竇忒殺老婆。重重為人處。且道。廓然與不識。 是一般兩般。若是了底人分上。不言而諭。若 是未了底人。決定打作兩橛。諸方尋常皆道。 雪竇重拈一遍。殊不知。四句頌盡公案了。後 為慈悲之故。頌出事跡。因茲暗渡江。豈免生 荊棘。達磨本來茲土。與人解粘去縛。抽釘拔 楔。剗除荊棘。因何却道生荊棘。非止當時。諸 人即今脚跟下。已深數丈。闔國人追不再來。 千古萬古空相憶。可殺不丈夫。且道。達磨在 什麼處。若見達磨。便見雪竇末後為人處。雪 竇恐怕人逐情見。所以撥轉關捩子。出自己 見解云。休相憶。清風匝地有何極。既休相憶。 爾脚跟下事。又作麼生。雪竇道。即今箇裏匝 地清風。天上天下有何所極。雪竇拈千古萬 古之事。拋向面前。非止雪竇當時有何極。爾 諸人分上亦有何極。他又怕人執在這裏。再 著方便高聲云。這裏還有祖師麼。自云有。雪 竇到這裏。不妨為人。赤心片片。又自云。喚來 與老僧洗脚。太殺減人威光。當時也好。與 本分手脚。且道。雪竇意在什麼處。到這裏。喚 作驢則是。喚作馬則是。喚作祖師則是。如何 名邈。往往喚作雪竇使祖師去也。且喜沒交 涉。且道。畢竟作麼生。只許老胡知。不許老胡 會。
text_en: He circles and coils within empty space, naturally not offending blade or edge. If you lack this kind of skill, the moment you pick it up you are hurt by the edge and your hand is cut. If you have eyes to see, watch him lift and set down, praise and blame. Using only four lines, he wipes it clean and pins down a single gong’an. In general, verses on old cases are just Chan spoken by a roundabout route—grasping the main outline of the ancient and settling the case, that’s all. Xuedou gave him a squeeze; right at the start he says: “The noble truth is vast and open—how could one ever discern it?” Under his first line, Xuedou plants this line—no harm calling it extraordinary. But tell me: in the end, how do you discern it? Even if you have iron eyes and copper pupils, you still cannot grope it out. Here, can emotional consciousness be used to divine and measure it? Therefore Yunmen said: like striking sparks from stone, like a flash of lightning. This bit does not fall into mental contrivance, thought, or imagining. If you wait until you open your mouth, what can it accomplish? When calculating thoughts arise, the hawk has already flown past Silla. Xuedou says: you patch-robed monks under heaven— how could you ever discern it? Who stands before me? Add this “still says ‘I do not know’ ”—this is Xuedou being far too grandmotherly, helping people layer upon layer. Tell me: “vast and open” and “I do not know”— are they the same or different? For one who is done, it is understood without speaking. For one who is not done, they will surely split it into two pieces. Everywhere, people ordinarily say: Xuedou re-lifted it once more. They do not realize: the four-line verse already exhausts the whole case. After that, out of compassion, he versified the events: “Because of this he secretly crossed the river—how could thorns and brambles not grow?” Bodhidharma originally came to this land to loosen stickiness and remove bindings for people, to pull nails and extract wedges, to clear away brambles. Why then say “brambles grow”? Not only back then—among you people, right under your heels even now, it is already several fathoms deep. “The whole nation pursued him, but he did not return.” “Through a thousand ages, ten thousand ages, they vainly remember.” How mortifying—no man of resolve! Tell me: where is Bodhidharma right now? If you see Bodhidharma, then you see where Xuedou finally helps people. Xuedou feared people would chase emotional views, so he turned the pivotal hinge and brought out his own understanding, saying: “Do not remember; a clear wind circles the earth—what limit could it have?” Since you should not remember— what about the matter right under your heels—how is it? Xuedou says: right now, here, the earth is encircled by a clear wind—throughout heaven above and earth below, what limit could there be? Xuedou picks up the affairs of a thousand ages, ten thousand ages and tosses them before your face. It was not only that in Xuedou’s time there was no limit—among you people too, what limit is there? And then he feared people would get stuck right here, so again Employing expedient means, he shouted, “Is there still a patriarch here?” He answered himself, “There is.” Xuedou has arrived here, and it’s not amiss to help people. His bare sincerity comes in pieces. And he says again, “Call him here to wash this old monk’s feet.” That cuts down a man’s dignity too much. Yet back then it was fine—treating him with proper hands and feet. Tell me, where is Xuedou’s intent? Right here—call him a donkey and it is; call him a horse and it is; call him a patriarch and it is. How does the name miss the mark? Time and again they call him “Xuedou” and send the patriarch off. Fortunately there’s no entangling involvement. Tell me—after all, how is it? Only the old barbarian is allowed to know; the old barbarian is not allowed to understand.

text_zh: 垂示云。乾坤窄。日月星辰一時黑。直饒棒如 雨點。喝似雷奔。也未當得向上宗乘中事。設 使三世諸佛。只可自知。歷代祖師全提不起。 一大藏教詮注不及。明眼衲僧自救不了。到 這裏。作麼生請益。道箇佛字。拖泥帶水。道箇 禪字。滿面慚惶。久參上士不待言之。後學初 機直須究取。
text_en: raindrops and the shouts like rushing thunder, it still wouldn’t match what belongs to the supreme vehicle. Even the Buddhas of the three times can only know it themselves; the patriarchs of successive generations cannot bring it up at all. The whole Tripitaka and its commentaries do not reach it. Even a clear-eyed patch-robed monk cannot save himself. When you reach here, how do you ask for instruction? Say the word “Buddha” and you drag mud and carry water. Say the word “Zen” and your face fills with shame. Those seasoned adepts need not be mentioned. Beginners and later students must investigate straight through.
[2] Case: Zhaozhou addressed the assembly, saying: “The supreme Way is not difficult; What is this old fellow doing? Do not strike up this tangle of vines. Neither hard nor easy.

text_zh: 【二】舉趙州示眾云這老漢作什麼。莫打這葛藤至道無難非難非易 唯嫌揀擇眼前是什麼。三祖猶在纔有語言。是揀擇是 明白兩頭三面。少賣弄。魚行水濁。鳥飛落毛老僧不在明白裏賊身 已露。這老漢向什麼處去是汝還護惜也無敗也。也有一箇半箇時 有僧問。既不在明白裏。護惜箇什麼也好與一 拶。舌拄上齶州云。我亦不知拶殺這老漢。倒退三千僧云。和尚 既不知。為什麼却道不在明白裏看走向什麼處去。逐教 上樹去州云。問事即得。禮拜了退賴有這一着。這老賊。
text_en: it only dislikes choosing and rejecting. As soon as there are words, that is choosing and rejecting; that is What is right before your eyes? The Third Patriarch is still here. clarity. This old monk is not within clarity—do you still cherish it or not?” At that time Two ends, three faces; show off less. When fish move, the water turns muddy; when birds fly, feathers fall. The thief's body is already exposed. Where is this old fellow going? Ruined. Still, there is one or half of one. a monk asked, “Since you are not within clarity, what is there to cherish?” Zhaozhou said, “I don’t know either.” The monk said, “Master, Fine, give him one squeeze; the tongue presses against the palate. Squeeze this old fellow to death; retreat three thousand. since you don’t know, why then did you say you are not within clarity?” Zhaozhou said, “Ask and you’ll get it.” The monk bowed and withdrew. Watch where he runs off to. Chase him and make him climb a tree. Thanks to this one move. This old bandit

text_zh: 趙州和尚。尋常舉此話頭。只是唯嫌揀擇。此 是三祖信心銘云。至道無難。唯嫌揀擇。但莫 憎愛。洞然明白。纔有是非。是揀擇。是明白。 纔恁麼會。蹉過了也。鉸釘膠粘。堪作何用。州 云。是揀擇。是明白。如今參禪問道。不在揀擇 中。便坐在明白裏。老僧不在明白裏。汝等還 護惜也無。汝諸人既不在明白裏。且道。趙 州在什麼處。為什麼却教人護惜。五祖先師 當說道。垂手來似過爾。爾作麼生會。且道。作 麼生是垂手處。識取鉤頭意。莫認定盤星。這 僧出來。也不妨奇特。捉趙州空處。便去拶他。 既不在明白裏。護惜箇什麼。趙州更不行棒 行喝。只道。我亦不知。若不是這老漢。被他拶 著。往往忘前失後。賴是這老漢。有轉身自在 處。所以如此答他。如今禪和子。問著也道。我 亦不知不會。爭奈同途不同轍。這僧有奇特 處。方始會問。和尚既不知。為什麼却道不在 明白裏。更好一拶。若是別人。往往分疏不下。 趙州是作家。只向他道。問事即得。禮拜了退。 這僧依舊無奈這老漢何。只得飲氣吞聲。此 是大手宗師。不與爾論玄論妙。論機論境。一 向以本分事接人。所以道。相罵饒爾接嘴。相 唾饒爾潑水。殊不知。這老漢。平生不以棒喝 接人。只以平常言語。只是天下人不奈何。蓋 為他平生無許多計較。所以橫拈倒用。逆行 順行。得大自在。如今人不理會得。只管道。趙 州不答話。不為人說。殊不知。當面蹉過。
text_en: comes from the Third Patriarch’s Inscription on Faith in Mind: “The supreme Way is not difficult; it only dislikes choosing and rejecting. Only do not hate or love, and it will be clear of itself. As soon as there is right and wrong, that is choosing and rejecting; that is clarity.” If you understand it like that, you’ve already missed it. Cutting and nailing, gluing and sticking—what use is that? Zhaozhou said: “That is choosing and rejecting; that is clarity.” Nowadays, those who investigate Zen and inquire into the Way—if they are not in choosing and rejecting, they sit in clarity. “This old monk is not within clarity—do you all still cherish it or not?” Since you people are not within clarity, tell me—where is Zhaozhou? Why then does he tell people to cherish? The former master, the Fifth Patriarch, once said: “With hands hanging down, he comes as if passing by you.” How do you understand that? Tell me—what is the place of hands hanging down? Recognize the intent at the hook’s tip—do not take the fixed North Star for it. This monk stepped forward—he was indeed something special. He grabbed Zhaozhou at the empty spot and pressed him hard. “Since you are not within clarity, what is there to cherish?” Zhaozhou still did not use the staff or the shout—he only said, “I don’t know either.” If it weren’t for this old fellow, being pressed like that would often make one forget what came before and lose what comes after. Luckily this old fellow has a free turning place, so he answered him like this. Nowadays, Zen followers—when questioned they also say, “I don’t know, I don’t understand.” But what can be done? Same road, different tracks. This monk had a special point—only then could he ask: “Master, since you don’t know, why then did you say you are not within clarity?” An even better pressing. If it were someone else, they’d often be unable to explain it away. Zhaozhou was a genuine hand—he simply told him, “Ask and you’ll get it.” The monk bowed and withdrew. This monk still could do nothing to this old fellow; he could only swallow his anger and hold his tongue. This is a great master of the school—he won’t debate mystery or subtlety with you, won’t debate “occasion” or “state.” He only meets people with the matter at hand. Hence the saying: if you curse at him, he’ll let you have the last word; if you spit, he’ll let you splash water. People don’t realize it: this old fellow, all his life, did not meet people with staff and shout— only with ordinary speech. And yet no one under heaven can do anything with him. Because all his life he had none of those calculations. Therefore he can pick up and use things sideways and upside down, go against the current or with it, and attain great freedom. People today don’t grasp it; they only keep saying, “Zhaozhou doesn’t answer; he doesn’t explain for people,” not realizing they miss it right in front of their faces.

The supreme Way is not difficult—at the edge of words, at the edge of phrases. One has many kinds; two has no twofold. At the horizon the sun rises, the moon sets; before the railing the mountains are deep, the water cold. When the skull’s knowing has a triple koan. His mouth full of frost, what is he saying? When fish move, the water turns muddy. Split into seven pieces and eight fragments.

text_zh: 至道無難三重公案。滿口含霜。道什麼言端語端魚行水濁。七花八裂。 搽胡也一有多種分開好。只一般。有什麼了期二無兩般何堪。 四五六七。打葛藤作什麼天際日上月下覿面相呈。頭上漫漫。脚下漫漫。切 忌昂頭低頭檻前山深水寒一死更不再活。還覺寒毛卓竪麼髑髏識 盡喜何立棺木裏瞠眼。盧行者是它同參枯木龍吟銷未乾 咄。枯木再生花。達磨遊東土難難邪法難扶。倒一說。這裏是什麼所在。說難說易揀 擇明白君自看瞎。將謂由別人。賴值自看。不干山僧事。
text_en: Smearing it up. Better to separate it. It is just the same; what end is there? How can it bear it? Four, five, six, seven. Why strike up entangling vines? Present it face to face. Boundless above the head, boundless beneath the feet. Absolutely avoid raising the head or lowering the head. Once dead, never alive again. Do you still feel your hairs bristle? is exhausted, what joy could stand? A dragon’s cry in a withered tree—the thaw has not yet dried. Staring with eyes wide open inside the coffin. The layman Lu is his fellow participant. Hard, hard— Bah! A withered tree blooms again. Bodhidharma roams the eastern land. Deviant Dharma is hard to support. Turn it upside down and speak: what place is this? Say hard, say easy. choosing and rejecting, clarity—sir, you see for yourself. Blind! You would think it was because of others; luckily you can see for yourself. It has nothing to do with this mountain monk.
Xuedou knew where it landed, so he composed the verse like this. “The supreme Way is not difficult,” and then he followed it with

text_zh: 雪竇知他落處。所以如此頌。至道無難。便隨 後道。言端語端。舉一隅不以三隅反。雪竇道。 一有多種。二無兩般。似三隅反一。爾且道。什 麼處是言端語端處。為什麼一却有多種。二 却無兩般。若不具眼。向什麼處摸索。若透 得這兩句。所以古人道。打成一片。依舊見。山 是山。水是水。長是長。短是短。天是天。地是 地。有時喚天作地。有時喚地作天。有時喚山 不是山。喚水不是水。畢竟怎生得平穩去。風 來樹動。浪起船高。春生夏長。秋收冬藏。一種 平懷。泯然自盡。則此四句頌頓絕了也。雪 竇有餘才。所以分開結裹算來也。只是頭上 安頭道。至道無難。言端語端。一有多種。二無 兩般。雖無許多事。天際日上時月便下。檻前 山深時水便寒。到這裏。言也端。語也端。頭頭 是道。物物全真。豈不是心境俱忘。打成一片 處。雪竇頭上太孤峻生。末後也漏逗不少。若 參得透見得徹。自然如醍醐上味相似。若是 情解未忘。便見七花八裂。決定不能會如此 說話。髑髏識盡喜何立。枯木龍吟銷未乾。只 這便是交加處。這僧恁麼問。趙州恁麼答。州 云。至道無難。唯嫌揀擇。纔有語言。是揀擇是 明白。老僧不在明白裏。是汝還護惜也無。時 有僧便問。既不在明白裏。又護惜箇什麼。州 云。我亦不知。僧云。和尚既不知。為什麼却道 不在明白裏。州云。問事即得。禮拜了退。此是 古人問道底公案。雪竇拽來一串穿却。用頌 至道無難。唯嫌揀擇。如今人不會古人意。只 管咬言嚼句。有甚了期。若是通方作者。始能 辨得這般說話。不見僧問香嚴。如何是道。嚴 云。枯木裏龍吟。僧云。如何是道中人。嚴云。 髑髏裏眼睛。僧後問石霜。如何是枯木裏龍 吟。霜云。猶帶喜在。如何是髑髏裏眼睛。霜 云。猶帶識在。僧又問曹山。如何是枯木裏龍 吟。山云。血脈不斷。如何是髑髏裏眼睛。山云 乾不盡。什麼人得聞。山云。盡大地未有一箇 不聞。僧云未審龍吟是何章句。山云。不知是 何章句。聞者皆喪。復有頌云。枯木龍吟真見 道。髑髏無識眼初明。喜識盡時消息盡。當人 那辨濁中清。雪竇可謂大有手脚。一時與爾 交加頌出。然雖如是。都無兩般。雪竇末後有 為人處。更道難難。只這難難。也須透過始得。 何故。百丈道一切語言。山河大地。一一轉歸 自己。雪竇凡是一拈一掇。到末後須歸自己。 且道。什麼處是雪竇為人處。揀擇明白君自 看。既是打葛藤頌了。因何却道。君自看。好彩 教爾自看。且道。意落在什麼處。莫道諸人 理會不得。設使山僧到這裏。也只是理會不 得。
text_en: “at the edge of words, at the edge of phrases.” Raise one corner and you don’t use the other three to turn it back. Xuedou said, “One has many kinds; two has no twofold.” It’s like the three corners turning back the one. Tell me—what place is the edge of words and the edge of phrases? Why does “one” have many kinds, and “two” have no twofold? If you don’t have eyes, where will you grope? If you penetrate these two lines, then as the ancients said, you beat it into one piece—yet you still see: mountains are mountains, water is water; long is long, short is short; heaven is heaven, earth is earth. Sometimes you call heaven “earth”; sometimes you call earth “heaven.” Sometimes you call mountains “not mountains,” call water “not water.” In the end, how do you go on steadily? Wind comes and trees move; waves rise and boats lift. Spring is born, summer grows; autumn harvests, winter stores. One kind of level heart—vanishing and ending of itself—and these four lines of the verse are cut off at once. Xuedou had surplus talent, so he split it apart and wrapped it up, calculating it out. But this is just putting a head on top of a head, saying: “The supreme Way is not difficult. At the edge of words, at the edge of phrases. One has many kinds. Two has no twofold.” Though there aren’t that many matters, when the sun rises at the horizon, the moon then sets; before the railing, when the mountains are deep, the water is cold. When you reach here, words are at the edge, phrases are at the edge; every head is the Way; each thing is wholly real. Isn’t this forgetting both mind and objects, beaten into one piece in that place? Xuedou’s head is too solitary and steep; in the end he also lets out quite a lot. If you investigate through and see through, it naturally resembles the finest taste of ghee. If emotional interpretation has not been forgotten, you will see it split into seven pieces and eight fragments; you certainly cannot understand talk like this. “When the skull’s knowing is exhausted, what joy could stand? A dragon’s cry in a withered tree—the thaw has not yet dried.” This is exactly the crossing point. The monk asked like this; Zhaozhou answered like this. Zhaozhou said: “The supreme Way is not difficult; it only dislikes choosing and rejecting. As soon as there are words, that is choosing and rejecting; that is clarity. This old monk is not within clarity—do you still cherish it or not?” At that time a monk then asked: “Since you are not within clarity, what is there to cherish?” Zhaozhou said: “I don’t know either.” The monk said: “Master, since you don’t know, why then did you say you are not within clarity?” Zhaozhou said: “Ask and you’ll get it.” The monk bowed and withdrew. This is an old case of questioning the Way. Xuedou dragged it over and strung it together, using a verse for “The supreme Way is not difficult; it only dislikes choosing and rejecting.” People today don’t understand the ancients’ intent; they only keep biting words and chewing phrases—when will that ever end? Only a master with thorough understanding can discern speech like this. Haven’t you seen a monk ask Xiangyan, “What is the Way?” Xiangyan said, “A dragon’s cry in a withered tree.” The monk said, “What is a person in the Way?” Xiangyan said, “Eyes in a skull.” Later the monk asked Shishuang, “What is a dragon’s cry in a withered tree?” Shishuang said, “It still carries joy.” “What are eyes in a skull?” Shishuang said, “It still carries knowing.” The monk then asked Caoshan, “What is a dragon’s cry in a withered tree?” Caoshan said, “The bloodline is unbroken.” “What are eyes in a skull?” Caoshan said, “It does not dry out.” “Who can hear it?” Caoshan said, “Across the whole earth there is not a single person who does not hear it.” The monk said, “I wonder what lines the dragon’s cry is.” Caoshan said, “I do not know what lines they are; those who hear it all perish.” There is also a verse: “A dragon’s cry in a withered tree truly sees the Way; in a skull without knowing, the eyes first brighten. When joy and knowing are exhausted, the news is exhausted; how can a person discern the clear within the turbid?” Xuedou could be said to have great skill—at once he brought it together and versified it for you. Yet even so, there are no two kinds at all. At the end Xuedou has a place where he helps people, saying again, “Hard, hard.” Just this “hard, hard”—you must pass through it to get it. Why? Baizhang said: all language, mountains and rivers and the great earth—each and every one turns back to oneself. Whenever Xuedou picks up and puts down, in the end it must return to oneself. Tell me, where is Xuedou’s place of helping people? “Choosing and rejecting, clarity—sir, you see for yourself.” Since he already spun out a vine-tangle verse, why then does he say, “You see for yourself”? Fine luck— he lets you see for yourself. Tell me, where does the intent land? Don’t say you people can’t understand it. Even if this mountain monk came to this point, I too would only be unable to understand it— unable to understand it.
3 In his instruction he said: one pivot, one circumstance; one word, one phrase—just to sketch an entry point.

text_zh: 垂示云。一機一境。一言一句。且圖有箇入處。 好肉上剜瘡。成窠成窟。大用現前不存軌則。 且圖知有向上事。蓋天蓋地又摸索不著。恁 麼也得。不恁麼也得。太廉纖生。恁麼也不得。 不恁麼也不得。太孤危生。不涉二塗。如何即 是。請試舉看。
text_en: Carving a wound into good flesh—making nests and pits. When great function appears before you, it keeps no fixed rules. Just try to know there is the matter beyond; it covers heaven and covers earth, yet you cannot grope it out. So, thus is fine; not thus is fine too—too fussy. Thus is not fine either. Not thus is not fine either—too lone and perilous. It does not fall into two roads—so what is it, then? Please try to raise an example and see.
Case 3: When Master Ma was unwell, the head of the monastery asked, This fellow leaks and hints a lot, dragging others along with him.

text_zh: 【三】舉馬大師不安這漢漏逗不少。帶累別人去也院主問。和 尚近日。尊候如何四百四病一時發。三日後不送亡僧。是好手。仁義道中 大師云。日面佛月面佛可殺新鮮。養子之緣。
text_en: “Master, how has your honored condition been lately?” The four hundred and four illnesses erupt at once. Not escorting the dead monk after three days is skillful. In the way of benevolence and righteousness, The great master said, “Sun-Face Buddha, Moon-Face Buddha.” how fresh and deadly! The karma of raising children
Master Ma was unwell. The head of the monastery asked, “Master, how has your honored condition been lately?” The great

text_zh: 馬大師不安。院主問。和尚近日尊候如何。大 師云日面佛月面佛。祖師若不以本分事相 見。如何得此道光輝。此箇公案。若知落處便 獨步丹霄。若不知落處。往往枯木巖前差路 去在。若是本分人到這裏。須是有驅耕夫之 牛。奪飢人之食底手脚。方見馬大師為人處。 如今多有人道。馬大師接院主。且喜沒交涉。 如今眾中多錯會瞠眼云。在這裏。左眼是日 面。右眼是月面。有什麼交涉。驢年未夢見在。 只管蹉過古人事。只如馬大師如此道。意在 什麼處。有底云。點平胃散一盞來。有什麼巴 鼻。到這裏。作麼生得平穩去。所以道。向上一 路千聖不傳。學者勞形如猿捉影。只這日面 佛月面佛。極是難見。雪竇到此。亦是難頌。却 為他見得透。用盡平生工夫。指注他。諸人要 見雪竇麼。看取下文。
text_en: master said, “Sun-Face Buddha, Moon-Face Buddha.” If the patriarchs did not meet by way of the essential matter, how could this Way shine with such radiance? In this public case, if you know where it lands, then you stride alone in the cinnabar sky. If you do not know where it lands, you often take a wrong road right in front of Deadwood Cliff. If you are an essential person and reach here, you must have hands and feet that can drive off a plowman’s ox and snatch away a hungry man’s food—only then do you see what kind of person Master Ma was. Nowadays many say, “Master Ma was responding to the head of the monastery.” Luckily, that has nothing to do with it. Many in the assembly misunderstand, glaring and saying, “It’s right here—his left eye is Sun-Face, his right eye is Moon-Face—what’s the big deal?” They haven’t even dreamed of it in the year of the donkey. They just keep missing what the ancients were doing. Tell me, when Master Ma spoke like this, where was his intent? Some say, “Bring a cup of Pingwei Powdered Decoction.” What’s the use of that? When you get here, how will you go on steadily? Therefore it is said: the road beyond is not transmitted by a thousand sages. Students wear themselves out like apes grabbing at shadows. This “Sun-Face Buddha, Moon-Face Buddha” is extremely hard to see. Even Xuedou, coming to this, found it hard to versify—yet because he saw through it, he used the work of his whole life to point directly at it. Do you all want to see Xuedou? Look at what follows.
Sun-Face Buddha, Moon-Face Buddha—what are the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns? Open your mouth and you see your guts. Like two mirrors facing each other, there is no image in between.

text_zh: 日面佛月面佛開口見膽。如兩面鏡相照於中無影像五帝三皇 是何物太高生。莫謾他好。可貴可賤二十年來曾苦辛自是爾落 草。不干山僧事。啞子喫苦瓜為君幾下蒼龍窟何消恁麼。莫錯用心 好。也莫道無奇特屈愁殺人。愁人莫向愁人說堪述向阿誰說。說與愁人愁殺人明 眼衲僧莫輕忽更須子細。咄。倒退三千。
text_en: What are they, really? For twenty years I endured bitter hardship; for your sake, how many times I went down into the azure dragon’s cave—humbling, yet worth telling. Too lofty. Do not casually praise it. It can be precious, it can be cheap. It is you yourself who fall into the weeds. It has nothing to do with this mountain monk. A mute eats bitter gourd. Why bother like that? Do not misapply the mind. Fine. And do not say there is nothing extraordinary. Sorrow kills people. A sorrowful person should not speak to a sorrowful person. To whom will you speak? Speak to a sorrowful person and sorrow kills people. Clear-eyed patchrobed monks, do not take it lightly. You must be even more careful. Bah! Retreat three thousand.
When Shenzong was on the throne, he claimed this verse mocked the state, so he would not allow it to be entered into the canon.

text_zh: 神宗在位時。自謂此頌諷國。所以不肯入藏。 雪竇先拈云。日面佛月面佛。一拈了。却云。五 帝三皇是何物。且道。他意作麼生。適來已說 了也。直下注他。所以道。垂鉤四海。只釣獰 龍。只此一句已了。後面雪竇自頌他平生所 以用心參尋。二十年來曾苦辛。為君幾下蒼 龍窟。似箇什麼。一似人入蒼龍窟裏取珠相 似。後來打破漆桶。將謂多少奇特。元來只消 得箇五帝三皇是何物。且道雪竇語。落在什 麼處。須是自家退步看。方始見得他落處。豈 不見。興陽剖侍者。答遠錄公問。娑竭出海 乾坤震。覿面相呈事若何。剖云。金翅鳥王 當宇宙。箇中誰是出頭人。遠云。忽遇出頭。又 作麼生。剖云。似鶻捉鳩。君不信。髑髏前驗始 知真。遠云。恁麼則屈節當胸退身三步。剖云。 須彌座下烏龜子。莫待重遭點額回。所以 三皇五帝亦是何物。人多不見雪竇意。只管 道諷國。若恁麼會。只是情見。此乃禪月題公 子行云。錦衣鮮華手擎鶻。閑行氣貌多輕忽。 稼穡艱難總不知。五帝三皇是何物。雪竇道。 屈堪述。明眼衲僧莫輕忽。多少人向蒼龍窟 裏。作活計。直饒是頂門具眼。肘後有符。明眼 衲僧。照破四天下。到這裏。也莫輕忽。須是子 細始得。
text_en: Xuedou first picked it up, saying, “Sun-Face Buddha, Moon-Face Buddha.” Once he had picked it up, he then said, “The Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns—what are they?” Tell me, what was his intent? Just now it has already been said outright—he went straight in on him. Therefore it is said: he casts a hook across the four seas, fishing only for fierce dragons. With just this one line, it is finished. After that, Xuedou himself versified what he had devoted his whole life to investigating: “For twenty years I endured bitter hardship; for your sake, how many times I went down into the azure dragon’s cave.” What is that like? It is like someone entering the azure dragon’s cave to fetch a pearl— just so. Later he smashed the lacquer bucket, thinking it was something extraordinary; yet in the end it only took “What are the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns?” Tell me—where do Xuedou’s words land? You must step back and look for yourself; only then do you begin to see where they land. Don’t you see: Attendant Pou of Xingyang answered Elder Yuanlu’s question: “When Sagara comes out of the sea, heaven and earth quake. Face-to-face, what is the matter presented?” Pou said, “The Golden-Winged Bird King rules the universe. In this, who is the one who comes out on top?” Yuan said, “If you suddenly meet someone who comes out on top, then what then?” Pou said, “Like a falcon seizing a dove. If you don’t believe it, test it in front of a skull—only then will you know it’s true.” Yuan said, “In that case, bend your pride to your chest and step back three paces.” Pou said, “You little turtle under Mount Sumeru’s seat—don’t wait until you get your forehead tapped again and sent back.” Therefore, “The Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors—what are they?” Many people do not see Xuedou’s meaning and just keep saying it mocked the state. If you understand it like that, it is only emotional opinion. This is what Chan-yue wrote in his verse on Gongzi Xing: “In bright brocade he holds a hawk in hand; strolling at ease, his air makes many treat him lightly. He never knows the hardship of farming—what are the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns?” Xuedou said, “Humbled, yet worth telling. Clear-eyed patchrobed monks, do not take it lightly.” How many people, down in the azure dragon’s cave, make their living there. Even if you have eyes on the crown of your head and a talisman behind your elbow—clear-eyed patchrobed monks who illuminate the four worlds—when you get here, do not take it lightly. You must be meticulous—only then will it do.

text_zh: 夾山下三箇點字。諸人還會麼。有時將一莖 草。作丈六金身用。有時將丈六金身。作一莖 草用。德山本是講僧。在西蜀講金剛經。因教 中道。金剛喻定。後得智中。千劫學佛威儀。萬 劫學佛細行。然後成佛。他南方魔子。便說即 心是佛。遂發憤。擔疏鈔行脚。直往南方。破這 魔子輩。看他恁麼發憤。也是箇猛利底漢。初 到澧州。路上見一婆子賣油糍。遂放下疏鈔。 且買點心喫。婆云。所載者是什麼。德山云。金 剛經疏鈔。婆云。我有一問。爾若答得。布施 油糍作點心。若答不得。別處買去。德山云。但 問。婆云。金剛經云。過去心不可得。現在心不 可得。未來心不可得。上座欲點那箇心。山無 語。婆遂指令去參龍潭。纔跨門便問。久嚮龍 潭。及乎到來。潭又不見。龍又不現。龍潭和 尚。於屏風後。引身云。子親到龍潭。師乃設禮 而退。至夜間入室。侍立更深潭云。何不下去。 山遂珍重。揭簾而出。見外面黑却回云。門外 黑。潭遂點紙燭度與山。山方接潭便吹滅。山 豁然大悟。便禮拜。潭云。子見箇什麼便禮拜。 山云。某甲自今後。更不疑著天下老和尚舌 頭。至來日。潭上堂云。可中有箇漢。牙如劍 樹。口似血盆。一棒打不回頭。他時異日。向孤 峯頂上。立吾道去在。山遂取疏鈔。於法堂 前。將火炬舉起云。窮諸玄辯。若一毫置於太 虛。竭世樞機。似一滴投於巨壑。遂燒之。後聞 溈山盛化。直造溈山。便作家相見。包亦不解。 直上法堂。從東過西。從西過東。顧視云無無。 便出。且道。意作麼生。莫是顛麼。人多錯會。 用作建立。直是無交涉。看他恁麼。不妨奇特。 所以道。出群須是英靈漢。敵勝還他師子兒。 選佛若無如是眼。假饒千載又奚為。到這裏 須是通方作者。方始見得。何故。佛法無許多 事。那裏著得情見來。是他心機那裏有如許 多阿勞。所以玄沙道。直似秋潭月影。靜夜鐘 聲。隨扣擊以無虧。觸波瀾而不散。猶是生死 岸頭事。到這裏亦無得失是非。亦無奇特玄 妙。既無奇特玄妙。作麼生會他從東過西。從 西過東。且道。意作麼生。溈山老漢。也不管 他。若不是溈山。也被他折挫一上。看他溈山 老作家相見。只管坐觀成敗。若不深辯來風。 爭能如此。雪竇著語云。勘破了也。一似鐵橛 相似。眾中謂之著語。雖然在兩邊却不住在 兩邊。作麼生會他道勘破了也。什麼處是勘 破處。且道勘破德山。勘破溈山。德山遂出 到門首。却要拔本。自云。也不得草草。要與溈 山掀出五臟心肝法戰一場。再具威儀却回 相見。溈山坐次。德山提起坐具云。和尚溈山 擬取拂子。德山便喝。拂袖而出。可殺奇特。眾 中多道。溈山怕他有甚交涉。溈山亦不忙。所 以道。智過於禽獲得禽。智過於獸獲得獸。智 過於人獲得人。參得這般禪。盡大地森羅萬 象。天堂地獄。草芥人畜。一時作一喝來。他亦 不管掀倒禪床。喝散大眾。他亦不顧。如天之 高。似地之厚。溈山若無坐斷天下人舌頭。底 手脚。時驗他也大難。若不是他一千五百人 善知識。到這裏也分疎不下。溈山是運籌帷 幄。決勝千里。德山背却法堂。著草鞋便出去。 且道他意作麼生。爾道德山是勝是負。溈山 恁麼是勝是負。雪竇著語云。勘破了也。是他 下工夫。見透古人聱訛極則處。方能恁麼。不 妨奇特。訥堂云。雪竇著兩箇勘破。作三段判。 方顯此公案。似傍人斷二人相似。後來這老 漢。緩緩地至晚方問首座。適來新到在什麼 處。首座云。當時背却法堂。著草鞋出去也。溈 山云。此子已後向孤峯頂上。盤結草庵呵佛 罵祖去在。且道他意旨如何。溈山老漢不是 好心。德山後來呵佛罵祖。打風打雨。依舊不 出他窠窟。被這老漢見透平生伎倆。到這裏 喚作溈山與他受記得麼。喚作澤廣藏山。理 能伏豹得麼。若恁麼且喜沒交涉。雪竇知此 公案落處。敢與他斷更道。雪上加霜又重拈 起來教人見。若見得去。許爾與溈山德山雪 竇同參。若也不見。切忌妄生情解。
text_en: of grass and use it as a sixteen-foot golden body. Sometimes you take a sixteen-foot golden body and use it as a single blade of grass. Deshan was originally a lecturer-monk, lecturing on the Diamond Sutra in Western Shu. Because in the teachings it says the diamond is a metaphor for samadhi, and later, in the wisdom teachings, it says: for a thousand kalpas you learn the Buddha’s deportment; for ten thousand kalpas you learn the Buddha’s fine conduct; only then do you become Buddha. Those southern demon fellows then said, “Mind itself is Buddha.” So he roused himself in anger, shouldered his commentaries and traveled on foot straight to the south to smash those demon types. Seeing him so incensed, he truly was a fierce fellow. When he first arrived in Lizhou, on the road he saw an old woman selling fried cakes. He set down his commentaries, and bought a snack to eat. The woman said, “What are you carrying?” Deshan said, “Diamond Sutra commentaries.” The woman said, “I have a question. If you can answer it, I will give you these fried cakes as a gift for your snack. If you can’t answer, buy elsewhere.” Deshan said, “Just ask.” The woman said, “The Diamond Sutra says: the past mind cannot be obtained; the present mind cannot be obtained; the future mind cannot be obtained. Senior monk, which mind do you want to ‘refresh’?” Deshan had nothing to say. The woman then pointed him to go see Longtan. As soon as he crossed the threshold he asked, “I have long admired Long tan, but now that I have arrived, the pool is not in sight and the dragon does not appear.” The master Longtan, from behind a screen, leaned out and said, “You have personally arrived at Longtan.” Deshan then bowed in respect and withdrew. At night he entered the room and stood waiting deep into the night. Longtan said, “Why don’t you go down?” Deshan said his farewells and lifted the curtain to go out. Seeing it was dark outside, he turned back and said, “Outside the door it’s dark.” Longtan then lit a paper candle and handed it to him. Just as Deshan received it, Longtan blew it out. Deshan suddenly awakened and bowed. Longtan said, “What did you see that you bow like this?” Deshan said, “From now on, I will no longer doubt the tongues of the old masters under heaven.” The next day Longtan ascended the hall and said, “In here there is a fellow whose teeth are like sword trees and whose mouth is like a basin of blood. Strike him with a staff and he won’t turn his head. One day, another day, he will go to a solitary peak top and establish my Way.” Deshan then took his commentaries and, in front of the Dharma hall, raised a torch and said, “Exhaust all subtle debate—like placing a single hair in vast emptiness. Drain the world’s pivotal mechanisms—like casting a drop into a great ravine.” Then he burned them. Later he heard that Weishan’s teaching was flourishing, so he went straight to Weishan and met him like a true adept. Bao did not understand it either. He went straight up into the Dharma hall, crossed from east to west, then from west to east, looked around and said, “No, no.” Then he left. Tell me—what was his intent? Was he mad? Many people misunderstand, using it to prop things up—yet it truly has nothing to do with that. Look at him like this; it is not without its strangeness. Therefore it is said: to stand out from the crowd you must be a heroic, numinous person; to beat a rival, you need a lion’s cub. If in selecting Buddhas you lack such eyes, then even after a thousand years what good would it be? When you reach here, you must be a master of all directions before you can begin to see it. Why? The Buddha Dharma isn’t that complicated. A matter like this leaves no room for sentimental opinions. Where in his mind could there be so much fuss? Therefore Master Xuansha said: it is just like the moon’s reflection in an autumn pool, like a bell sounding in a quiet night—struck without ever being diminished, met by waves and ripples without being scattered. Still, this is a matter on the shore of birth and death. When you get here, there is no gain or loss, no right or wrong, and no strange, mysterious marvel. Since there is nothing strange or mysterious, how will you understand him going from east to west, from west to east? Tell me—what is the point? Old man Guishan doesn’t bother with him at all. If it weren’t Guishan, he would have been roughed up once. Look at Guishan that seasoned old hand meeting him—he just sits and watches success and failure. If he didn’t discern the incoming wind deeply, how could it be like this? Xuedou added a remark: “He has seen through it.” It is like an iron stake all the same. The assembly calls this an appended remark. Though it stands on both sides, it does not abide on either side. How do you understand his saying “He has seen through it”? Where is the place that is seen through? And tell me—seen through Deshan, seen through Guishan. Deshan then went out to the gate, wanting to pull it up by the roots. He said to himself, “I mustn’t be careless. I want to have a Dharma battle with Guishan, lay bare his innards—then, after composing myself with proper demeanor, I’ll go back to meet him again.” Guishan was seated. Deshan lifted up his sitting mat and said, “Master Guishan—” Guishan reached to take up his whisk; Deshan gave a shout, flicked his sleeves, and walked out. How astonishing! In the assembly many say, “Guishan was afraid of him—what does that have to do with it?” Guishan wasn’t flustered either. So it is said: If your wisdom surpasses birds, you catch birds; if it surpasses beasts, you catch beasts; if your wisdom surpasses people, you catch people. If you investigate this kind of Chan, then across the whole earth, all the myriad forms and phenomena—heaven and hell, weeds and people and animals—if they all at once give a single shout, he still doesn’t bother. If they overturn the meditation bench, if they shout and scatter the great assembly, he still doesn’t care. Like the height of heaven, like the thickness of earth. If Guishan did not have the means to sit and cut off the tongues of everyone under heaven, it would be very hard to test him. If it weren’t for his fifteen hundred people, good friends of the Way, even here it would still be hard to sort out. Guishan is one who plans within the tent, deciding victory a thousand miles away. Deshan turned his back on the Dharma hall, put on his straw sandals, and went out. Tell me—what was his intent? Do you say Deshan won or lost? Guishan, in this way—was it winning or losing? Xuedou’s appended remark says: “He has seen through it.” This is because he applied effort and saw through the ancients’ most knotty, contentious point—only then can it be like this. It certainly is not hindered from being astonishing. Netang said: Xuedou wrote two “seen through” remarks, making a three-part judgment. Only then does this gong’an become clear—like a bystander judging between two people. Later this old fellow, slowly, not until evening, asked the head monk, “Where is the newcomer from earlier now?” The head monk said, “At the time he turned his back on the Dharma hall and went out in straw sandals.” Gui- shan said, “In the future this fellow will go to the top of a solitary peak, build a grass hut, and scold the Buddha and curse the patriarchs.” Tell me—what is his meaning? Old Guishan is not kindhearted. Later Deshan indeed scolded the Buddha and cursed the patriarchs, storming and raging, yet still he did not leave his own nest. This old fellow saw through all his life’s tricks. At this point, do you call it Guishan giving him a prediction? Do you call it “a marsh broad, a storehouse of mountains”? Can principle subdue a leopard? If it is like that, then happily it has nothing to do with it. Xuedou knew where this gong’an lands, and dared to make a verdict; he further said, “Adding frost on top of snow,” and again picked it up to show people. If you can see it, I permit you to join Guishan, Deshan, and Xue- dou in the same investigation. If you do not see it, strictly avoid giving rise to reckless sentimental interpretations.
One seen through, two seen through—adding frost on snow, he once nearly fell into danger. The words are still in the ear. Pass the double koan.
