text_zh: 【二六】舉。僧問百丈。如何是奇特事言中有響。句裏呈機。驚殺 人。有眼不曾見丈云。獨坐大雄峯凜凜威風四百州。坐者立者二俱敗缺 僧禮拜伶俐衲僧。也有恁麼人。要見恁麼事丈便打作家宗師。何故來言不豊。 令不虛行。
text_en: people. Having eyes, yet never seeing. A grim, bristling might across four hundred prefectures; sitting and standing alike are both defeated and flawed. The monk bowed; Baizhang immediately struck him. Quick-witted patch-robed monks—there are such people, too—who want to see such a matter. A true master of masters—why do his words not come in plenty? The command does not go forth in vain.
Having eyes in a critical moment, not caring about danger or death—therefore it is said: If you don’t enter the tiger’s den, how will you get

text_zh: 臨機具眼。不顧危亡。所以道。不入虎穴。爭得 虎子。百丈尋常如虎插翅相似。這僧也不避 死生。敢捋虎鬚便問。如何是奇特事。這僧也 具眼。百丈便與他擔荷云。獨坐大雄峯。其僧 便禮拜。衲僧家須是別未問已前意始得。這 僧禮拜。與尋常不同。也須是具眼始得。莫 教平生心膽向人傾。相識還如不相識。只這 僧問。如何是奇特事。百丈云。獨坐大雄峯。僧 禮拜。丈便打。看他放去則一時俱是。收來則 掃蹤滅跡。且道他便禮拜意旨如何。若道是 好。因甚百丈便打他作什麼。若道是不好。他 禮拜有什麼不得處。到這裏須是識休咎別 緇素。立向千峯頂上始得。這僧便禮拜。似捋 虎鬚相似。只爭轉身處。賴值百丈頂門有眼。 肘後有符。照破四天下。深辨來風。所以便打。 若是別人無柰他何。這僧以機投機。以意遣 意。他所以禮拜。如南泉云。文殊普賢。昨夜三 更。起佛見法見。各與二十棒。貶向二鐵圍山 去也。時趙州出眾云。和尚棒教誰喫。泉云。王 老師有什麼過。州禮拜。宗師家等閑不見他 受用處。纔到當機拈弄處。自然活鱍鱍地。五 祖先師常說。如馬前相撲相似。爾但常教見 聞聲色一時坐斷。把得定作得主。始見他百 丈。且道放過時作麼生。看取雪竇頌出云。
text_en: the tiger cub? Baizhang was ordinarily like a tiger with wings. This monk also did not avoid life and death; he dared to stroke the tiger’s whiskers and asked: What is an extraordinary matter? This monk too had eyes. Baizhang then shouldered it for him, saying: Sitting alone on Great Hero Peak. The monk then bowed. For a patch-robed monk, it must be distinct from the intent before the question was asked. This monk’s bowing was not like the usual. It too requires eyes. Don’t pour out your lifelong heart and guts to others; even acquaintances should be as if not acquainted. Just this: the monk asked: What is an extraordinary matter? Baizhang said: Sitting alone on Great Hero Peak. The monk bowed; Baizhang struck him. See: when he lets go, all of it at once is so; when he gathers it in, he sweeps away traces and erases tracks. Now tell me: what was the intent of his bowing? If you say it was good, then why did Baizhang strike him? If you say it was not good, then what is wrong with his bowing? When you reach here, you must know fortune and misfortune and distinguish black robes and white. Only then can you stand atop a thousand peaks. This monk bowed, like stroking the tiger’s whiskers. It only lacked the place to turn the body. Fortunately, Baizhang had eyes on the crown of his head, and a talisman behind his elbow—illuminating and breaking open the four worlds, keenly discerning the wind that comes. Therefore he struck. If it were someone else, there’d be no way to deal with him. This monk used the moment to meet the moment, used intent to send off intent. That is why he bowed. As Nanquan said: Manjushri and Samantabhadra, last night at the third watch, raised a view of Buddha and a view of Dharma—each gets twenty blows, banished to the two Iron Encircling Mountains they go. Then Zhaozhou stepped forward and said: Master, who should eat these blows? Nanquan said: Old Wang the teacher—what fault does he have? Zhaozhou bowed. In the house of a lineage master, you do not casually see where he makes use of it; once you reach the point where he takes it up right on the spot, it is naturally lively and leaping. The Fifth Patriarch formerly often said: It is like grappling in front of a horse. You must always have seeing, hearing, sounds and forms all at once cut off. Grasp it firmly and be the master of it; only then do you see Baizhang. Now tell me: when he lets it pass, how is it? Look at Xuedou’s verse:

In the patriarchs’ domain they crisscross—celestial colts; in the teaching gate, One appears in five hundred years; among a thousand or ten thousand there is one, or half of one—son inheriting the father’s work.

text_zh: 祖域交馳天馬駒五百年一間生。千人萬人中有一箇半箇。子承父業　化 門舒卷不同途已在言前。渠儂得自由。還他作家手段電光石火 存機變劈面來也。左轉右轉。還見百丈為人處也無堪笑人來捋虎 鬚好與三十棒。重賞之下必有勇夫。不免喪身失命。放過闍黎一著
text_en: unfurling and rolling up, not the same road. It is already before the words. He gets his freedom—grant him the methods of a true hand. Lightning flash, flint spark— the pivot of change is kept alive. It comes straight at your face. Turn left, turn right—do you still see where Baizhang acted for people, or not? Laughable are those who come to stroke the tiger’s whiskers. Give him thirty blows. Where heavy rewards are offered, brave men will appear—yet one cannot avoid losing body and life. Let the acharya off by one move.
Xuedou saw it through, and only then composed the verse. A celestial colt travels a thousand miles in a day, running across

text_zh: 雪竇見得透。方乃頌出。天馬駒日行千里。橫 行竪走。奔驟如飛。方名天馬駒。雪竇頌百丈 於祖域之中。東走向西。西走向東。一來一往。 七縱八橫。殊無少礙。如天馬駒相似。善能交 馳。方見自由處。這箇自是得他馬祖大機大 用。不見僧問馬祖。如何是佛法大意。祖便打 云。我若不打爾。天下人笑我去在。又問。如何 是祖師西來意。祖云。近前來向爾道。僧近前。 祖劈耳便掌云。六耳不同謀。看他恁麼得大 自在。於建化門中。或卷或舒。有時舒不在卷 處。有時卷不在舒處。有時卷舒俱不在。所以 道同塗不同轍。此頌百丈有這般手脚。雪竇 道。電光石火存機變。頌這僧如擊石火似閃 電光。只在些子機變處。巖頭道。却物為上。逐 物為下。若論戰也。箇箇立在轉處。雪竇道。機 輪曾未轉。轉必兩頭走。若轉不得。有什麼用 處。大丈夫漢。也須是識些子機變始得。如今 人只管供他欵。彼他穿却鼻孔。有什麼了期。 這僧於電光石火中。能存機變。便禮拜。雪竇 道堪笑人來捋虎鬚。百丈似一箇大蟲相似。 堪笑這僧去捋虎鬚。
text_en: and running straight, galloping as if flying—only then is it called a celestial colt. Xuedou’s verse praises Baizhang within the patriarchs’ domain: running east toward west, running west toward east—coming and going, seven vertical, eight horizontal, with not the slightest obstruction—like a celestial colt, skilled at crisscrossing and racing. Only then do you see the place of freedom. This is precisely having obtained Mazu’s great pivot and great functioning. Haven’t you seen a monk ask Mazu: What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Mazu immediately struck him, saying: If I don’t strike you, people everywhere will laugh at me. Another asked: What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Mazu said: Come closer and I’ll tell you. The monk came closer. Mazu slapped him across the face and said: Six ears do not share the same scheme. See how he thus attains great freedom. Within the gate of establishing and transforming, sometimes he rolls up, sometimes he unfurls; sometimes unfurling is not within rolling up, place. Sometimes the rolling up is not in the unrolling; sometimes the rolling up and unrolling are both not there. Therefore, they say: same road, different tracks. In this verse, Baizhang has such a knack. Xuedou says: Like lightning, like sparks from striking stone, he preserves the pivot of adaptation. He praises this monk as sparks from struck stone, like flashing lightning light. It all lies in that bit of adaptive pivot. Yantou said: Rejecting things is above; chasing things is below. If you speak of the struggle, each one stands at the turning point. Xuedou said: If the mechanism’s wheel has not yet turned, once it turns it must run to both ends. If it cannot turn, what use is there? A true man must also recognize a bit of adaptive pivot. Nowadays people only keep supplying him with provisions; the other party bores through their nostrils. What end will there be? This monk, amid lightning and sparks from stone, could preserve the adaptive pivot, and so he bowed. Xuedou said: It’s laughable, someone comes to stroke the tiger’s whiskers. Baizhang is like a great beast. It’s laughable that this monk went to stroke the tiger’s whiskers.

text_en: blow the fire. Not sparing your eyebrows, set that aside for now—when entering the tiger’s den, how is it? Try to bring it up and see.

text_zh: 【二七】舉。僧問雲門。樹凋葉落時如何是什麼時節。家破 人亡。人亡家破雲門云。體露金風撐天拄地。斬釘截鐵。淨裸裸赤灑灑。 平步青霄。
text_en: the people are gone. People gone, family broken. Propping up heaven and bracing earth; cutting nails and slicing iron—clean and naked, bare and bright. Walking level into the blue sky.
If you can realize it right here, only then do you see where Yunmen meets people. If not,

text_zh: 若向箇裏薦得。始見雲門為人處。其或未然。 依舊只是指鹿為馬。眼瞎耳聾。誰人到這境 界。且道雲門為復是答他話。為復是與他酬 唱。若道答他話。錯認定盤星。若道與他唱和。 且得沒交涉。既不恁麼。畢竟作麼生。爾若 見得透。衲僧鼻孔。不消一揑。其或未然。依舊 打入鬼窟裏去。大凡扶竪宗乘。也須是全身 擔荷。不惜眉毛。向虎口橫身。任他橫拕倒拽。 若不如此。爭能為得人。這僧致箇問端。也不 妨嶮峻。若以尋常事看他。只似箇管閑事底 僧。若據衲僧門下。去命脈裏覷時。不妨有妙 處。且道樹凋葉落是什麼人境界。十八問中。 此謂之辨主問。亦謂之借事問。雲門不移易 一絲毫。只向他道。體露金風。答得甚妙。亦不 敢辜負他問頭。蓋為他問處有眼。答處亦端 的。古人道。欲得親切。莫將問來問。若是知音 底。舉著便知落處。爾若向雲門語脈裏討。便 錯了也。只是雲門句中。多愛惹人情解。若作 情解會。未免喪我兒孫。雲門愛恁麼騎賊馬 趁賊。不見僧問。如何是非思量處。門云。識情 難測。這僧問。樹凋葉落時如何。門云。體露金 風。句中不妨把斷要津不通凡聖。須會他舉 一明三。舉三明一。爾若去他三句中求。則腦 後拔箭。他一句中須具三句。函蓋乾坤句。隨 波逐浪句。截斷眾流句。自然恰好。雲門三句 中。且道用那句接人。試辨看。頌曰。
text_en: it is still just calling a deer a horse—blind eyes, deaf ears. Who reaches this realm? Tell me, was Yunmen answering his words, or was he trading lines with him? If you say he answered him, you mistake the fixed star. If you say he was harmonizing with him, you at least avoid irrelevance. Since it’s not like that, what is it, after all? If you see through it, a patch-robed monk’s nostrils need not be pinched even once. If not, still you get driven into a ghost cave. In general, to uphold the school’s vehicle, you must with your whole body shoulder the burden, not sparing your eyebrows, throw yourself across the tiger’s mouth, letting it drag you sideways or pull you down. If not like this, how could you work for people? This monk raised this question-point, and it is not without steepness. If you look at it as an ordinary matter, he seems like a monk who minds other people’s business. But judged within the gate of patch-robed monks, looking into the lifeline, there is no harm in saying there is something subtle there. Now tell me: when trees wither and leaves fall, whose realm is that? Among the eighteen questions, this is called a discerning-the-host question; it is also called a borrowing-the-occasion question. Yunmen did not shift a hair’s breadth; he only said to him: The body reveals the golden wind. The reply is exceedingly fine, and it also does not dare fail the point of the question. For his asking-place has eyes, and the answering-place is also straight and true. The ancients said: If you want it intimate, do not use a question to ask a question. If it is one who knows the tune, once it is raised, he immediately knows where it lands. If you go fishing in Yunmen’s verbal pulse, then you have already missed it. It’s just that in Yunmen’s phrases he often likes to provoke sentimental interpretations. If you take it as a sentimental interpretation, you won’t avoid losing my sons and grandsons. Yunmen likes to ride the thief’s horse to chase the thief. Didn’t you see a monk ask: What is the place beyond thinking? Yunmen said: Discriminating feelings are hard to measure. This monk asked: When trees wither and leaves fall, how is it? Yunmen said: The body reveals the golden wind. In this phrase he does not fail to block the vital pass, allowing no traffic for ordinary or holy. You must understand his raising one to illuminate three, raising three to illuminate one. If you go seeking in his three phrases, then an arrow is pulled from the back of your head. Within his one phrase, the three phrases must be present: the phrase that encloses heaven and earth; the phrase that follows waves and chases currents; the phrase that cuts off the multitude of streams. Naturally it fits perfectly. Among Yunmen’s three phrases, tell me, which phrase does he use to meet people? Try to discern it. Verse says:

text_en: empty contrivance. Therefore it is said: whenever you ask about a matter, you must recognize a bit of like and dislike. If you don’t recognize high and low, advance and retreat, don’t recognize purity and contact, and you babble whatever comes to mouth, what benefit is there? Whenever you speak and breathe out words, it must be like pincers, like shears—having hooks and locks; it must be continuous and unbroken. This monk’s asking-place has a guiding principle; Yunmen’s answering-place is the same. Yunmen commonly meets people with three phrases; this is the ultimate standard. Xuedou’s verse on this case is similar to his verse on the Dalong case. With three phrases it can be discerned; within one phrase, three phrases are contained. If you can discern it, you penetrate beyond the three phrases altogether. One arrowhead in far-off space—an arrowhead is the metal point of an arrow. It shoots too far; you must quickly fix your eyes on it to see. If you see it clearly, then beneath a single phrase you can unfold the great thousand worlds like grains of sand. Here, having finished the verse, Xuedou still has talent to spare; therefore he opens it up and chants: Over the wide plain, cool gusts rustle and sweep; across the long sky, sparse rain is misty and dim. Tell me—is it mind or is it scene, is it dark mystery or is it subtle wonder? The ancients said: Each and every dharma does not hide; in ancient and modern times it is always revealed. He asked: when trees wither and leaves fall, how is it? Yunmen said: the body reveals the golden wind. Xuedou’s intent is just to make it one scene. Right before your eyes now, the wind blows and brushes—if it is not a southeast wind, it is a northwest wind. You must straightaway understand it just like that. If you further make a Zen-and-Dao kind of understanding, it has nothing to do with it. Don’t you see—the long-sitting guest of Shaolin who has not yet returned: when Bodhidharma had not yet returned to the Western Heaven, he faced the wall for nine years, quietly and still. Tell me—is that trees withering and leaves falling, or tell me is that the body revealing the golden wind? If you go from here, all ordinary and holy of past and present, the vast heaven and earth are hammered into one piece—only then do you see Yunmen and Xuedou’s true way of meeting people. Quietly leaning on Bear’s Ears, cluster after cluster. Bear’s Ears is Shaolin on Mount Song near the western capital. The front mountain has thousands of clusters, and the back mountain also has thousands of clusters. Where do you all see from? Do you still see where Xuedou meets people? It is also like the numinous tortoise dragging its tail.

text_zh: 【二八】舉。南泉參百丈涅槃和尚。丈問。從上諸 聖。還有不為人說底法麼和尚合知。壁立萬仞。還覺齒落麼 泉云。有落草了也。孟八郎作什麼。便有恁麼事丈云。作麼生是不 為人說底法看他作麼生。看他手忙脚亂。將錯就錯。但試問看泉云。不 是心。不是佛。不是物果然納敗闕。果然漏逗不少丈云。說了 也莫與他說破。從他錯一平生。不合與他恁麼道泉云。某甲只恁麼。 和尚作麼生賴有轉身處。與長即長。與短即短。現長則就丈云。我 又不是大善知識。爭知有說不說看他手忙脚亂。藏身露 影。去死十分。爛泥裏有刺。恁麼那。賺我泉云。某甲不會乍可恁麼。賴 值不會。會即打爾頭破。賴值這漢只恁麼丈云。我太殺為爾說了 也雪上加霜。龍頭蛇尾作什麼。

text_en: Straight down from head to toe, not even one eyebrow hair remains—still it is a bit short. Mind-is and mind-is-not—Master Shou called these affirming interpretation and negating interpretation. This is the Nirvana master, Chan Master Fazheng. In former times at Baizhang he served as West Hall; he opened the fields and spoke the great meaning. At that time Nanquan had already seen Mazu, but he was just going about to various places to decide and test. Baizhang posed this one question—it is very hard to answer—saying: of those from the sages of old, is there still a dharma not spoken for people? If it were this mountain monk, I would cover my ears and leave, watching this old fellow’s whole muddle. If it were a real adept, seeing him ask like this, he would immediately see through him. Nanquan simply went by what he saw and said there is. He too is like Meng Baluo. Baizhang then took the mistake and followed it, and next said: what is the dharma not spoken for people? Nanquan said: Not mind, not Buddha. Not a thing. This fellow greedily watches the moon in the sky and loses the pearl in his palm. Baizhang said: Spoken. What a pity—he pierced it for him with a note. At the time, he should have simply struck him across the back with a staff, to make him know pain and itch. Even so, tell me: at what point is the speaking done? According to Nanquan’s view: not mind, not Buddha, not a thing—he never spoke anything. Now I ask you all: why then say, Spoken? His words leave no trace either. If you say he did not speak, why then did Baizhang say it like that? Nanquan is one who can adapt; immediately he pressed forward and said: I am just like this—Master, how are you? If it were someone else, they would inevitably be unable to avoid coming off clumsy and out of step. But Baizhang is an adept; his answering place is not without its peculiar wonder, and so he saying, “I’m not some great spiritual friend either. How would I know whether there is speaking or not speaking?” Nanquan then said, “I don’t understand.” Did he truly understand and say “I don’t understand,” or was he really not understanding? Baizhang said, “I’ve already explained it for you too much.” Tell me, what place is the place of speaking? If they were mud-ball fellows, the two would just muddle together. If both were adepts, it is like a bright mirror set on a stand. In truth, the first two were both adepts; the latter two both let it pass. If you are a man with eyes, clearly test it. But tell me, how do you test him? Look at Xuedou’s verse, where he sang:

Patriarchs and Buddhas have never been for people. Each keeps to his own boundary; if there is a branch, cling to the branch. Remember the original footing in your heart—entering hell is like an arrow.

text_en: Patch-robed monks, past and present, race with lowered heads; a bright mirror stands on the platform. Wear out straw sandals, snap the staff, and hang the bowl bag high. The images arrayed are each distinct. Fall, and break. Break the mirror and meet me face to face. Each one faces south and looks at the Northern Dipper. Do you still see this old monk riding the Buddha hall out through the mountain gate? In Silla it once ascended the hall; in Great Tang the drum has not yet been struck. The dipper handle hangs down. You do not even know where it lands—where is it? There’s nowhere to seek it; when you pick up the nostrils, you lose the mouth. Blind—what a pity. A bowl falls to the ground; a plate shatters into seven or eight pieces. Where did you get this news? If it really is so, then strike.

text_en: the land of Radiant Splendor, ending at the Bati River—between those two, he never once spoke a single word. Said like this—tell me, is it speaking or not speaking? Now the Dragon Palace fills the ocean treasury; then how is it not speaking? Haven’t you seen what Master Xiushan said: “If all Buddhas had not appeared in the world, there would be the forty-nine years of teaching. If Bodhidharma had not come from the West, Shaolin would have its subtle secret.” He also said, “The Buddhas have never appeared in the world, and there is not a single dharma given to people. They only observe the minds of living beings, respond to the illness according to the occasion, give medicine and prescribe methods; thus there are the three vehicles and the twelvefold teachings. In truth, patriarchs and Buddhas, from ancient times to the present, have never for people spoken. This very not-for-people is exactly worth investigating. This mountain monk often says: if you add a single sentence, sweet as honey—look closely, it is precisely poison. If you split the spine with a staff at once, slap the mouth on the spot, and shove him out—only then is it intimate, for the sake of people. Patch-robed monks, past and present, race with lowered heads. Everywhere they ask “is it?” and also ask “isn’t it?” They ask the Buddha, ask the patriarchs, ask upward, ask downward. Even so, if you haven’t reached this ground, you can’t avoid it. It is like a bright mirror on its stand, with images all distinct. All it takes is one sentence to distinguish it clearly. The ancients said, “The ten thousand forms and all phenomena are what a single dharma seals.” And they also said, “All phenomena and the ten thousand forms are wholly rounded within this.” Master Shenxiu said, “The body is the bodhi tree; the mind is like a bright mirror-stand. Constantly polish it diligently; do not let it gather dust.” Daman said, “He’s only outside the gate.” Xuedou said it like this: tell me, is it inside the gate or outside the gate? You people each have an ancient mirror. All phenomena and the ten thousand forms—long and short, square and round—each appears within it. If you go to understand it in terms of long and short, in the end you won’t be able to find it. Therefore Xuedou said: a bright mirror stands on its platform, the images arrayed are distinct—yet it must be that each one faces south and looks at the Northern Dipper. Since it is facing south, why does it look at the Northern Dipper? If you can understand it like this, then you see the place where Baizhang and Nanquan met. These two lines of verse praise Baizhang’s pressing. Baizhang said, “I’m not some great spiritual friend either; how would I know whether there is speaking or not speaking?” Xuedou when he came to this, if he versified it he would fall into dead water. Fearing people would misunderstand, he then lifted it up himself and said: “Right now, before your eyes, the dipper handle hangs down—where else will you go to seek it? As soon as you grab the nostrils, you lose the mouth; if you grab the mouth, you lose the nostrils as well.”

text_en: does this get destroyed or not?” Dasui said, “Destroyed.” What is this thing? This one line cannot be grasped by patch-robed monks under heaven—scratching in advance, waiting for the itch. The monk said, “In that case, it goes along with it.” A holeless iron hammer is hurled right at your face, wiping out the nostrils. Before you open your mouth, it has already been seen through. Dasui said, “It goes along with it.” Turning within the word-thread of an immeasurable great person—sure enough, you misrecognize it. The first arrow is still light; the later arrow is deep. Just this—how many people cannot find it. As the water rises, the boat rises; the more mud, the bigger the Buddha. If you say follow him, where is it? text_en: County in Dongchuan. He visited more than sixty spiritual friends. In former times, at Guishan’s assembly he served as the cook. One day Guishan asked, “You’ve been here for several years, yet you still don’t know how to bring a question and show it—how about that?” Dasui said, “What should you have me ask to make it?” Guishan said, “You just don’t know to ask, ‘What is Buddha?’” Dasui used his hand to cover Guishan’s mouth. Guishan said, “After this, you won’t even find someone to sweep the ground.” Later he returned to Sichuan. First, by the roadside at Pengkou Mountain, he boiled tea to receive travelers, for three years. Only afterward did he come forth in the world, founding a monastery and residing at Dasui. A monk asked, “When the kalpa fire rages and the great thousand worlds are all destroyed, I wonder: is this destroyed or not?” This monk was only relying on doctrinal meaning to ask. In the teachings it says: formation, abiding, decay, emptiness; when the three disasters arise in a kalpa, the destruction reaches to the third dhyana heaven. This monk, from the start, didn’t know where the critical point of the saying lands. Tell me, what kind of person is this? Many make an interpretive explanation, saying: “This is the original nature of sentient beings.” Dasui said, “Destroyed.” The monk said, “In that case, it goes along with it.” Dasui said, “It goes along with it.” Just this—how many people make interpretive explanations and cannot find it. If you say “it goes along with it,” where is it? If you say “it doesn’t go along with it,” then how is it? Haven’t you seen it said: “If you want it to be intimate, don’t use a question to ask a question.” Later a monk asked Master Xiushan, “When the kalpa fire rages and the great thousand worlds are all destroyed, I wonder: is this destroyed or not?” Master Xiushan said, “Not destroyed.” The monk said, “Why is it not destroyed?” The master said, “Because it is the same as the great thousand.” “Destroyed” also blocks and kills people; “not destroyed” also blocks and kills people. Since that monk didn’t understand Dasui’s words, it’s no wonder he kept this matter on his mind. So he held onto this question and went straight to Touzi Mountain in Shuzhou. Touzi asked, “Where have you come from lately?” The monk said, “Dasui in Western Shu.” Touzi said, “What sayings does Dasui have?” The monk then raised the previous exchange. Touzi burned incense and bowed, saying, “In Western Shu an ancient Buddha has appeared in the world. You should quickly return.” The monk returned again to Dasui, but Dasui had already passed away. The monk was utterly frustrated. Later the Tang monk Jingzun inscribed on Dasui: “Clearly there is no other dharma—who says only Yinnan can? One sentence, ‘it goes along with it,’ and patch-robed monks run over a thousand mountains. Crickets chirp cold among the courtyard leaves; ghosts at night bow to the shrine-lamp. After chanting, outside the lonely window, he paces with regret that he cannot bear.” Therefore Xuedou later brings out these two lines in his verse. Now, too, you must not take it as “destroyed,” and you must not take it as “not destroyed.” In the end, how do you understand it? Look closely, right now.

text_en: had eyes or lacked eyes. If one word matched, they stayed; if one word did not match, they left. Look at Magu going to Zhangjing: he circled the meditation seat three times, shook his staff once, and stood upright. Zhangjing said, Yes, yes. The killing blade, the life-giving sword. It must be a person of the house. Xuedou said, Wrong. It falls into two sides. If you understand it by going to the two sides, you won’t see Xuedou’s intent. He stood upright; tell me, what is it about? Why did Xuedou instead say wrong? Where is his wrong? Zhangjing said yes; where is the yes? Xuedou is like sitting and reading a verdict. Magu carried off that one character yes and then went to see Nanquan. Just the same, he circled the meditation seat three times, shook his staff once, and stood upright. Nanquan said, Not, not. The killing blade, the life-giving sword. It must be a true master of the house. Xuedou said, Wrong. Zhangjing said yes, yes; Nanquan said not, not. Are they the same or different? The first said yes; why is that also wrong? The latter said not; why is that also wrong? If you can realize it under Zhangjing’s phrase, you cannot even save yourself. If you can realize it under Nanquan’s phrase, you can take the patriarchs and buddhas as your teachers. Even so, a monk must affirm it for himself before it counts. Don’t just seize on people’s eloquence. Since his question was the same, why does one say yes and one say not? If you are a person of broad capacity who has gained great liberation, you must have another way of living. If you do not forget the mechanism and the situation, you will certainly get stuck on these two ends. If you want to clearly distinguish ancient and modern and sit cutting off the tongues of everyone under heaven, you must clearly take up these two wrongs. When it comes to Xuedou’s later verse, he also only versifies these two wrongs. Xuedou wants to lift up the lively, living place, and so it is like this. If you are a man with blood under the skin, naturally you won’t make interpretations inside words and phrases. You won’t make principles on the donkey-tethering stake. Some say Xuedou made these two wrongs on behalf of Magu; what does it have to do with anything? They do not know that the ancients’ remarks lock off the vital checkpoint. This side is also it, that side is also it, yet in the end it is not on these two ends. Qing the storehouse master said, Carrying the staff and circling the meditation seat, both yes and not are wrong. In truth it also isn’t here. Haven’t you seen Yongjia go to Caoxi to see the Sixth Patriarch: he circled the meditation seat three times, shook his staff once, and stood upright. The patriarch said, A monk possesses three thousand dignified forms and eighty thousand subtle practices. Great Virtue, from what direction have you come, giving rise to great arrogance? Why did the Sixth Patriarch say he gave rise to great arrogance? Here it is not said to be yes, and not said to be not. Yes and not are both donkey-tethering stakes. Only Xuedou’s placing of two wrongs is somewhat better. Ma- gu said, Zhangjing said yes; master, why do you say not? This old fellow does not spare his eyebrows, and he lets out quite a lot. Nanquan said, Zhangjing is indeed yes; you are not. Nanquan can be called seeing the rabbit and releasing the hawk. Qing the storehouse master said, Nanquan is far too sloppy. Not, then stop. Instead he gave him a further path: This is turned by the power of wind, and in the end it will decay and collapse. The Perfect Enlightenment Sutra says, My present body is a combining of the four elements: hair and body hair, nails and teeth; skin, flesh, tendons, bones; marrow and brain, grime and color, all return to earth. Spit and snot, pus and blood all return to water. Warmth returns to fire. Movement and turning return to wind. When the four elements each separate from this illusory body, where will it be? Magu carrying his staff and circling the meditation seat, since it is turned by the power of wind, will in the end decay and collapse. Tell me, in the end, where is the matter that illuminates the mind’s source? When it comes to here, you also must be a man cast from raw iron. Haven’t you seen the scholar Zhang Zhuo? He called on Chan Master Zang of Xitang and asked, Are mountains, rivers, and the great earth existent or nonexistent? The buddhas of the three times, are they existent or nonexistent? Zang said, Existent. Scholar Zhang Zhuo said, Wrong. Zang said, What person have you previously called on? Zhang said, I called on the master of Jingshan. Whatever I asked about, Jingshan always said nonexistent. Zang said, What family do you have? Zhang said, I have a mountain wife and two foolish, stubborn ones. Then he asked, What family does Jingshan have? Zhang said, Jingshan is an ancient buddha; master, don’t slander him. Zang said, When you reach the level of Jingshan, then you can say nonexistent to everything. Zhang Zhuo lowered his head and that was all. In general, a true master wants to help people loosen what clings and remove bonds, pull nails and extract wedges. You cannot merely hold to one side, pushing left then turning right, pushing right then turning left. Just look at Yangshan going to Zhongyi to thank Xiejie. Zhongyi saw him coming and clapped his hands on the meditation seat and said, Master. Yangshan then stood on the east side, then on the west side, then stood in the center. After that he thanked Xiejie, then stepped back and stood behind. Zhongyi He said, “Where did you get this samadhi from?” Yangshan said, “From the seal of Caoxi, I took it off there and brought it out.” Zhongyi said, “Tell me—using this samadhi, whom does Caoxi receive? Yangshan said, “He receives the awakened in a single night.” Then Yangshan again asked Zhongyi, “Master, where did you get this samadhi from?” Zhongyi said, “I got this samadhi from Mazu. Speaking like this—wouldn’t that be to raise one and make three clear? Those who see the root and chase the branches—fellows like that. Longya addressed the assembly, saying, “Those who study must break through the patriarchs and buddhas before it will do. Master Xinfeng said, ‘When you see the words and teachings of the patriarchs and buddhas, treat them like a mortal enemy. Only then do you have a share in study. If you cannot break through, you will be deceived by the patriarchs and buddhas.’ At that time there was a monk who asked, ‘Do the patriarchs and buddhas still have any intention to deceive people?’ Longya said, ‘Tell me—do rivers and lakes have any intention to obstruct people?’ And he also said, ‘Though rivers and lakes have no intention to obstruct people, it is simply that people of the time cannot pass through. Therefore rivers and lakes instead become an obstruction to people. You must not say that rivers and lakes do not obstruct people. Though the patriarchs and buddhas have no intention to deceive people, it is simply that people of the time cannot penetrate through. Therefore the patriarchs and buddhas instead become deceivers of people. You must not say that the patriarchs and buddhas do not deceive people. If you can break through the patriarchs and buddhas, then you pass beyond the patriarchs and buddhas. Yet you must embody the intent of the patriarchs and buddhas—only then is it in accord with what is above. The ancients were the same. If you have not broken through, and you just study buddhas and study patriarchs, then for ten thousand kalpas there will be no time of attainment. Again he asked, ‘How can one avoid being deceived by the patriarchs and buddhas?’ Longya said, ‘You must awaken by yourself. When you get here, it must be like this to succeed.’ Why? ‘To help people, you must help them through. text_en: adds two turning words, threads them into a single strand, and then brings out the verse. “This wrong, that wrong—strictly avoid picking it up and discarding it.” Xuedou’s meaning is: wrong here, wrong there— strictly avoid picking it up and discarding it. If you pick it up and discard it, you go astray. It must be like this: establish these two wrongs, and straightaway the waves of the four seas are level and the tides of the hundred streams recede—how delightful, pure wind and bright moon. If you can understand within these two wrongs, there isn’t the slightest thing left. Mountains are mountains, waters are waters. The long are long, the short are short. Five days a wind, ten days a rain. Therefore it is said: the waves of the four seas are level, the tides of the hundred streams recede. After that he versifies Magu holding up his staff: “The ancient goad—its wind is high over the twelve gates.” The ancients used a whip as a goad. In the house of patch-robed monks, the staff is the goad. At the Queen Mother of the West’s Jasper Pool In the Matters of the Patriarchal Courtyard, the old record cites the Sutra of Raising the Staff. there are twelve vermilion gates. The ancient goad is precisely the staff. The clear wind above it is higher than the twelve vermilion gates. The places where the Son of Heaven and Indra dwell likewise each have twelve vermilion gates. If you understand these two wrongs, light is born on the head of the staff— you won’t even need the ancient goad. The ancients said, “Recognize the staff, and the work of a lifetime of study is finished.” They also said, “It is not a matter of empty forms and false matters; this is the Tathagata’s precious staff itself, a true trace.” Things of this kind. When you arrive here, tumbling head over heels, at all times you attain great freedom. “Gate after gate has a road, empty and desolate.” Though there is a road, it is only empty and desolate. When Xuedou gets here, he feels he has let something slip, so he breaks it open for you again. Yet even so, there is also a place that is not desolate. Even an adept—when there is no illness—still must first go ask for some medicine to take.

Senior Seat Ding was such a fellow: struck by Linji’s slap, when he rose from bowing he immediately knew where he had landed. He was a man from the north, most plain and direct. Yantou then asked, “Where have you come from?” Ding said, “Linji.” Yantou said, “Ten thousand blessings to the master.” Ding said, “He has already passed on.” Yantou said, “The three of us went especially to pay our respects, but our good fortune is shallow and meager, and we met his return to stillness. We wonder: while the master was alive, what sayings did he have? Please, Senior Seat, raise one or two for us to see.” Ding then raised Linji’s words from one day when he addressed the assembly, saying: “On the red flesh lump there is a true person of no rank, constantly coming in and out through the face-gate of you people. Those who have not yet proven it, look, look!” At that time a monk stepped out and asked, “What is the true person of no rank?” Linji immediately grabbed him and said, “Speak, speak!” The monk tried to consider it; Linji immediately shoved him away and said, “True person of no rank—what dried shit-stick is that?” Then he returned to the abbot’s quarters. Yantou, without noticing, stuck out his tongue. Qinshan said, “Why not say ‘not the true person of no rank’?” Ding grabbed him and said, “The true person of no rank and the not-true person of no rank—how far apart are they? Quick, speak, quick!” Qinshan had no words—his face turned sallow, then green. Yantou and Xuefeng came forward and bowed, saying, “This newly ordained one doesn’t know good from bad and has offended the Senior Seat. We beg for compassion—please let him go.” Ding said, “If not for these two old fellows, I would kill this bed-wetting brat.” Again, returning from a meal offering in Zhenzhou, he rested on a bridge and met three lecture-masters. One asked, “What is the deep place of the Chan river, where one must reach the very bottom?” Ding grabbed him and was about to throw him off the bridge. The other two lecture-masters hurriedly pleaded, “Stop, stop! He is the one who offended the Senior Seat—please show compassion.” Ding said, “If not for you two lecture-masters, I’d let him reach the bottom.” Look at such methods—this is entirely Linji’s function. Look at this one question and one answer: clearly distinct. Why then did Yunmen say, These words are all for the sake of compassion; they are talk that falls into the weeds? When the ancients came here, it was like a bright mirror on a stand, a shining pearl in the palm: when a barbarian comes, a barbarian appears; when a Han comes, a Han appears. Even a single fly could not pass beyond their discernment. Tell me, how is it that for the sake of compassion there is talk that falls into the weeds? It is fine if it is steep and perilous. When you reach this ground, you still must be a true fellow to be able to pick it up. Yunmen raised it and said, This monk personally came from Mount Lu. Why then did Yangshan say, Venerable, you have not toured the mountains? Weishan one day asked Yangshan, If a monk comes from the various places, what will you use to test him? Yangshan said, I have a place to test from. Weishan said, Try raising it for me. Yangshan said, When I usually see a monk come, I only raise my fly-whisk toward him and say, Do the various places still have this? When he has something to say, I only say to him, This we will set aside for now; how about that one? Weishan said, This is the fangs and claws of a person of the beyond. Have you not seen how Mazu asked Baizhang, Where have you come from? Baizhang said, From the mountain below. Mazu said, Did you meet anyone on the road? Baizhang said, I did not. Mazu said, Why did you not meet anyone? Baizhang said, If I had met someone, I would have brought it up to the master. Mazu said, Where did you get this news? Baizhang said, I have faults and offenses. Mazu said, It is actually this old monk who has faults and offenses. Yangshan's question to the monk is just like this. At that time, when he asked, Have you visited Five Old Peaks, if the monk were a true fellow, he would only say, Trouble. Instead he said he had not been there. Since this monk was not capable, why did Yangshan not act according to the command and avoid all the entangling vines that follow? Instead he said, Venerable, you have not toured the mountains. Therefore Yunmen said, These words are all for the sake of compassion; they are talk that falls into the weeds. If it were talk that comes out of the weeds, it would not be like this.

text_en: here, one hand lifts, one hand grips. White clouds in layers, the red sun shines bright. It is greatly like grass thick and soft, mist dense and veiling. Here there is not the slightest bit that belongs to the ordinary, not the slightest bit that belongs to the holy. Across the whole world nothing has been hidden; not one thing can be covered over. This is what is called the realm of no-mind: in cold you do not hear cold, in heat you do not hear heat. Altogether it is a great gate of liberation. Glancing left, no flaw; looking right, already old. Master Lanzan lived in seclusion in a stone chamber on Mount Heng. Tang Dezong heard of his name and sent an envoy to summon him. The envoy arrived at his chamber and proclaimed, The Son of Heaven has issued a decree; the venerable one should rise and give thanks for the favor. Zan was stirring a cow-dung fire, then took roasted taro to eat. In the cold his tears hung down to his chin, yet he never answered. The envoy laughed and said, Let me urge the venerable one to wipe away your tears. Zan said, How could I have the leisure to wipe tears for worldly people? In the end he did not rise. The envoy returned and reported. Dezong greatly admired and praised him. Like this, pure and clear, plainly white, not taking orders from others. Truly it is held fast and steady, as if cast from raw iron. Take, for example, Shandao the master: after being expelled, he never again became a monk; people called him the Stone Chamber ascetic. Whenever he stepped onto the pestle, he forgot to move his feet. A monk asked Linji, "The Stone Chamber ascetic forgets to move his feet— what is the meaning of this?" Linji said, "Drowning in a deep pit." Fayen’s Verse on Perfecting True Nature says: When principle reaches the utmost, feelings are forgotten—how could any analogy match it? In the end, the frosty night moon, carried along by circumstance, falls into the stream before us. Fruit ripens and the monkeys grow heavy; the mountains stretch long, as if the road were lost. Raise your head— the lingering light is there; it turns out he lives to the west. Xuedou said, "Haven’t you seen? Hanshan’s walking is too early—ten years and he cannot return, forgetting the road he came by." Hanshan’s poem says: If you would find a place to settle your body, Hanshan can be kept for long. A faint breeze stirs the secluded pines; listen closely, the sound only gets better. Below there are grey-haired men, babbling as they read Huang-Lao; ten years and they cannot return, forgetting the road they came by. Yongjia also said: Mind is the root, dharmas are dust; the two are like marks on a mirror. When the marks and grime are gone, the light first appears; when mind and dharmas are both forgotten, nature is the real. When you reach here—like a fool, like a stump—only then do you see this koan. If you do not reach this ground, you only run about in words—what understanding is there?

text_en: him for the night. Then he asked, "Where have you just come from?" Wuzhuo said, "The South." Wenshu said, "In the South, how is the Buddhadharma maintained?" Wuzhuo said, "Bhikshus of the latter age seldom uphold the precepts." Wenshu said, "How many monks?" Wuzhuo said, "Perhaps three hundred, perhaps five hundred." Wuzhuo then asked Wenshu, "How is it maintained here?" Wenshu said, "Ordinary and sage dwell together; dragons and snakes are mixed." Wuzhuo said, "How many monks?" Wenshu said, "Three-three in front, three-three behind." Then they drank tea. Wenshu lifted up a glass cup and said, "Does the South still have this?" Wuzhuo said, "No." Wenshu said, "Then what do you usually use to drink tea?" Wuzhuo had no words, and so took his leave and departed. Wenshu told the youth Junti to see him to the gate. Wuzhuo asked the youth, "Just now you said three-three in front, three-three behind—how many is that?" The youth said, "Venerable sir!" Wuzhuo answered. The youth said, "How many is it?" Wuzhuo again asked, "What monastery is this?" The youth pointed behind Vajra. Wuzhuo turned his head; the conjured monastery and the youth had all vanished, not to be seen. It was only an empty valley. Later, that place was called Vajra Cave. Later a monk asked Fengxue, "What is the lord within Clear and Cool Mountain?" Fengxue said, "Not even a single phrase can spare you." Wuzhuo asked; to this day he is still taken for a wandering monk. If you want to penetrate it plainly and truly, with your feet planted on solid ground, realize it right beneath Wuzhuo’s words—then even if you dwell in a cauldron of boiling soup or among furnace coals, you will not hear heat; if you dwell upon cold ice, you will not hear cold. If you want to penetrate it so it is solitary, perilous, steep, and austere—like the Vajra King’s jeweled sword—realize it beneath Wenshu’s words; then water cannot splash you, wind cannot enter you. Haven’t you seen Dizang of Zhangzhou ask a monk, "Where have you just come from?" The monk said, "The South." Dizang said, "How is the Buddhadharma there?" The monk said, "They discuss it in great bustle." Dizang said, "How does that compare to my place here— farming the fields to earn food to eat?" Tell me: compared with Wenshu’s reply, is it the same or different? Some say Wuzhuo’s reply is not so, while Wenshu’s reply has dragons and has snakes, has ordinary and has sage—what does it have to do with anything? Can you clearly discern "three-three in front, three-three behind" or not? The earlier arrow is still light; the later arrow goes deep. Tell me: how many is it? If you break through here, a thousand phrases, ten thousand phrases are just one phrase. If beneath this one phrase you can cut it off and hold it steady, then in due course you arrive at this realm.

text_en: Xuedou merely picked it up again and did not truly verse it. But consider a monk who asked Fayen, "What is a single drop of water from Caoxi?" Fayen said, "It is a single drop of water from Caoxi." And a monk asked the master Langya Jue, "The original nature is pure—how did mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?" Jue said, "The original nature is pure—how did mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?" You cannot call that merely picking it up again. Mingzhao the One-Eyed Dragon also versified its meaning: "A device that covers heaven and earth: it spreads through the world of sands, surpassing monasteries. Everywhere you look, Wenshu is holding a dialogue; within the words you do not know to open the Buddha-eye—turn your head and you only see the green mountain crags." "Spreads through the world of sands, surpassing monasteries" points to the conjured monastery in the grass hut; it is what is called a device that works with both provisional and real. "Everywhere you look, Wenshu is holding a dialogue"; within the words you do not know to open the Buddha-eye; turn your head and you only see the green mountain crags. At just such a time, can you call it the realm of Wenshu, Samantabhadra, and Avalokiteshvara? In any case, it is not that principle. Xuedou merely altered Mingzhao’s use, yet there are stitches and seams. "A thousand peaks coil and bend, their color like indigo" does not harm the edge nor cut the hand. Within the line there is provisional and real, principle and fact. "Who says Wenshu was holding a dialogue?" One night of dialogue, yet not knowing it was Wenshu. Later Wuzhuo served as kitchen steward on Wutai Mountain; Wenshu would appear over the porridge pot. Wuzhuo would grab the porridge-stirring paddle and strike him. Even so, it was still like drawing the bow after the thief has passed. Back then, when he asked, "How is the Buddhadharma in the South maintained?" he should have brought the staff down across his back at once—still that would have been closer. Ridiculous—how many monks at Clear and Cool Mountain! In Xuedou’s laugh there is a knife; if you understand where this laugh is, then you will see his saying "three-three in front and three-three behind."

text_en: and the like. His adaptive function was swift. If someone asked for instruction, he gave instruction; if they wanted a verse, he gave a verse. If you wanted a meeting of adepts, he would give you a meeting of adepts. Yangshan’s ordinary functioning was foremost. One day he and Changsha were enjoying the moon when Yangshan pointed to the moon and said, "Everyone has this, but they cannot use it." Changsha said, "Exactly so. Then I’ll ask you to use it." Yangshan said, "You try using it and see." Changsha took one step and knocked Yangshan down. Yangshan got up and said, "Uncle Master, you’re like a great beast!" Later people called him Cen the Great Beast. One day, when he returned from roaming the mountains, the head monk—also someone from his assembly— asked, "Master, where have you been?" Changsha said, "Roaming the mountains." The head monk said, "What places did you go to?" Changsha said, "At first I followed the fragrant grasses away; then I chased the falling blossoms back." Only someone who sits cutting off the ten directions can do this. The ancients, in their coming and going, never failed to keep this matter in mind. Look at how guest and host trade places; meeting the occasion, they cut straight through—neither yields an inch. Since it was roaming the mountains, why ask, "To what places did you go?" If it were today’s Zen fellows, they would say, "I went to Jiasan Pavilion and came back." Look at the ancients: not the slightest calculating over principles, and no place to cling. Therefore he said, "At first I followed the fragrant grasses away; then I chased the falling blossoms back." The head monk then followed his intent and said, "It greatly resembles springtime." Changsha said, "It even surpasses autumn dew dripping on lotus." Xuedou said, "Thanks for the reply words." It stands in for the final line, and yet it too falls to both sides. Ultimately it is not on these two sides. In the past there was Scholar Zhangzhuo, who saw a thousand Buddhas a named scripture—then he asked about the hundreds and thousands of buddhas: we only hear their names; we do not know what country and land they dwell in—do they still transform beings or not? Sha said: after Cui Hao inscribed his poem on Yellow Crane Tower, did any scholar ever inscribe one there again? Zhuo said: no one ever inscribed one. Sha said: when you have leisure, inscribe a piece yourself— that would be fine. Cen Dachong, in his dealings all his life, was straight to the point—pearls turning, jade revolving—he wanted people to understand right in their faces. The verse says:
When the great earth is free of the slightest dust, whose eyes do not Who is it that throws open the windows and sits facing the eaves? You cannot be lacking this at all—then the world is at peace.

text_en: Yangshan said, “Have you been to Five Elders Peak?” The monk said, “I haven’t been there.” Yangshan said, “Acarya, you have not yet toured the mountains.” Distinguish black and white and see whether it is the same or different—when you get here, you must have all contrivances exhausted and all consciousness forgotten: mountains, rivers, the great earth; grass and weeds; people and beasts—without the slightest seepage. If it is not so, the ancients called it still being in a superb and wondrous realm. Have you not seen Yunmen say: even if mountains, rivers, and the great earth have not the tiniest fault, you are still being turned by things. Not seeing a single form is only half a lifting up; you must further know there is a time of full lifting up—one upward opening—then you can sit securely. If you penetrate it, as of old, mountain is mountain and water is water; each abides in its own place, each matches its own essence—like clapping hard for a blind person. Zhaozhou said: at the rooster’s crow, in the chou hour, sorrowfully I rise and still there are leaks. I have not even a skirt or short shirt; the shape of a kasaya I have only a little, yet my underpants have no crotch and my trousers have no opening. On my head, three to five pecks of blue-gray ash—originally it was for cultivation and for benefiting people; who would have known it would instead turn into muttering. If you truly reach this realm, whose eyes do not open? Let it be seven topsy-turvies and eight tumbles—every place is this realm; all of it is this time. In the ten directions there are no walls; on all sides there is likewise no gate. Therefore it says: first follow the fragrant grasses and go, then chase the fallen blossoms and return. Xue- dou is quite clever: he merely sticks one line on the left side, and one line on the right side— just like a poem. A gaunt crane perches on a cold tree; a wild ape howls on an ancient terrace. Xuedou leads it up to here, then feels his own leakage; suddenly he says, “Changsha’s meaning is boundless.” Bah! Like waking up from a dream. Though Xuedou gives a shout, it does not yet cut off completely. If it were this mountain monk, it would not be so: “Changsha’s meaning is boundless”—dig the ground deeper and bury it.

text_en: there appeared one named Puhua. As the master was nearing death, he said to the assembly, “Is there anyone who can depict my true likeness?” The assembly all drew portraits and presented them; the master scolded them all. Puhua came forward and said, “I can depict it.” The master said, “Why not present it to this old monk?” Puhua immediately did a somersault and left. The master said, “From now on this fellow will receive people like a mad wind.” One day he addressed the assembly, saying, “In the three realms there is no dharma—where can one seek the mind? The four great elements are originally empty; the Buddha relies on what to abide? The pivot does not move; still quiescence leaves no trace. Presented face to face, there is nothing more— no remaining matter. Xuedou picked up two lines to make a verse—truly unalloyed gold and uncut jade. Have you not seen it said: to cure an illness, one need not donkey-camel medicine. Why does this mountain monk say, “With a harmonious voice I strike”? Only because he bears the cangue and passes through the accusation. The ancients said: when you hear the phrase beyond the sound, do not seek it in your thoughts. Now tell me, what is his intent like? It is like rushing streams crossing a blade-edge; lightning turns, stars fly. If you speculate and ponder, even if a thousand buddhas appear in the world, you still will not be able to grope it out. If you go deep into the innermost, penetrating to bone and marrow, seeing through to the bottom, Panshan is a complete defeat. If you take his words and “understand the essential,” turning left and right, Panshan will only get a single stake. If you drag mud and carry water, turning in the heap of sounds and forms, you have not even dreamed of Panshan. The ancestral master Wuzu said: only by passing through to the other side do you have a share of freedom. Have you not seen the Third Patriarch say: if you cling to it, losing measure, you surely enter a deviant path; if you let it go, the essential nature naturally has no coming or going. If here you say “no Buddha, no dharma,” you again fall into a ghost cave. The ancients called it the deep pit of liberation. It was originally a good cause yet it draws an evil result. Therefore it is said: even a person with nothing to do and nothing going on still runs into the hardship of golden locks. You must exhaust it to the very end. If in the place of no words you can speak, and in the place where you cannot act you can act, this is called the turning point. In the three realms there is no dharma—where can one seek the mind? If you make it into an emotional interpretation, you die right under his words. Xuedou’s insight has seven piercings and eight holes; therefore he composed this verse:
In the three realms there is no dharma—where can one seek the mind? White The words are still in the ear. No need to raise it again—check it yourself. He strikes, saying: What is this?

text_zh: 三界無法何處求心。雪竇頌得。一似華嚴境 界。有者道。雪竇無中唱出。若是眼皮綻底。終 不恁麼會。雪竇去他傍邊。貼兩句道。白雲為 蓋。流泉作琴。蘇內翰見照覺。有頌云。溪聲便 是廣長舌。山色豈非清淨身。夜來八萬四千 偈。他日如何舉似人。雪竇借流泉。作一片長 舌頭。所以道。一曲兩曲無人會。不見九峯虔 和尚道。還識得命麼。流泉是命。湛寂是身。千 波競起是文殊家風。一亘晴空。是普賢境界。 流泉作琴。一曲兩曲無人會。這般曲調。也 須是知音始得。若非其人。徒勞側耳。古人道。 聾人也唱胡家曲。好惡高低總不聞。雲門道。 舉不顧即差互。擬思量。何劫悟。舉是體。顧是 用。未舉已前。朕兆未分已前見得。坐斷要津。 若朕兆纔分見得。便有照用。若朕兆分後見 得。落在意根。雪竇忒殺慈悲。更向爾道。却似 雨過夜塘秋水深。此一頌曾有人論量。美雪 竇有翰林之才。雨過夜塘秋水深。也須是急 著眼看。更若遲疑。即討不見。
text_en: Some say Xuedou sings it out of nothing; if you are someone whose eyelids have split open, in the end you will not understand it that way. Xuedou steps to the side and sticks on two lines, saying: “White clouds as a canopy; running springs as a zither.” Su Neihan, seeing illumination and awakening, had a verse saying: the sound of the stream is precisely the broad, long tongue; are not the mountain colors the pure body? Last night, eighty-four thousand gathas—how will you raise them to someone another day? Xuedou borrows the running springs to make a single piece of long tongue; therefore it says, “One tune, two tunes—no one understands.” Have you not seen Jiufeng Qian the master say: do you recognize life? Running springs are life; clear stillness is the body. A thousand waves competing to rise is Manjushri’s family style; a single stretch of clear sky is Samantabhadra’s realm. Running springs as a zither—one tune, two tunes—no one understands. A melody like this requires a true connoisseur. If it is not the right person, it is futile to cock your ear. The ancients said: even a deaf person sings a barbarian tune; likes and dislikes, high and low, he never hears at all. Yunmen said: raise it without regard and it is already off; if you try to think about it, in what kalpa will you awaken? Raising is essence; regarding is function. If before it is raised, before the first signs have split, you can see it, you sit cutting off the crucial pass. If as soon as the signs split you can see it, there is illumination and function. If after the signs split you see it, it falls into the mind-root. Xuedou is far too compassionate; he tells you further: it is like “after the rain, in the night pond, autumn waters are deep.” People have once weighed and discussed this single verse, praising Xue- dou for having the talent of a Hanlin. “After the rain, in the night pond, autumn waters are deep”—you must look quickly and sharply; if you hesitate, you will not find it.

更有在。仰山云有。只是年代深遠。不欲舉似 和尚。溈山。云雖然如是。吾亦要知。但舉看。 仰山云。一人指南吳越令行。遇大風即止。此 乃讖風穴也。穴初參雪峯五年。因請益。臨濟 入堂。兩堂首座齊下一喝。僧問臨濟。還有賓 主也無。濟云。賓主歷然。穴云。未審意旨如 何。峯云。吾昔與巖頭欽山。去見臨濟。在途中 聞已遷化。若要會他賓主話。須是參他宗派 下尊宿。穴後又見瑞巖常自喚主人公。自云 喏。復云。惺惺著。他後莫受人瞞却。穴云。自 拈自弄。有什麼難。後在襄州鹿門與廓侍者 過夏。廓指他來參南院。穴云。入門須辨主。端 的請師分。一日遂見南院。舉前話云。某甲 特來親覲。南院云。雪峯古佛。一日見鏡清。清 問近離甚處。穴云。自離東來。清云。還過小江 否。穴云。大舸獨飄空。小江無可濟。清云。鏡 水圖山。鳥飛不渡。子莫盜聽遺言。穴云。滄溟 尚怯蒙輪勢。列漢飛帆渡五湖。清竪起拂子 云。爭奈這箇何。穴云。這箇是什麼。清云。果 然不識。穴云。出沒卷舒。與師同用。清云。杓 卜聽虛聲。熟睡饒譫語。穴云。澤廣藏山理 能伏豹。清云。赦罪放愆。速須出去。穴云。出 即失。乃便出至法堂上。自謂言。大丈夫。公案 未了。豈可便休。却回再入方丈。清坐次。便 問。某適來輒呈騃見。冐瀆尊顏。伏蒙和尚 慈悲。未賜罪責。清云。適來從東來。豈不是翠 嚴來。穴云。雪竇親棲寶蓋東。清云。不逐亡羊 狂解息。却來這裏念詩篇。穴云。路逢劍客須 呈劍。不是詩人莫獻詩。清云。詩速祕却。略借 劍峯穴云。󱓒首甑人携劍去。清云。不獨觸風 化。亦自顯顢頇。穴云。若不觸風化。焉明古佛 心。清云。何名古佛心。穴又云再許允容。師今 何有清云。東來衲子菽麥不分。穴云。只聞不 以而以。何得抑以而以。清云。巨浪湧千尋。澄 波不離水。穴云。一句截流萬機寢削。穴便禮 拜。清以拂子點三點云。俊哉。且坐喫茶。風穴 初到南院。入門不禮拜。院云。入門須辨主。 穴云。端的請師分。院左手拍膝一下。穴便 喝。院右手拍膝一下。穴亦喝。院舉左手云。這 箇即從闍黎。又舉右手云。這箇又作麼生。穴 云。瞎院遂拈拄杖。穴云。作什麼。某甲奪却拄 杖。打著和尚。莫言不道。院便擲下拄杖云。今 日被這黃面浙子。鈍置一上。穴云。和尚大似 持鉢不得。詐道不飢。院云。闍黎莫曾到此間 麼。穴云。是何言歟。院云。好好借問。穴云。也 不得放過。院云。且坐喫茶。爾看俊流自是機 鋒峭峻。南院亦未辨得他。至次日南院只作 平常問云。今夏在什麼處。穴云。鹿門與廓侍 者同過夏。院云。元來親見作家來。又云他 向爾道什麼。穴云。始終只教某甲一向作主。 院便打推出方丈云。這般納敗缺底漢。有什 麼用處。穴自此服膺。在南院會下作園頭。一 日院到園裏問云。南方一棒作麼生商量。穴 云。作奇特商量。穴云。和尚此間作麼生商量。 院拈棒起云。棒下無生忍。臨機不讓師。穴於 是豁然大悟。是時五代離亂。郢州牧主請師 度夏是。時臨濟一宗大盛。他凡是問答垂示。 不妨語句尖新。攢花簇錦。字字皆有下落。一 日牧主。請師上堂。示眾云。祖師心印。狀似鐵 牛之機。去即印住。住即印破。只如不去不住。 印即是不印即是。何故。不似石人木馬之機。 直下似鐵牛之機。無爾撼動處。爾才去即印 住。爾才住即印破。教爾百雜碎。只如不去不 住。印即是不印即是。看他恁麼垂示可謂鉤 頭有餌。是時座下有盧陂長老。亦是臨濟下 尊宿。敢出頭來與他對機。便轉他話頭。致箇 問端。不妨奇特。道某甲有鐵牛之機。請師不 搭印。爭奈風穴是作家。便答他道。慣釣鯨鯢 澄巨浸。却嗟蛙步輾泥沙。也是言中有響。 雲門云。垂鉤四海只釣獰龍。格外玄機為尋 知已。巨浸乃十二頭水牯牛。為鉤餌。却只釣 得一蛙出來。此語且無玄妙。亦無道理計較。 古人道。若向事上覻則易。若向意根下卜度 則沒交涉。盧陂佇思。見之不取千載難逢。可 惜許。所以道。直饒講得千經論。一可臨機下 口難。其實盧陂要討好語對他。不欲行令。被 風穴一向用攙旗奪皷底機鋒。一向逼將去。 只得沒奈何。俗諺云。陣敗不禁苕菷掃。當初 更要討鎗法敵他。等爾討得來。即頭落地。 牧主亦久參風穴。解道佛法與王法一般。穴 云。爾見箇什麼。牧主云。當斷不斷返招其亂。 風穴渾是一團精神。如水上葫蘆子相似。捺 著便轉。按著便動。解隨機說法。若不隨機翻 成妄語。穴便下座。只如臨濟有四賓主話。夫 參學之人。大須子細。如賓主相見。有語論賓 主往來。或應物見形。全體作用。或把機權喜 怒。或現半身。或乘獅子。或乘象王。如有真正 學人便喝。先拈出一箇膠盆子。善知識不辨 是境。便上他境上。作模作樣。便學人又喝。 前人不肯放下。此是膏肓之病。不堪醫治。喚 作賓看主。或是善知識。不拈出物。隨學人 問處便奪。學人被奪。抵死不放。此是主看賓。 或有學人。應一箇清淨境。出善知識前。知識 辨得是境。把他拋向坑裏。學人言。大好善知 識。知識即云。咄哉不識好惡。學人禮拜。此喚 作主看主。或有學人。披枷帶鎖。出善知識前。 知識更與他安一重枷鎖。學人歡喜。彼此不 辨。呼為賓看賓。大德山僧所舉。皆是辨魔揀 異。知其邪正。不見僧問慈明。一喝分賓主。照 用一時行時如何。慈明便喝。又雲居弘覺禪 師示眾云。譬如獅子捉象亦全其力。捉兔亦 全其力。時有僧問。未審全什麼力。雲居云。不 欺之力。看他雪竇頌出　󱓒堅堯切通作梟斷首倒縣。
text_en: was planting pines. Huangbo said: In the deep mountains, what are you doing planting so many pines? Linji said: First, to make scenery for the monastery gate; second, to serve as signposts for later people. Having said that, he hoed the ground once. Huangbo said: Even so, you have already taken twenty blows. Linji struck the ground once more and said: Hush, hush. Huangbo said: Our school will greatly flourish in the world through you. Weishan Zhe said: Linji like this is like taking a fall on flat ground. Even so, when facing danger he does not change—only then is he called a true man. Huangbo said: Our school will greatly flourish in the world through you—like doting on a child and not noticing its ugliness. Later, Weishan asked Yangshan: At that time Huangbo entrusted it only to Linji. Was there anyone else? Yangshan said: There was, but the era is far removed; I do not wish to bring it up before you, master. Weishan said: Even so, I want to know—just raise it and let me see. Yangshan said: One man points south—Wu and Yue carry out the command; when a great wind is met, it stops. This was a prophecy of Fengxue. At first Fengxue studied under Xuefeng for five years. Because he asked for instruction, Linji entered the hall; the head monks of the two halls together gave a shout. A monk asked Linji: Are there still guest and host or not? Linji said: Guest and host are distinct. Fengxue said: I do not yet understand the meaning—how is it? Xuefeng said: Long ago I went with Yantou and Qinshan to see Linji, but on the road we heard he had already passed away. If you want to understand his talk of guest and host, you must study elders in his lineage. Later Fengxue saw Ruiyan, who always called to his own “true person,” saying to himself, Yes. Then he said: Stay awake; later do not let people fool you. Fengxue said: Picking it up yourself and playing with it yourself—what’s difficult about that? Later, at Lumen in Xiangzhou, he spent the summer with Attendant Kuo, who pointed him to go study with Nanyuan. Fengxue said: Entering the gate, you must discern the host; I earnestly ask the master to differentiate. One day he went to see Nanyuan and brought up the earlier words, saying: I have come specially to pay my respects in person. Nanyuan said: Xuefeng is an old Buddha. One day he met Jingqing. Jingqing asked: Where have you just come from? Fengxue said: I came from the east. Jingqing said: Did you cross Little River? Fengxue said: A great vessel drifts alone in empty space; Little River is not something to be crossed. Jingqing said: Mirror waters and painted mountains—birds can fly but do not cross. Don’t steal-hear leftover words. Fengxue said: Even the blue sea still fears the force of armored ships; set sails across the ranks of rivers and cross the Five Lakes. Jingqing raised the whisk and said: What about this? Fengxue said: What is this? Jingqing said: As expected, you do not recognize it. Fengxue said: Appearing and vanishing, rolling up and unfurling—we use it together. Jingqing said: Divining by ladle and tortoise, listening to empty sounds; deep sleep is full of babble. Fengxue said: Broad marshes hide mountains; in principle you can subdue leopards. Jingqing said: Forgive crimes and release faults—quickly get out. Fengxue said: If I go out, I lose it. So he went out to the Dharma hall and said to himself: A great man—if a public case is unresolved, how could I just stop? He turned back and re-entered the abbot’s quarters. Jingqing was sitting; Fengxue then asked: Just now I rashly presented a foolish view and presumed upon your honored presence. I have received the master’s compassion and have not been blamed. Jingqing said: Just now you came from the east—wasn’t it from Cuiyan? Fengxue said: Xuedou personally perches east of the jeweled canopy. Jingqing said: Not chasing the lost sheep, the mad explanations cease—yet you come here reciting poems. Fengxue said: When you meet a swordsman on the road, you must show your sword; if he is not a poet, do not offer poems. Jingqing said: Quickly hide the poem; lend me the sword’s edge for a moment. Fengxue said: The man at the first steamer carries the sword away. Jingqing said: Not only do you touch off a response to conditions, you also reveal your own dullness. Fengxue said: If I do not touch off a response, how would the old Buddha’s mind be made clear? Jingqing said: What is called the old Buddha’s mind? Fengxue again said: Grant me another allowance—what do you have now, master? Jingqing said: A patched-robed fellow from the east cannot even tell beans from barley. Fengxue said: I have only heard of taking what is not taken—how could you suppress taking what is taken? Jingqing said: Great waves surge a thousand fathoms; the clear ripples do not leave the water. Fengxue said: One phrase cuts off the current; the ten thousand activities are laid to rest and pared away. Fengxue then bowed in homage. Jingqing tapped three times with the whisk and said: Splendid! Sit and have tea. When Fengxue first arrived at Nanyuan, he entered without bowing. Nanyuan said: Entering the gate, you must discern the host. Fengxue said: I earnestly ask the master to differentiate. Nanyuan slapped his left knee once with his left hand; Fengxue then shouted. Nanyuan slapped his right knee once with his right hand; Fengxue also shouted. Nanyuan raised his left hand and said: This comes from you, practitioner. Then he raised his right hand and said: And what about this one? Fengxue said: Blind! Nanyuan then picked up his staff. Fengxue said: What are you doing? I will seize the staff and strike the master with it—don’t say I didn’t warn you. Nanyuan immediately threw down the staff and said: Today I’ve been dulled once by this yellow-faced fellow from Zhejiang. Fengxue said: The master is very much like someone unable to hold a bowl, yet pretending not to be hungry. Nanyuan said: Practitioner, haven’t you ever come here before? Fengxue said: What kind of words are those? Nanyuan said: Ask well, ask well. Fengxue said: I won’t let it pass either. Nanyuan said: Sit and have tea. You see—this fine fellow naturally has sharp and steep edge. Even Nanyuan had not yet discerned him. By the next day, Nanyuan simply asked in the ordinary way: Where were you this summer? Fengxue said: At Lumen, spending the summer with Attendant Kuo. Nanyuan said: So you really have personally met a master. And he asked: What did he say to you? Fengxue said: From start to finish he only taught me to always be the host. Nanyuan then struck him and drove him out of the abbot’s room, saying: A fellow like this, taking in defeat and defects—what use is he? From then on Fengxue submitted in his heart and served in Nanyuan’s assembly as the garden head. One day Nanyuan came to the garden and asked: How do they discuss “a single blow” in the south? Fengxue said: They discuss it in an extraordinary way. Fengxue asked: Master, how do you discuss it here? Nanyuan raised his staff and said: Under the staff, the patience of the unborn; meeting the moment, not yielding even to the master. Fengxue suddenly had great awakening. At that time, during the upheavals of the Five Dynasties, the prefect of Yingzhou invited the master to spend the summer. In those days the Linji school was flourishing greatly. In all his question-and-answer instructions, his phrases were sharp and fresh, gathered like flowers and brocades; every word had its landing. One day the prefect invited the master to ascend the hall. He instructed the assembly, saying: The Patriarchs’ mind-seal is like the mechanism of an iron ox: go and it stamps and holds; stay and it stamps and breaks. But if neither going nor staying, stamping is not-stamping, and not-stamping is stamping. Why? It is not like the mechanism of a stone man or wooden horse. Straight on, it is like the mechanism of an iron ox—there is nowhere you can shake it. The moment you go, it stamps and holds; the moment you stay, it stamps and breaks. It shatters you into a hundred fragments. But if neither going nor staying, stamping is not-stamping and not-stamping is stamping. Seeing him instruct like this, it can be said there is bait on the hook. At that time among the seats was Elder Lupei, also a venerable elder in the Linji line, who dared step forward to meet him on the spot. He then turned the topic and posed a question-point—indeed extraordinary—saying: I have the mechanism of the iron ox; I ask the master not to apply the stamp. But Fengxue was a master; he answered: Long used to fishing whales and sea-dragons in the clear vast deep, yet I sigh at a frog’s steps trampling mud and sand. His words had an echo within them. Yunmen said: Casting the hook into the four seas, he only fishes ferocious dragons; the extraordinary profound mechanism is to seek a true one who knows. The vast deep is the twelve-headed water buffalo used as hook and bait, yet he only fished up a single frog. These words have no mystique, and there is no principle to weigh and calculate. The ancients said: If you look at it in things, it is easy; if you divine and measure beneath the root of intention, it has nothing to do with it. Lupei paused in thought—seeing it and not taking it is hard to meet in a thousand years. What a pity. Thus it is said: Even if you can expound a thousand sutras and treatises, once you face the moment, it is hard to speak. In truth, Lupei wanted to seek a pleasing phrase to answer him, not wishing to carry out the command; but Fengxue consistently used the edge that seizes the banner and snatches the drum, pressing him onward without pause. With no choice but to submit. As the common saying goes: when the battle is lost, you cannot forbid even a rush broom from sweeping. At the outset you still wanted to go fetch spear techniques to fight him. By the time you fetch them, your head will already be on the ground. The Prefect Mu had long studied under Fengxue, and understood that the Buddha Dharma and the king’s law are the same. Fengxue said, What do you see? The Prefect Mu said, If what should be cut off is not cut off, it only invites further disorder. Fengxue was wholly a single mass of spirit, like a gourd floating on water. Press it and it turns; hold it down and it moves. He could speak the Dharma according to the occasion; if he did not accord with the occasion, it would turn into false speech. Fengxue then descended from the seat. Now Linji has the talk of four guest and host. As for those who study the Way, you must be very careful. When guest and host meet, there are words discussing the guest and host coming and going; or responding to things as forms appear, functioning with the whole body; or wielding devices and expedients in joy and anger; or manifesting half the body; or riding a lion; or riding an elephant king. If there is a true student, he gives a shout. First he produces a lacquer basin. If a good spiritual friend cannot discern it as a circumstance, he climbs onto that circumstance, putting on airs and posturing. Then the student shouts again. The one in front refuses to put it down. This is an illness lodged in the vitals, beyond treatment. This is called the guest watching the host. Or there is a good spiritual friend who does not bring out any thing, but whatever the student asks, he immediately snatches away. The student, once snatched from, will not let go even to the death. This is the host watching the guest. Or there is a student who presents a pure, clean circumstance before a good spiritual friend. The friend discerns it as a circumstance and flings it into a pit. The student says, What a fine good spiritual friend! The friend at once says, Tsk! You do not know good from bad. The student bows. This is called the host watching the host. Or there is a student wearing a cangue and chains who comes before a good spiritual friend. The friend adds another layer of cangue and chains. The student is delighted. Neither side can discern it. This is called the guest watching the guest. What the monks of Great Deshan cited is all about distinguishing demons and selecting what differs, knowing what is crooked and what is straight. Have you not seen a monk ask Ciming: With one shout you separate guest and host; when illumination and function operate at the same time, what then? Ciming immediately shouted. And Master Yunju Hongjue instructed the assembly, For example, when a lion seizes an elephant, it uses all its strength; when it seizes a rabbit, it also uses all its strength. At that time a monk asked, What strength is it that is used in full? Yunju said, The strength that does not deceive. Look at Xuedou’s verse as it comes forth. Hard as iron, sharp through and through—like an owl, severing heads and hanging them upside down.
Capture Lu Po, stride the iron ox, the three mysteries; Among thousands upon thousands, one must still display skill. A defeated general is not beheaded again.

text_zh: 擒得盧陂跨鐵牛千人萬人中。也要呈巧藝。敗軍之將不再斬　三玄 戈甲未輕酬當局者迷。受災如受福。受降如受敵楚王城畔朝 宗水說什麼朝宗水。浩浩充塞天地。任是四海也須倒流喝下曾令却倒 流不是這一喝截却爾舌頭。咄。驚走陝府鐵牛。嚇殺嘉州大象
text_en: spear and armor are not repaid lightly. Those inside the game are confused. Receive disaster as if receiving blessing; accept surrender as if accepting an enemy. By the walls of the King of Chu’s city, the waters flow toward the sea in homage; What talk of waters returning to the sea? Vast and flooding, it fills heaven and earth—though it be the four seas, they too must flow backward. under a shout, it once was made to flow back. If not for this one shout cutting off your tongue—tsk! It startles the iron ox of Shan Prefecture into flight, and scares the great elephant of Jiazhou to death.
Xuedou knew that Fengxue had such a house style, so he versified: Capture Lu Po

text_zh: 雪竇知風穴有這般宗風。便頌道。擒得盧陂 跨鐵牛。三玄戈甲未輕酬。臨濟下有三玄三 要。凡一句中須具三玄。一玄中須具三要。僧 問臨濟。如何是第一句。濟云。三要印開朱 點窄。未容擬議主賓分。如何是第二句。濟 云。妙辨豈容無著問。漚和不負截流機。如 何是第三句。濟云。但看棚頭弄傀儡。抽牽 全藉裏頭人。風穴一句中便具三玄戈甲。七 事隨身。不輕酬他。若不如此。爭奈盧陂何。後 面雪竇要出臨濟下機鋒。莫道是盧陂假饒 楚王城畔。洪波浩渺白浪滔天。盡去朝宗。只 消一喝。也須教倒流。
text_en: and stride the iron ox. The three mysteries’ spear and armor are not repaid lightly. Under Linji there are the three mysteries and the three essentials. In every single phrase, the three mysteries must be present; within one mystery, the three essentials must be present. A monk asked Linji, What is the first phrase? Linji said, When the seal of the three essentials is opened, the vermilion dot is narrow; before deliberation is allowed, host and guest are distinguished. What is the second phrase? Linji said, Subtle discernment does not allow Wuzhu’s question; Ouhe does not fail the device that cuts off the stream. What is the third phrase? Linji said, Just watch the puppets played atop the shed; pulling and hauling wholly relies on the person inside. In one phrase Fengxue already embodies the three mysteries’ spear and armor. The seven affairs attend the body; he does not repay him lightly. If it were not like this, what could he do about Lu Po? Later, Xuedou wants to bring out the edge of Linji’s devices. Do not say Lu Po is a fake; even if by the walls of the King of Chu’s city the vast flood surges and white waves billow to the sky, all going to pay homage to the sea—still it takes only one shout, and it must be made to flow backward.

text_zh: 垂示云。途中受用底。似虎靠山。世諦流布底。 如猿在檻。欲知佛性義。當觀時節因緣。欲煅 百鍊精金。須是作家爐韛。且道大用現前底。 將什麼試驗。
text_en: is like a monkey in a cage. If you want to know the meaning of Buddha-nature, you must observe time, season, and conditions. If you want to forge refined gold a hundred times over, it must be an expert’s furnace and bellows. Tell me: when great function appears before you, with what will you test it?
