text_en: you see not seeing, it naturally is not the appearance of that not seeing. If you do not see the place of my not seeing, it naturally is not a thing—how is it not you? When Xuedou reaches here, he does not quote the sutra text to the end; quoting it in full makes it clear. The sutra says: If what is seen is a thing, then you also can see my seeing. If you see the same, it is called seeing me. When I do not see, why do you not see the place of my not seeing? If you see not seeing, it naturally is not that appearance of not seeing. If you do not see the place of my not seeing, it naturally is not a thing. How is it not you? Too many words to record. Ananda’s intent was this: the world, lanterns, pillars—everything can have a name; he also wanted the World-Honored One to point out this subtle essence, original clarity—what is it called, what thing is it—so that I may see the Buddha’s intent. The World-Honored One said, I see the incense stand. Ananda said, I also see the incense stand; that is the Buddha’s seeing. The World-Honored One said, If I see the incense stand, then you can know. If I do not see the incense stand, how do you see? Ananda said, When I do not see the incense stand, that is seeing the Buddha. The Buddha said, When I say I do not see, that is my own knowing. When you say you do not see, that is your own knowing. Another person’s not seeing— how can you know it? The ancients said: when you reach here, you can only know it yourself. You cannot speak of it to others. Just as the World-Honored One said: When I do not see, why do you not see the place of my not seeing? If you see not seeing, it naturally is not the appearance of that not seeing. If you do not see the place of my not seeing, it naturally is not a thing—how is it not you? If you say you take seeing to be a thing, you still cannot brush away traces. When I do not see, it is like an antelope hanging its horns—sound and traces, even its breath, are all cut off. Where will you go to grope for it? The sutra’s intent first lets go to break through, then snatches away to break through. Xuedou, bringing forth a verse with an eye for the teaching, does not versify a thing; nor does he versify seeing and not seeing. He only versifies seeing the Buddha.

text_en: Sutra. A monk asked Yangshan, When the master sees people ask about Zen and ask about the Way, you make a circle, and inside it you write the character ox; what is your intent in this? Yangshan said, This too is an idle matter. If you suddenly understand, it does not come from outside. If you suddenly do not understand, you definitely do not recognize it. Let me ask you: the old worthies of all directions point to you and indicate which is your buddha-nature— is it the speaking one, the silent one? Could it be the one that neither speaks nor is silent? Or is it all of them? Or is it none of them? If you take the speaking one to be it, you are like a blind person feeling the elephant’s tail. If you take the silent one to be it, you are like a blind person feeling the elephant’s ear. If you take the one that neither speaks nor is silent to be it, you are like a blind person feeling the elephant’s trunk. If you say every single thing is it, you are like a blind person feeling the elephant’s four legs. If you say none of it is, you throw away the elephant itself and fall into empty views. Such is what the blind crowd sees: they only name vague differences upon the elephant. If you want it good, absolutely do not grope the elephant. Do not say seeing and awareness are it; also do not say they are not. The Patriarch said, Bodhi originally has no tree; the bright mirror also has no stand. Originally there is not a single thing—how could dust and grime cling? And he also said, The Way originally has no form or appearance; wisdom is the Way. One who makes this understanding is called true prajna. A clear-eyed person sees the elephant and gets its whole body; as the Buddha sees nature, so it is. The whole ox comes from Zhuangzi: Butcher Ding carved an ox, never once seeing its whole ox. Following the pattern, he cut; the blade moved freely, at ease. There was no need to force the hand. When he only lifted his eyes, horns, hooves, and flesh all at once resolved themselves. Thus for nineteen years, his knife stayed sharp as if freshly honed on the whetstone—this is called the whole ox. Even though it is so extraordinary, Xue- dou said, Even if you achieve this, the whole elephant and whole ox are still no different from an eye-film. From the beginning, all who do it are together named gropers. Even a genuine adept—go in there and grope and you will not find it. From Kashyapa on, down to the Patriarchs of India and this land, the old masters under heaven are all merely named gropers. Xuedou bluntly said: now if you want to see the yellow-headed old fellow—therefore it is said, if you want to see, then see right away. If you still want to search, only then you will see—then it is a thousand miles, ten thousand miles. The yellow-headed old fellow is the yellow-faced old one. You now want to see: in every instant, in every speck of dust, it is halfway along the road. It is commonly said: one mote, one land; one leaf, one Shakyamuni. Throughout the three-thousand great-thousand worlds, all the fine dust—see it only within a single mote. Even then, you are still halfway along the road. Over there there is still another halfway along the road. Tell me, where is it? Even old Shakyamuni himself does not know—how could this mountain monk possibly speak it? Eye-film. text_zh: 長慶保福在雪峯會下。常互相舉覺商量。一 日平常如此說話云。寧說阿羅漢有三毒。不 說如來有二種語。梵語阿羅漢。此云殺賊。以 功能彰名。能斷九九八十一品煩惱。諸漏已 盡。梵行已立。此是無學阿羅漢位。三毒即是 貪嗔癡。根本煩惱。八十一品。尚自斷盡。何況 三毒。長慶道。寧說阿羅漢有三毒。不說如來 有二種語。大意要顯如來無不實語。法華經 云。唯此一事實。餘二則非真。又云。唯有一乘 法。無二亦無三。世尊三百餘會。觀機逗教。應 病與藥。萬種千般說法。畢竟無二種語。他 意到這裏。諸人作麼生見得。佛以一音演說 法。則不無長慶要且未夢見如來語在。何故 大似人說食終不能飽。保福見他平地上說 教遂問。作麼生是如來語。慶云。聾人爭得聞。 這漢知他幾時。在鬼窟裏作活計來也。保福 云。情知爾向第二頭道。果中其言。却問師兄 作麼生是如來語。福云。喫茶去。鎗頭倒被別 人奪却了也。大小長慶。失錢遭罪。且問諸人。 如來語還有幾箇。須知恁麼見得。方見這兩 箇漢敗缺。子細檢點將來。盡合喫棒。放一 線道與他理會。有底云。保福道得是。長慶道 得不是。只管隨語生解。便道有得有失。殊不 知。古人如擊石火。似閃電光。如今人不去他 古人轉處看。只管去句下走。便道長慶當時 不便用。所以落第二頭。保福云。喫茶去。便 是第一頭。若只恁麼看。到彌勒下生。也不見 古人意。若是作家。終不作這般見解。跳出這 窠窟。向上自有一條路。爾若道聾人爭得聞 有什麼不是處。保福云喫茶去。有什麼是處。 轉沒交涉。是故道。他參活句。不參死句。這因 緣與遍身是通身是因緣一般。無爾計較是 非處。須是爾脚跟下。淨裸裸地。方見古人相 見處。五祖老師云。如馬前相撲相似。須是眼 辨手親。這箇公案。若以正眼觀之。俱無得失 處。辨箇得失。無親疎處。分箇親疎。長慶也須 禮拜保福始得。何故這箇些子。巧處用得好。 如電轉星飛相似。保福不妨牙上生牙。爪上 生爪。頌云。
text_en: day he said as usual, Better to say an arhat has the three poisons, not to say the Tathagata has two kinds of speech. In Sanskrit, arhat; here it means slayer of thieves. It is named by its function and capability: it can cut off the nine times nine, eighty-one grades of afflictions. All outflows have already ended; the holy conduct has been established. This is the position of a no-more-learning arhat. The three poisons are greed, anger, and delusion—the root afflictions. Even the eighty-one grades are cut off; how much more the three poisons. Changqing said, Better to say an arhat has the three poisons than to say the Tathagata has two kinds of speech. The main intent is to reveal that the Tathagata has no untrue speech. The Lotus Sutra says, Only this one matter is true; the other two are not real. It also says, There is only one vehicle dharma, not two and not three. Across more than three hundred assemblies, the World-Honored One observed capacities and applied teachings, matching sickness with medicine, teaching the dharma in ten thousand ways—yet in the end there are not two kinds of speech. His intent reaches here—how do you all see it? The Buddha expounds the dharma with a single sound; that is not absent. But Changqing has not even dreamed of Tathagata speech yet—why? It is like someone talking about food and never becoming full. Baofu saw him preaching on level ground and so asked, What is Tathagata speech? Changqing said, Deaf people—how could they hear it? This fellow—who knows how long he has been making a living in a ghost cave. Baofu He said: I knew you would head for the second point—sure enough you hit the mark. Then he asked the senior brother, What is the Tathagata’s speech? Baofu said: Go drink tea. Instead, the spear point was seized by someone else and taken away. Big Changqing—losing money and incurring punishment. Now I ask all of you: How many kinds of Tathagata’s speech are there? You must see it like this to see these two fellows’ defects. If you examine it carefully, they both deserve a beating. Letting a single thread out so they can understand—some say Baofu spoke rightly and Changqing spoke wrongly. They just keep forming interpretations from the words, saying there is gain and there is loss—without realizing that the ancients were like striking sparks from stone, like the flash of lightning. People today do not look where the ancients turned; they only run under the phrases, and then say that Changqing at the time did not use it well, so he fell into the second point, while Baofu’s “Go drink tea” is the first point. If you only look at it this way, even when Maitreya descends you still will not see the ancients’ intent. A master would never make such an understanding; he would leap out of this nest and pit—above there is naturally a road. If you say, how could a deaf person hear, what is not the case? When Baofu says “Go drink tea,” what is the case? Turn it and there is no connection. Therefore it is said: He studies living phrases, not dead phrases. This causal nexus is the same as “cause-and-conditions through the whole body.” There is no place for you to calculate right and wrong. You must stand on your own heels, completely bare, and only then see where the ancients met each other. The Fifth Patriarch, the old master, said: It is like grappling in front of a horse—you must have eyes to discern and hands that are intimate. If you view this public case with the true eye, there is no place of gain or loss at all. If you distinguish gain and loss, there is no place of closeness or distance; if you divide closeness and distance, Changqing too must bow to Baofu to make it so. Why? This little bit is used well at the skillful point, like lightning turning and stars flying. Baofu is not hindered from growing teeth on teeth, claws on claws. The verse says:
First and second points—crouching dragon, In my king’s treasury there is no such thing. A model for past and present—why follow the crooked and chase the evil?

In dead water how could there be a dragon’s lair? If it is first and second, that is exactly making a living in still water. You must be in vast flooding waves, white breakers reaching heaven—only then is there a dragon’s lair. Just like earlier it said: A clear pool does not allow an azure dragon to coil. Haven’t you seen it said: Dead water does not hide a dragon. And it is also said: The crouching dragon always fears the clear blue pool. Therefore it is said: Where there is no dragon, moon-waves are clear—wind calm and waves still. Where there is a dragon, without wind waves rise. It is just like Baofu saying “Go drink tea”—exactly windless waves rising. Here Xuedou at this point, all at once packs up your emotional interpretations and versifies it. He has lingering resonance, forming it into coherent writing; as before, he stays within it and sets one eye there—also not amiss, extraordinary—yet he says: edgy Chan traveler, edgy Chan traveler, in the third month at Yu Gate his forehead is marked. Xuedou disliked his final line for leaking and dangling, so he cut it off and only versified the three lines. If a clay Buddha crosses water, it rots away. If a golden Buddha crosses through a furnace, it melts away. If a wooden Buddha crosses fire, it burns up. What is hard to understand? In Xuedou’s one hundred verses on old cases, full of calculations and vine-tangling, only these three verses straightaway have the breath of a patched-robed monk. Even so, these verses are still not easy to understand. If you can penetrate these three verses, then I allow you to stop your wandering study.

text_zh: 泥佛不渡水。神光照天地。這一句頌分明了。 且道為什麼却引神光。二祖初生時。神光燭 室亘於霄漢。又一夕神人現。謂二祖曰。何久 于此。汝當得道時至。宜即南之。二祖以神遇 遂名神光。久居伊洛。博極群書。每嘆曰。孔 老之教祖述風規。近聞達磨大師住少林。乃 往彼晨夕參扣。達磨端坐面壁。莫聞誨勵。光 自忖曰。昔人求道。敲骨出髓。刺血濟飢。布髮 掩泥。投崖飼虎。古尚若此。我又何如。其年十 二月九日夜大雪。二祖立於砌下。遲明積雪 過膝。達磨憫之曰。汝立雪於此。當求何事。二 祖悲淚曰。惟願慈悲開甘露門。廣度群品。達 磨曰。諸佛妙道曠劫精勤。難行能行。非忍而 忍。豈以小德小智輕心慢心。欲冀真乘。無有 是處。二祖聞誨勵。向道益切。潛取利刀。自斷 左臂。致于達磨前。磨知是法器。遂問曰。汝 立雪斷臂。當為何事。二祖曰。某甲心未安。乞 師安心。磨曰。將心來。與汝安。祖曰。覓心了 不可得。達磨云。與汝安心竟。後達磨為易其 名曰慧可。後接得三祖燦大師。既傳法隱於 舒州皖公山。屬後周武帝破滅佛法沙汰僧。 師往來太湖縣司空山。居無常處。積十餘載 無人知者。宣律師高僧傳。載二祖事不詳。三 祖傳云。二祖妙法不傳於世。賴值末後依前 悟他當時立雪。所以雪竇道。立雪如未休。何 人不雕偽。立雪若未休。足恭諂詐之人皆效 之。一時只成雕偽。則是諂詐之徒也。雪竇頌 泥佛不渡水。為什麼。却引這因緣來用。他參 得意根下無一星事。淨裸裸地方頌得如此。 五祖尋常教人看此三頌。豈不見洞山初和 尚有頌示眾云。五臺山上雲蒸飯。古佛堂前 狗尿天。剎竿頭上煎䭔子。三箇胡孫夜簸 錢。又杜順和尚道。懷州牛喫禾。益州馬腹脹。 天下覓醫人。灸猪左膊上。又傅大士頌云。空 手把鋤頭。步行騎水牛。人從橋上過。橋流水 不流。又云。石人機似汝。也解唱巴歌。汝若似 石人。雪曲應須和。若會得此語。便會他雪竇 頌　足將樹反過也。
text_en: But tell me, why does it bring in Shen Guang? When the Second Patriarch was first born, a divine light shone through the room and reached the sky. And one night a spirit appeared and said to the Second Patriarch: Why have you long stayed here? The time for you to attain the Way has arrived; you should go south at once. The Second Patriarch, meeting the divine, was thus named Shen Guang. He long lived in the Yi and Luo region, exhaustively studying many books, often sighing: The teachings of Confucius and Lao only transmit the models and rules of the ancestors. Recently I heard that Master Bodhidharma resides at Shaolin, so I went there morning and evening to inquire. Bodhidharma sat upright facing the wall, and no instruction was heard. Guang thought to himself: People of old seeking the Way knocked bone to bring out marrow, pricked blood to relieve hunger, spread their hair to cover mud, threw themselves off cliffs to feed tigers—if the ancients were like this, what about me? That year, on the ninth night of the twelfth month, there was heavy snow. The Second Patriarch stood below the steps; by dawn the snow had piled up past his knees. Bodhidharma pitied him and said: You stand in snow here—what matter do you seek? The Second Patriarch wept and said: I only beg compassion to open the gate of sweet dew and widely ferry all beings. Bodhi- dharma said: The Buddhas’ wondrous Way requires diligence over vast kalpas—doing what is hard to do, enduring what is not to be endured. How could you, with small virtue and small wisdom, with a frivolous mind and arrogant mind, hope for the true vehicle? There is no such place. Hearing this admonition, the Second Patriarch’s resolve for the Way grew more urgent. He secretly took a sharp knife and cut off his left arm, placing it before Bodhidharma. Bodhidharma knew he was a vessel of the Dharma and asked: You stood in snow and cut off your arm—what is it for? The Second Patriarch said: My mind is not at peace; I beg the master to pacify my mind. Bodhidharma said: Bring me your mind, and I will pacify it for you. The patriarch said: Searching for the mind, it cannot be found. Bodhidharma said: I have pacified your mind for you. Later Bodhidharma changed his name to Huike. Later he received the Third Patriarch, Master Can. After transmitting the Dharma, he hid away at Wangong Mountain in Shuzhou. During the time when Emperor Wu of Later Zhou destroyed Buddhism and purged monks, the master traveled to and from Sikong Mountain in Taihu County, living without a fixed place, for more than ten years, with no one knowing. In Master Xuan’s Biographies of Eminent Monks, the Second Patriarch’s affairs are not detailed. The Third Patriarch’s record says: The Second Patriarch’s wondrous Dharma was not transmitted in the world; only because at the end one still relied on the former did he awaken to that standing in snow. Therefore Xuedou said: If standing in snow had not ceased, who would not carve and counterfeit? If standing in snow had not ceased, people of excessive deference and flattery would all imitate it, and all at once it would only become carved counterfeit—mere flattery and fraud. Xuedou’s verse says: A clay Buddha does not cross water—why then does it bring in this causal story to use? He investigated until beneath the root of intention there was not a single speck of matter; only then could he versify like this, on naked, bare ground. The Fifth Patriarch often taught people to look at these three verses. Haven’t you seen that early on, Master Dongshan also had a verse instructing the assembly, saying: On Mount Wutai, clouds steam rice; before the old Buddha hall, the sky is dog piss. On top of the temple flagpole, a frying pan; three barbarian brats at night winnow coins. And Master Dushun said: In Huaizhou, cattle eat grain; in Yizhou, horses’ bellies swell. Searching the world for a doctor, you moxa a pig’s left foreleg. And Layman Fu’s verse says: Empty- handed, he holds a hoe; walking, he rides a water buffalo. People pass over the bridge; the bridge flows but the water does not flow. And he also said: The stone man’s mechanism is like yours; he too can sing Ba songs. If you are like the stone man, you should harmonize with the snow song. If you can understand these words, then you will understand Xuedou’s verses completely. Turning the tree upside down.

text_zh: 金佛不渡罏。人來訪紫胡。此一句亦頌了也。 為什麼却引人來訪紫胡。須是作家罏鞴始 得。紫胡和向。山門立一牌。牌中有字云。紫胡 有一狗。上取人頭。中取人腰。下取人脚。擬議 則喪身失命。凡見新到便喝云。看狗。僧纔回 首。紫胡便歸方丈。且道為什麼却咬趙州不 得。紫胡又一夕夜深於後架叫云。捉賊捉賊。 黑地逢著一僧。攔胸捉住云。捉得也捉得也。 僧云。和尚不是某甲。胡云。是則是。只是不肯 承當。爾若會得這話。便許爾。咬殺一切人。處 處清風凜凜。若也未然。牌中數箇字。決定不 奈何。若要見他。但透得盡方見。頌云。
text_en: Why then bring in “someone comes to visit Zihu”? Only a master’s furnace and bellows will do it. Zihu once set it up: at the monastery gate a signboard was erected, and on it were written the characters: Zihu There is a dog: above it takes a man's head, in the middle it takes a man's waist, below it takes a man's feet. If you speculate, you lose your body and your life. Whenever he saw a newly arrived monk he would shout: Watch the dog! As soon as the monk turned his head, Zihu would return to the abbot's room. Tell me, why could it not bite Zhaozhou? Zihu again, one night deep in the dark, called out from behind the racks: Catch the thief, catch the thief! In the pitch dark he met a monk, grabbed him across the chest and said: Caught him, caught him! The monk said: Venerable, it is not me. Hu said: It is, it is—only you refuse to take responsibility. If you can understand this saying, I will allow you to bite to death everyone. Everywhere the pure wind is sharp and bracing. If it is not so, a few words on a placard will certainly not do anything. If you want to see it, only when you penetrate it completely will you see. The verse says:

text_zh: 木佛不渡火。常思破竈墮。此一句亦頌了。雪 竇因此木佛不渡火。常思破竈墮。嵩山破竈 墮和尚不稱姓字。言行叵測隱居嵩山。一日 領徒。入山塢間有廟甚靈。殿中唯安一竈。遠 近祭祀不輟。烹殺物命甚多。師入廟中。以拄 杖敲竈三下云。咄汝本塼土合成。靈從何來。 聖從何起。恁麼烹殺物命。又乃擊三下。竈乃 自傾破墮落。須臾有一人。青衣峨冠。忽然立 師前設拜曰。我乃竈神。久受業報。今日蒙師 說無生法。已脫此處。生在天中。特來致謝。師 曰。汝本有之性非吾強言。神再拜而沒。侍者 曰。某甲等久參侍和尚。未蒙指示。竈神得何 徑旨。便乃生天。師曰。我只向伊道。汝本塼土 合成。靈從何來。聖從何起。侍僧俱無對。師 云。會麼。僧云。不會。師云。禮拜著。僧禮拜。師 云。破也破也墮也墮也。侍者忽然大悟。後有 僧舉似安國師。師歎云。此子會盡物我一如。 竈神悟此則故是。其僧乃五蘊成身。亦云破 也墮也。二俱開悟。且四大五蘊。與塼瓦泥土。 是同是別。既是如此。雪竇為什麼道。杖子忽 擊著。方知辜負我。因甚却成箇辜負去。只是 未得拄杖子在。且道雪竇頌木佛不渡火。為 什麼却引破竈墮公案。老僧直截與爾說。他 意只是絕得失情塵意想。淨裸裸地。自然見 他親切處也。
text_en: Dou, because of this saying, A wooden Buddha does not pass through fire; always think of breaking the stove and letting it collapse, tells of Songshan's Stove-Breaking Venerable, who did not give his surname or personal name. His words and actions were unfathomable; he lived in seclusion on Mount Song. One day he led his disciples into a mountain hollow where there was a very efficacious shrine. In the hall there was only a single stove installed. From far and near the sacrifices never ceased, and they cooked and killed many living creatures. The master entered the shrine and with his staff struck the stove three times, saying: Hey! You are originally made of brick and clay—where does your numinous power come from? Where does your holiness arise? You have them cook and kill living creatures like this! Then he struck it three more times, and the stove toppled over and broke, collapsing. After a short while there was a person in green robes with a tall cap, who suddenly stood before the master, bowed, and said: I am the stove spirit. I have long borne karmic retribution. Today I have received the master's teaching of the unborn dharma; I have already been freed from this place, and am born in the heavens. I have come especially to give thanks. The master said: Your nature was originally so; it is not something I forced with words. The spirit bowed again and vanished. The attendant said: We have long attended and studied under the master, yet have not received instruction. By what direct path did the stove spirit gain the essential point, and immediately be born in the heavens? The master said: I only said to it: You are originally made of brick and clay— where does your numinous power come from? where does your holiness arise? The attendant monks all had no reply. The master said: Do you understand? The monk said: I do not understand. The master said: Keep bowing. The monk bowed. The master said: Broken, broken; collapsed, collapsed. The attendant suddenly had a great awakening. Later there was a monk who brought this up to National Teacher Anguo. The teacher sighed and said: This fellow fully understood that things and self are one thus. The stove spirit awakening to this is of course so. That monk is a body formed of the five aggregates, and he too said: broken and collapsed. Both opened awakening. Now, are the four elements and five aggregates the same as, or different from, bricks, tiles, and mud? Are they the same or different? Since it is like this, why does Xuedou say: When the staff suddenly strikes, only then you know you have betrayed me? Why does it become a betrayal? It is only that the staff has not yet been obtained. Tell me, when Xuedou versifies A wooden Buddha does not pass through fire, why does he bring in the case of Stove-Breaking Venerable? This old monk will tell you straight: his intent is only to cut off notions of gain and loss, emotional dust and imaginings. Naked and cleanly, you will naturally see the intimate place.
97 The instruction says: Pick up one and put down one—this is not yet an adept. Raise one and illuminate three—still it deviates

text_zh: 垂示云。拈一放一。未是作家。舉一明三。猶乖 宗旨。直得天地𨺗變四方絕唱。雷奔電馳雲 行雨驟。傾湫倒嶽甕瀉盆傾。也未提得一半 在。還有解轉天關能移地軸底麼。試舉看。
text_en: from the main point. Even if heaven and earth change and the four directions fall silent; thunder runs, lightning darts, clouds move and rain lashes; pools overturn, peaks topple; jars pour out, basins tip over—you still have not lifted even half of it. Is there anyone who can turn the heavenly barrier and move the earth's axle? Try to raise it and see.

text_zh: 【九七】舉。金剛經云。若為人輕賤放一線道。又且何妨是人 先世罪業驢駝馬載應墮惡道陷墮了也以今世人輕賤 故酬本及末。只得忍受先世罪業向什麼處摸索。種穀不生豆苗則為消 滅雪上加霜又一重。如湯消氷。
text_en: in a former life had karma of wrongdoing that should fall into an evil path; because in the present life people despise him, Donkeys, camels, and horses carry it, yet it falls into a pit. therefore the karma of wrongdoing from former lives is thereby Repaying root and branch alike—you can only endure it. text_en: into an evil path; because in the present life people despise him, the karma of wrongdoing from former lives is thereby extinguished. Going only by ordinary explication, this is a common discussion in the sutra. Xuedou picked it up to versify this intent, wanting to smash the livelihoods in the doctrinal school's ghost cave. Prince Zhaoming classified this section as being able to purify karmic obstacles. The general intent in the teachings says this sutra has efficacy. Such a person in a former life created karma for hell; because the power of goodness was strong, it had not yet been received. Because in the present life people despise him, the former-life karma is extinguished. Therefore this sutra can extinguish the karma of wrongdoing from immeasurable kalpas, turning heavy into light, turning light so it is not received, and again obtain the Buddha fruit of awakening. According to the doctrinal school, to recite these twenty-odd pages of sutra is then called holding the sutra. What does that have to do with it? Some say the sutra itself has efficacy. If so, then try putting a scroll in an idle place and see—does it have any response or not? Fayuan said: To realize the Buddha ground is called holding this sutra. In the sutra it says: All Buddhas, and the dharma of all Buddhas' unsurpassed, complete awakening, all come from this sutra. Now tell me, what do you call this sutra? Is it the yellow scroll with red roller-ends kind? Do not mistakenly take the fixed star for it. Diamond is a metaphor for the dharma body's solidity: therefore things cannot destroy it. Because it is useful, it can crush all things. If you set it against a mountain, the mountain is crushed; set it against the sea, and the sea is drained. Taking the metaphor to reveal the name, the dharma is also thus. This prajna has three kinds: first, real-mark prajna; second, contemplative prajna; third, textual prajna. Real-mark prajna is true wisdom—it is the great matter beneath all your heels. It shines through past and present, utterly beyond knowledge and views. Naked and clean, bare and bright is it. Contemplative prajna is true realm—throughout the twelve periods of day and night, it emits light and moves the earth; hearing sounds and seeing forms is it. Textual prajna is that which can explicate words and letters—namely, the speaker and listener right now. Now tell me, is it prajna or is it not prajna? The ancients said: Everyone has one scroll of sutra. They also said: The hand does not hold a sutra scroll, yet constantly turns such a sutra. If you go by the sutra's efficacy, how could it be only turning heavy to make it light, turning light so it is not received? Even if it could match a sage, it would still not be wondrous. Do you not see Layman Pang listening to a lecture on the Diamond Sutra, asking the seat-master: This layman dares to have a small question—may I? The master said: If you have doubts, ask. Pang said: No self-mark and no person-mark. Since there are no self and person marks, who is there to lecture, and who is there to listen? The seat-master had no reply, and instead said: I interpret meaning based on the text; I do not know this intent. The layman then had a verse: No self and also no person—how could there be distant and close? I urge you, do not go through the seat; how could it compare to directly seeking the true? The nature of diamond prajna is beyond even the slightest speck of dust. I hear and believe and accept—altogether these are provisional names. This verse is best; clearly in one moment it is said. Guifeng classified the four-line verse: All forms whatsoever are illusory; if you see all forms as no-form, you then see the Tathagata. The meaning of these four lines is entirely the same as To realize the Buddha ground is called holding this sutra. It also says: If by form you see me, by sound you seek me, that person walks a deviant path and cannot see the Tathagata. This too is a four-line verse. But to take the one whose meaning is complete: a monk asked Huitang: What is the four-line verse? Huitang said: Even if words collapse, you still do not know. Here, regarding this sutra, Xuedou points out: If someone holds this sutra, it is precisely all of your native scenery, your original face. If you go by the Patriarchs' command in effect, this native scenery, this original face is also cut into three sections. The Buddhas of the three times and the twelvefold teachings cannot dissolve even a pinch. When you arrive here, even if you had ten thousand kinds of abilities, you still could not manage it. People today just keep reciting sutras, completely unaware what principle this is. They just say: How many have I recited in a day? They only recognize the yellow scrolls and red roller-ends, going around counting ink marks. They do not know it all arises from one's own original mind. This is only a bit of the turning-place. Master Dazhu said: If you pile up several chests of sutras in an empty room and look at them, do they emit light? It is only that a single thought from your own mind is merit and virtue. Why? The ten thousand dharmas all come from the mind itself. One thought is numinous; being numinous, it is unobstructed; being unobstructed, it transforms. The ancients said: The green green bamboo is entirely true thusness; the lush yellow flowers are nothing but prajna. If you see through it thoroughly, it is true thusness. If you suddenly have not seen it, then tell me: how do you call it true thusness? The Avatamsaka Sutra says: If a person wishes to fully know all Buddhas of the three times, he should contemplate the nature of the dharma realm: all is only mind-made. If you can recognize it, then meeting situations and conditions you are the host, you are the core. If you have not yet been able to make it clear, then submit and listen to the disposition. text_zh: 明珠在掌有功者賞。若有人持得此經。有功 驗者。則以珠賞之。他得此珠。自然會用。胡來 胡現。漢來漢現。萬象森羅。縱橫顯現。此是有 功勳。法眼云。證佛地者。名持此經。此兩句頌 公案畢。胡漢不來。全無伎倆。雪竇裂轉鼻孔。 也有胡漢來。則教爾現。若忽胡漢俱不來時。 又且如何。到這裏。佛眼也覻不見。且道是功 勳是罪業。是胡是漢。直似羚羊掛角。莫道聲 響蹤跡氣息也無。向什麼處摸索。至使諸天 捧花無路。魔外潛覻無門。是故洞山和尚。一 生住院。土地神覓他蹤跡不見。一日厨前拋 撒米麫。洞山起心曰。常住物色。何得作踐如 此。土地神遂得一見便禮拜。雪竇道。伎倆既 無。若到此無伎倆處。波旬也教失途。世尊 以一切眾生為赤子。若有一人。發心修行。波 旬宮殿。為之振裂。他便來惱亂修行者。雪竇 道。直饒波旬恁麼來。也須教失却途路無近 傍處。雪竇更自點胸云。瞿曇瞿曇識我也無。 莫道是波旬。任是佛來。還識我也無。釋迦老 子尚自不見。諸人向什麼處摸索。復云。勘破 了也。且道是雪竇勘破瞿曇。瞿曇勘破雪竇。 具眼者試定當看。
text_en: that proves true, then reward them with the pearl. Having obtained this pearl, they will naturally know how to use it. When a Hu comes, a Hu appears; when a Han comes, a Han appears. The ten thousand forms, dense and manifold, appear freely in all directions. This is merit. Fayan said: One who realizes the Buddha-ground is called one who upholds this scripture. These two lines of verse— the case is finished. When neither Hu nor Han comes, there are utterly no tricks. Xuedou twists and tears at the nostrils. If Hu and Han do come, then he has you make them appear. But if suddenly both Hu and Han do not come, then what? When you reach here, even the Buddha-eye cannot see it. Tell me: is it merit or is it karma of wrongdoing? Is it Hu or is it Han? It is like an antelope hanging by its horns—don’t say there is no sound, no trace, no breath. Where will you grope for it? This leaves the gods holding flowers with no road, and Mara and outsiders peeking with no gate. Therefore Master Dongshan, for his whole life residing in a monastery, could not be tracked by the local earth deity. One day, in front of the kitchen he scattered rice and flour. Dongshan had a thought and said: These are communal supplies—how can you waste them like this? The earth deity then managed to catch sight of him and immediately bowed in worship. Xuedou said: Since there are no tricks, if you reach this place of no tricks, you make even Papiyas lose the way. The World-Honored One takes all beings as his own children. If even one person arouses the resolve to practice, the palace of Papiyas is shaken and cracked. Then he comes to harass the practitioner. Xuedou said: Even if Papiyas comes like that, you must still make him lose the road, with nowhere nearby to cling to. Xuedou further pointed to his own chest and said: Gautama, Gautama—do you recognize me or not? Don’t say it is only Papiyas—let the Buddha himself come; would he recognize me or not? Even old Shakyamuni does not see it. Where will you all grope for it? Again he said: It has been seen through. Tell me: did Xuedou see through Gautama, or did Gautama see through Xuedou? Those with eyes, try to decide it and see.

text_en: the city of illusions and come out, how is it? Bao Shou said: A sharp sword does not cut a dead man. Siming said: Cut. Bao Shou then struck him. Siming said cut ten times; Bao Shou struck ten times, saying: This fellow— why be in such a hurry to die? Taking a corpse to meet the painful stick! And he drove him out with a shout. At that time there was a monk who asked Bao Shou: The monk who just questioned you had a lot of sense. The master skillfully received him. Bao Shou also struck and drove this monk out. Tell me: Bao Shou also drove this monk out—was it only because he spoke right and spoke wrong, or was there some other principle? What was the intent? Later, both became heirs to Bao Shou. One day Siming went out to meet Nanyuan. Nanyuan asked: Where have you come from? Siming said: From Xuzhou. Nanyuan said: What did you bring? Siming said: I brought a Jiangxi razor, to present to the master. Nanyuan said: If you came from Xuzhou, why do you have a Jiangxi razor? A-la-la-la. Tian- Siming pinched the West Courtyard’s hand once. The Courtyard said: Attendant, take it up. Siming brushed it once with his sleeve and left. The Courtyard said: Ah-la-la! ping once studied with a mountain master. Because of that, as he went around to various places, he picked up some radish- head Zen in his belly, and everywhere he casually opened his big mouth saying: I understand Zen, I understand the Way. He often said: Don’t say you understand the Buddha Dharma; you can’t even find someone to raise a phrase. The stink of dung fumes people. He just kept flaunting shallowness. But tell me: before the Buddhas appeared in the world, before the ancestral teacher came from the West, before there were questions and answers, before there were public cases—was there still Zen and the Way? The ancients, unable to avoid it, pointed according to the situation; later people called it a public case. Because the World-Honored One held up a flower and Kashyapa smiled; later Ananda asked Kashyapa: Besides the robe, what Dharma did the World-Honored One transmit separately? Kashyapa said: Ananda, Ananda. Ananda responded. Kashyapa said: Knock down the temple flagpole in front of the gate. Just as before he held up the flower, before Ananda asked—where would you get a public case? Yet you keep getting stamped and sealed by pumpkin seals from all directions and then say: I understand the Buddha Dharma—how extraordinary. Don’t let people know. Tianping was exactly like this. When Xiyuan called him over, he got two wrongs in a row, leaving him utterly flustered and frightened, unable to sort it out—before him no village, behind him no inn. Some say: The moment you speak of the meaning of coming from the West, you are already wrong. They do not realize where Xiyuan’s two wrongs land. Tell me: where do they land? Therefore it is said: He studied the living phrase, not the dead phrase. When Tianping raised his head, he had already fallen into the second, fallen into the third. Xiyuan said: Wrong. Yet he did not grasp the function right on the spot; he only said: I’ve got Zen in my belly—don’t mind him. Then he walked three or two steps again, and Xiyuan again said: Wrong—still pitch-dark as ever. Tianping came closer. Xiyuan said: Those two wrongs just now—were they Xiyuan’s wrong, or the senior’s wrong? Tianping said: From the start, wrong. Fortunately it has nothing to do with me. He was already on the seventh head, the eighth head. Xiyuan said: Stay here and spend the summer; I’ll discuss these two wrongs with you. Tianping left right then. It seemed like it, and yet it wasn’t; it was, and yet not quite; nor could you say it wasn’t—he just couldn’t keep up. Even so, there was still a bit of the breath of a patched monk. Later, after Tianping took charge of a monastery, he told the assembly: When I was traveling at first, I was blown by karmic winds and arrived at Master Siming’s place. He hit me with two wrongs in a row, and even kept me over the summer to discuss them with me. I didn’t say I was wrong then. When I set out and headed south, I already knew I was wrong. This fellow really said it. He only fell into the seventh head and the eighth head—trying to shake it off, claiming it had nothing to do with him. Nowadays when people hear him say: When I set out and headed south, I already knew I was wrong—they then go and speculate, saying: Before traveling, there wasn’t so much Buddha Dharma and Zen Way. But once you travel, you get hoodwinked by the heat of the various places. If, before traveling, you called earth heaven and called mountains water, luckily there wasn’t the tiniest matter. If you take it all in such a vulgar way, why not just buy a hat and wear it, and everyone gets by—what use is there? The Buddha Dharma is not this principle. If you discuss this matter, how could there be so many tangling vines? If you say I understand and he doesn’t, carrying a shoulder-pole of Zen, you run around under heaven—once a clear-eyed person sees through you, not a bit of it is usable. text_en: understands, but he cannot employ it. Usually he stares up into the clouds and says, How much Chan has he understood? Yet once he is cooked on the brazier, it turns out he cannot use even a bit of it. The former master, the Fifth Patriarch, said: there are people who study Chan like pounding rice cake inside a glass bottle—you cannot shift it at all; you cannot shake it out; touch it and it breaks. If you want it lively and nimble, just study shell-and-husk, leaky-basket Chan—go straight to a high mountain and throw yourself down; neither broken nor harmed. The ancients said: even if you can realize it before words, you are still stuck in the shell, deluded by the seal; even if you are perfectly clear beneath the phrase, you still cannot avoid wild views whenever you meet things. Pitiful and laughable is old Tianping, who then said he regretted traveling on pilgrimage back then. Xuedou said: pitiful that he could not speak it to others; laughable that he understood a whole bellyful of Chan yet could not put even a little of it to use. Wrong, wrong—these two wrongs. Some say, Tianping not understanding is the wrong. Others say: having no words is the wrong. What does it have to do with it? They do not know that these two wrongs are like sparks struck from stone, like a flash of lightning. This is the course and footing of one who is above: like taking up a sword to cut a man, going straight for his throat— only then is the life-root severed. If you can walk on this sword’s edge, then in seven releases and eight crossings, if you understand the two wrongs, then you can see how at West Cloister the pure breeze suddenly melts it away. Xuedou ascended the hall and raised this story, intending to say Wrong. I ask you: Xue- dou’s two wrongs—how do they compare to Tianping’s wrong? Study it for thirty years.

text_en: his reverence only deepened; in coming and going, in greeting and escorting, he personally attended the carriage. One day he brought up a question and asked the National Teacher: What is the regulating and taming of the ten bodies? The teacher said: Patron, you tread atop Vairocana’s crown. All his life the National Teacher had a spine as hard as raw iron; yet before an emperor he was like soft mud. Even though his reply was thin and petty, it still had something good in it. He said: if you want to understand, patron, you must tread atop Vairocana’s crown. Yet the emperor did not awaken, and instead said, I do not understand. After that the National Teacher was far too careless and fell into the weeds, adding a sentence on top of it: Do not mistake your own pure Dharma-body. It is said that every person is fully endowed; each one is perfectly complete. Watch how he lets go and gathers in—meeting enemies from eight sides. Did you not see it said: one who is good at being a teacher sets up instruction in response to the occasion, and trims the sail to the wind. If you only cling stubbornly to one corner, how can you turn and respond? Look at old Huangbo—how well he could receive people. When he met Linji, after three encounters he fiercely administered sixty blows; Linji immediately understood. But when it came to Chancellor Pei, the entanglements were far too many—how is this not being good at being a teacher? National Teacher Zhong, with skillful expedients, received Emperor Suzong, because he had methods for facing eight-sided attack. The ten-body regulating and taming is precisely the ten kinds of bodies of personal use. The three bodies—Dharma, reward, and transformation—are just the Dharma-body. Why is it that reward and transformation are not the true Buddha, nor are they the one who speaks Dharma? As for the Dharma-body, it is a single expanse of empty stillness, numinously bright, quiescent, and illuminating. Senior seat Fu of Taiyuan, at Guangxiao Monastery in Yangzhou, was lecturing on the Nirvana Sutra. A traveling monk—Jiaoshan’s monastic cook—was snowed in at the monastery and went to listen to the lecture. When the talk reached the three causes of Buddha-nature and the three virtues of the Dharma-body, he spoke at length of the wondrous principle of the Dharma-body. The cook suddenly laughed. Fu glanced over at him. When the lecture ended, he had the Chan monk invited and asked, saying: My understanding has always been narrow and poor; I explain meaning based on the text. Just now during the lecture, I saw you laugh. I must have fallen short somewhere—please tell me. The cook said: If the lecturer did not ask, I would not dare speak. Since you have asked, I cannot not speak. Truly, I was laughing that you do not know the Dharma-body. Fu said: Explained like this, what place is not it? The cook said: Please say it again. Fu said: The principle of the Dharma-body is like the great void: vertically it exhausts the three times; horizontally it spans the ten directions; it pervades the eight extremes, encompassing the two polarities; following conditions and responding to stimuli, it is nowhere not all-pervading. The cook said: I do not say your words are wrong; you only know matters at the measure-and-boundary of the Dharma-body. In truth you have not known where the Dharma-body is. Fu said: If so, then you, Chan monk, should explain it for me. The cook said: If so, then lecturer, suspend your lectures for ten days; in a quiet room sit upright in calm contemplation; gather the mind and collect the thoughts; let go of all conditions, good and bad, all at once; and investigate to the end on your own. Fu followed his words; from the first watch of night until the fifth, hearing the drums and horns sound, he suddenly accorded and awakened. He went and knocked at the Chan monk’s door. The cook said: Who is it? Fu said: It is I. The cook snapped: I teach you to uphold the great teaching and speak Dharma in the Buddha’s stead— why, in the middle of the night, are you like a drunk lying in the street? Fu said: All along, in lecturing on sutras, I have been twisting and pinching the nostrils of my living parents. From today onward, I will not dare do so again. Look at this extraordinary fellow—how could he merely recognize some bright, numinous awareness and fall in front of donkeys and behind horses? You must shatter karmic consciousness—there must not be the slightest trace to be found. Even then you only get half of it. The ancients said: do not raise the slightest mind of cultivating and learning; in the formless light you are always at ease. Only recognize what is constantly quiescent extinction; do not mistake sounds and forms. Only recognize numinous knowing; do not mistake deluded thoughts. Therefore it is said: even if an iron wheel spins atop your head, samādhi and wisdom, perfectly bright, are never lost. Bodhidharma asked the Second Patriarch: You stood in snow and cut off your arm— for what reason? The patriarch said: My mind is not at peace; I beg the master to pacify it. Dharma said: Bring me your mind, and I will pacify it for you. The patriarch said: I searched for the mind, and it cannot be found. Dharma said: I have pacified your mind for you. The Second Patriarch suddenly understood. Tell me, right at that moment, where is the Dharma-body? Changsha said: People who study the Way do not recognize the true, only because from long ago they recognized the spirit. The root of birth and death through countless kalpas—fools call it the original person. People today only recognize some bright, numinous awareness, and then stare wide-eyed, bulging their eyes, playing with spirit and soul—what does that have to do with it? Just as he said: do not mistake your own pure Dharma-body. And yet as for your own Dharma-body, you have not even dreamed of seeing it—so what is there to say about do not mistake? The doctrinal schools take the pure Dharma-body as the ultimate standard—so why not teach people to recognize it? Did you not see it said: if you recognize it, as before it is still not it—Bah! Fine, give him a blow. Only one who understands this intent will understand his saying, Do not mistake your own pure Dharma-body. Did you not see that Master Dongshan had three roads for receiving people: the mysterious road, the bird path, and the outstretched hand. Beginners who study the Way should for now walk these three roads. A monk asked the master: You usually teach students to walk the bird path—what, precisely, is the bird path? Dongshan said: You do not meet a single person. The monk said: How do you walk it? Dongshan said: You must go with no private footing beneath your feet. The monk said: If one walks the bird path, is that not the original face? Dongshan said: Venerable, why are you inverted? The monk said: Where am I inverted? text_en: the strong to oppress the weak, then sent a flying sword to take the strong one’s head. Therefore in the lineage teacher’s house, the brows hide a precious sword and the sleeve hangs a golden hammer, to cut off affairs of injustice. Great skill seems like clumsiness—Ba- ling’s answer, for this matter of leveling what is not level, was so extremely skillful that it instead looks clumsy. Why? Because he did not swing it right in front of your face, but instead went to a secluded place and, in one hidden cut, took a person’s head—and the person did not notice. Sometimes finger, sometimes palm—leaning to the sky, it shines on snow. If you understand it, it is like a sky-leaning long sword, stern and awe-inspiring. The ancients said: The mind-moon is solitary and round; its light swallows ten thousand forms. Light does not illuminate objects; objects do not remain. When light and objects are both forgotten, what is it then? This precious sword may appear on a finger, and suddenly appear in the palm. In the past, Steward Qing spoke to this point, raised his hand and said: Do you see it? It also need not be on the fingers. Xuedou passes by, borrowing the road, to let you see the ancients’ intent. Tell me, is there any place that is not the hair-blowing sword? Therefore it is said: When the third-tier waves rise high, a fish transforms into a dragon; fools still bail water from a night pond. The Record of the Ancestor’s Court Affairs Garden records in the Filial Son Biography: The consort of the King of Chu once, in summer, seeking coolness, embraced an iron pillar and conceived. Later she gave birth to an iron lump. The King of Chu ordered Ganjiang to forge it into a sword. After three years a pair of swords was made: one female, one male. Ganjiang secretly kept the male and presented the female to the King of Chu. The king hid it in a case, and often heard a mournful cry. The king asked his ministers. A minister said: The sword has female and male; the one that cries longs for the male. The king, greatly enraged, seized Gan- jiang and killed him. Ganjiang knew what would come, so he hid the sword inside a house pillar, and instructed his wife Moye, saying: When the sun rises at the north door, on the south mountain is a pine; the pine grows from stone; the sword is within it. Later his wife bore a son named Red-Brow. At fifteen he asked his mother: Where is my father? His mother recounted what happened before. After long reflection he split the pillar and got the sword, and day and night wished to avenge his father. The King of Chu also offered rewards and sought him, proclaiming: Whoever captures Red- Brow will be richly rewarded. Red-Brow then fled. Soon a guest said: You are Red-Brow, are you not? He said: Yes. The guest said: I am from Zengshan, and I can avenge your father. Red-Brow said: My father was innocent and was wrongfully harmed. Now you kindly remember him—what do you require? The guest said: I must obtain your head and the sword. Red-Brow then gave him the sword and his head. The guest took them and presented them to the King of Chu. The king was overjoyed. The guest said: I wish to boil oil and cook it. The king then threw it into a cauldron. The guest told the king: That head does not rot. The king came forward to look. From behind, the guest used the sword to strike at the king’s head and knocked it into the cauldron. Thereupon the two heads bit each other. The guest feared Red-Brow would not prevail, so he cut his own throat to help him. The three heads bit each other, and soon all rotted away. Xuedou said: This sword can In the Sichuan edition there is no such passage about the King of Chu. lean to the sky and shine on snow. It is commonly said: the light of a sky-leaning long sword can shine on snow. This use goes so far that: the great forge cannot grind it down. Even if the fine craftsman keeps wiping and polishing, it does not cease. The fine craftsman is Ganjiang. The old story makes itself clear. Xuedou after chanting, finally makes it clear: distinct, distinct—also not without strangeness. There is a special point, different from ordinary swords. Tell me, what is the special point? Coral branches, each branch holding up the moon—one could say it surpasses what came before and cuts off what comes after, uniquely occupying the world, with no equal match. Ultimately, how is it? All of you—your heads have fallen too. This old monk has another short verse:

text_en: Lifted and turned a hundred times, an old case—scattered among people today as grit in the eyes.

text_zh: 佛果圜悟禪師碧巖錄卷第十終 後序
text_en: Blue Cliff Record, Volume Ten, by the Chan master Foguo Yuanwu End. Postface Xuedou’s one hundred verses on the ancients are essential pointers for studying the Way in the monasteries. Within them he draws analogies

text_zh: 雪竇頌古百則。叢林學道詮要也。其間取譬 經論或儒家文史。以發明此事。非具眼宗匠 時為後學擊揚剖析。則無以知之。
text_en: from sutras and treatises, or from Confucian literature and history, to illuminate this matter. Without a lineage craftsman with eyes who at times strikes and raises it up, dissecting it for later students, there is no way to know it.
When the elder teacher Yuanwu was in Chengdu, I and others requested instruction on his explanations.

text_zh: 圜悟老師。在成都時。予與諸人請益其說。師 後住夾山道林。復為學徒扣之。凡三提宗綱。 語雖不同。其旨一也。門人掇而錄之。既二十 年矣。師未甞過而問焉。流傳四方。或致踳駁。 諸方且因其言以其道不能尋繹之。而妄有 改作。則此書遂廢矣。學者幸諦其傳焉。
text_en: Later, when the master lived at Jiashan Daolin, we again pressed him for it as students. In all, he raised the essentials of the school three times. Though the words differed, the meaning was one. Disciples gathered them and recorded them. It has been twenty years now, and the master has never corrected or questioned it. As it circulated in all directions, it sometimes became confused and faulty. In various places, because people could not trace and unfold his Way from his words, they rashly altered and rewrote them, and then this book was ruined. Students, please carefully examine its transmission.
Recorded by Ren Guan, You Wudang, on the last days of spring in the yisi year of the Xuanhe era.

text_zh: 宣和乙巳春暮上休。𭷔人關友無黨記。 重刊圜悟禪師碧巖集疏
text_en: Preface to the reprinting of the Blue Cliff Collection Commentary by the Chan master Yuanwu Xuedou’s one hundred verses on the ancients, with Yuanwu’s added annotations, are shown plainly to the monasteries.

text_zh: 雪竇頌古百則圜悟重下注脚。單示叢林。 永垂宗旨經也。學人機鋒捷出。大慧密室 勘辨。知無實詣。毀梓不傳權也。此書諸 佛正眼列祖大機。兩經鉗鎚。一無瑕纇。茲 欲與大慧長書並駕。同圜悟心要兼行。揭 杲日於迷途。指南鍼於慧海。快然一覩。開 彼群愚。相與圓成。不無利益。幸甚。
text_en: They are a scripture that forever transmits the school’s aim. When students’ sharp points spring forth swiftly, Dahui in the private room examined and discerned, and knew there was no real attainment, so he destroyed the woodblocks and did not transmit it, as a provisional measure. This book is the Buddhas’ true eye and the patriarchs’ great functioning. The two classics are tongs and hammer, without a single flaw. Now it is desired to run alongside Dahui’s long letter, carrying out together Yuanwu’s mind-essentials, raising the bright sun in a deluded path, and setting a compass needle in the sea of wisdom. With one swift look, it opens that crowd of the foolish, and together brings completion. It is not without benefit. How fortunate.
Moreover, at seventeen he already awakened through Yunmen and Muzhou, which can be called a verbal

text_zh: 右伏以。十七歲便悟雲門睦州。可道是口頭 三昧。二百年不見碧巖雪竇。忽遭渠手下一 交。怎忘得弓冶裘箕。莫斷却兒孫種草。隨人 去脚跟後轉。誰下得釣龍鉤。有箇具眼目底 來。不看作繫驢橛。此事當如筏喻。他時自 會筌忘。家家門戶透長安。前者呼後者應。種 種因緣歸大數。昔之廢今之興。莫怪山僧口 多。終是老婆心切。不讀東土書。安知西來意。 重興一代宗風。雖無南去雁。看取北來魚。便 有十分消息。持同文印。讀無盡燈。謹疏。
text_en: samadhi. For two hundred years there was no sight of Blue Cliff Xuedou; suddenly one is struck once by his hand, how could one forget the bow, the forge, the fur robe, the winnowing basket? Do not cut off the descendants’ seed of weeds. Following others, you turn after their heels. Who can cast the dragon-fishing hook? Let someone with eyes come forth, and do not take it as a donkey-tethering stake. This matter should be like the raft parable; later on you will naturally forget the fish trap. Every household’s gate passes through Chang’an; the one in front calls, the one behind responds. All kinds of causes and conditions return to the great tally. What was abandoned in the past now revives; do not blame this mountain monk for his many words, it is only an old woman’s urgent heart. If you do not read the books of this land, how will you know the meaning of the coming from the West? Reviving a generation’s school style: though there are no geese going south, look at the fish coming from the north, and then there is full news. Holding the seal of the shared script, reading the inexhaustible lamp, I respectfully submit this.
Written on the day of this month

text_zh: 今月　日疏 比丘淨日序
text_en: Preface by the bhikshu Jingri When the old patriarch Yuanwu lived at Jiashan, he compiled this book, wishing that later generations under heaven

text_zh: 圓悟老祖居夾山時。集成此書。欲天下後世 知有佛祖玄奧。豈小補哉。老妙喜深患學者 不根於道溺于知解。由是毀之。謂其父子之 間矛盾。可乎。今嵎中張居士重為板行。果何 謂哉。覽者宜自擇焉。大德壬寅中秋。住天童 第七世法孫比丘。淨日拜手謹書。
text_en: would know the mysterious depths of Buddhas and patriarchs. How could that be a small benefit? The old Miaoxi deeply worried that students were not rooted in the Way and drowned in learned interpretations; therefore he destroyed it, saying that between father and son there were contradictions. Could that be right? Now Layman Zhang of Yuzhong has again made woodblocks to print it. What does that mean, really? Readers should choose for themselves. Mid-autumn in the renyin year of the Dade era, residing at Tiantong, the seventh-generation dharma-grandson bhikshu Jingri respectfully wrote this with joined hands.

text_zh: 比丘𭤔陵序
text_en: Preface by the bhikshu Ling The Chan master Yuanwu commented on and sang Xuedou the master’s one hundred verses on the ancients, splitting open and deciding

text_zh: 圜悟禪師。評唱雪竇和尚頌古一百則。剖決 玄微。抉剔幽邃。顯列祖之機用。開後學之心 源。況妙智虛凝。神機默運。晶旭輝而玄扃洞 照。圓蟾升而幽室朗明。豈淺識而能致極哉。 後大慧禪師。因學人入室。下語頗異。疑之纔 勘而邪鋒自挫。再鞠而納欵。自降曰。我碧 巖集中記來。實非有悟。因慮其後不明根本。 專尚語言以圖口捷。由是火之以救斯弊也。 然成此書。火此書。其用心則一。豈有二哉。嵎 中張明遠偶獲寫本後冊。又獲雪堂刊本及 蜀本。校訂訛舛。刊成此書。流通萬古。使上根 大智之士。一覽而頓開本心。直造無疑之地。 豈小補云乎哉。延祐丁巳迎佛會日。徑山住 持比丘。𭤔陵拜書以為後序。
text_en: the subtle and mysterious, picking out the hidden and profound, revealing the patriarchs’ functioning, and opening the mind- source for later students. Moreover, wondrous wisdom is empty and congealed, the spiritual mechanism operates silently; crystal dawn shines and the dark gate is thoroughly illuminated; the full moon rises and the hidden chamber becomes bright. How could shallow knowledge bring one to the ultimate? Later the Chan master Dahui, because students entered the room and his words were quite different, doubted it and only after examination did the crooked edge collapse on its own; after a second pressing he confessed. He humbled himself, saying: In my Blue Cliff Collection notes, I truly had no awakening. Because I feared that later people would not understand the root, and would prize language alone to seek quick mouths, I therefore burned it to remedy this flaw. Yet compiling this book and burning this book come from a single intention. How could there be two? Layman Zhang of Yuzhong, Zhang Mingyuan, happened to obtain a later volume of a manuscript copy, and also obtained the Xuetang printed edition and a Shu edition, collated and corrected errors, and printed this book to circulate for ten thousand ages, so that those of superior faculties and great wisdom may glance once and suddenly open their original mind, directly reaching the ground of no doubt. How could this be called a small benefit? On the day of the Buddha-greeting assembly in the ding-si year of the Yanyou era, the resident of Jingshan, the bhikshu Ling, bowed and wrote this as a postface.

text_zh: 海粟老人馮子振序
text_en: Preface by the old man Haisu, Feng Zizhen In the Confucian school, Zigong had great merit for the sage of the eastern house. If a fine horse sees

text_zh: 儒門子貢極有功於東家聖人。藉令良馬見 鞭影而奔。皆如瞠若乎後之顏子。吾聖師遊 乎何言之天久矣。靈山會上。四眾海集。世尊 拈花宗旨。諸人罔措。獨迦葉尊者。微為之破 顏。與吾教中一唯之外口耳俱喪。同一頓徹懸 悟。當時曾參。不直下剖擊忠恕之祕鑰。豈惟 門人之惑滋甚。千載之下。何以祛一貫之迷 雲乎。異時成都佛果圜悟老禪。笏夾山丈室。 拈提雪竇頌古百則。其大弟子杲上座。懼學 人泥於言句。辜負從上諸祖。取老和尚舌頭。 一截併付烈焰。煙而颺之拉𣜂堆。自以巨壑 太虛投置毫滴。如古德德山賣弄油糍婆前。 此疏鈔已埃冷而無餘矣。野火燒不盡。春風 吹又生。花落碧巖。陽坡如繡。歷過去劫。死灰 復然。不知何許。許多葛藤。一一從嵎中張居 士手栽無影樹子上。全體敗露。直得般若無 說諸天雨花。百七八十年。衲僧驀地。橫穿鼻 孔。從前不曾嗅底寶熏。一旦水湧雲蒸。於八 萬四千毛孔。悉普悉遍。可謂甚深希有。難值 難遇之事。已而居士二子得心疾。或謂。勤寶 經杲上座燬板。居士不當拾遺燼。而日月光 景之故。受如是報。居士者疑其說。以質於予。 予謂。圜悟門人人人而杲上座。碧巖自碧。何 得有說杲上座。見月亡指。遂乃追尤古佛。毒 燎亘天。倒却剎竿。不放一綫。彼未甞識月者。 誰將乘一指而示之。或者又謂。杲上座火此 書。盟之社鬼者深重。居士二子之患正坐此。 予謂。當杲上座灼然秉炬時。煉得故紙通紅。 何緣密室通風。老勤巴命門舌根。別自有不 壞處。一星迸散。明月空山。張居士那裏得這 消息來。把天然一段西蜀錦機。依舊織作舊 日花樣。意者主林神陰為之地。訶護至今。料 亦是此書合出世因緣時節。清涼池上。針芥 相逢。則書寫讀誦。為人演說之功。應獲殊勝 福德。何況金石刻鏤。展轉流布。居士二子之 心疾根本。本不在此。客作漢。妄以情識卜度。 居士緣其目前不足計拔之禍福。亦以情識 卜度之。是相隨赴火坑也。豈不冤哉。冥驗記。 沛國周氏。三子並瘖。一日有客造門曰。君可 內省宿愆。忽猛憶兒時見燕窠三子。伺其母 出。各以一蒺藜吞之。斯須共斃。母還悲鳴而 去。常自悔責。客曰。君既知悔責。罪今免矣。 三子即皆能言。然則居士二子之病風喪心。 得無亦有可悔恨之事乎。談般若者。若為人 輕賤。是人先世罪業應墮惡道。以今世人輕 賤故。先世罪業即為消滅。居士能於此有省。 縱無始劫來所造諸業。當應時消滅。即君二 子之心疾。當如周氏三子之應時能言。可以 不疑。世尊住世。四十九年。六百函文字。覆藏 遍界。若從杲上座之說。萬年一念。更留踪跡 作麼。向上禪林無限尊宿有兩句。最端的曰。 任爾即心即佛。我但非心非佛。今而後有謗 如來正法輪者。君但應之曰。任汝說杲上座 底是。我只說勤老師底是。若不如是。即恐 燎却面門。四百四病一時發矣。將如居士二 子心疾何。不見古人道。養子方知父母恩。居 士學佛知恩。臨老懺悔。他日作家爐鞴。跳出 丈六金身。不知還見勤老師真箇揚眉竪拂 否。若還一句薦得。向道佛祖有誓。罪不重科。 莫殃及他家兒孫好。雖然如是。且得沒交涉。 是年延祐丁巳中元日。海粟老人馮子振題。
text_en: the shadow of a whip and runs, it is still like staring blankly compared to the later Yanzi. Our sacred teacher roamed long in the heaven beyond words. At the assembly on Vulture Peak, the fourfold community gathered like a sea; the World-Honored One held up a flower as the school’s essential point; everyone was at a loss. Only the venerable Kasyapa slightly broke into a smile. In our teaching too, outside the single cry, mouth and ears are both lost, the same sudden penetration and sudden awakening. If at that time there had been inquiry, but it did not directly split open and strike the secret key of loyalty and forgiveness, then not only would the disciples’ confusion have grown worse; a thousand years later, how could one dispel the delusion of the single thread of coherence? Later, in Chengdu, the old Chan master Foguo Yuanwu dwelled in the abbot’s room at Jiashan. He raised and presented Xuedou’s one hundred verses on the ancients. His great disciple, Senior Kegui, feared that students would cling to words and phrases and betray the patriarchs of old. He took the old master’s tongue, cut off a section and threw it into fierce flames, smoking it and scattering it to an ash heap. He regarded himself as casting a hair-tip drop into a vast void, like the old worthy Deshan showing off before the old woman selling fried cakes. This commentary had already turned to cold ash with nothing left. Wildfire cannot burn it all away; spring wind blows and it grows again. Flowers fall on Blue Cliff; the sunny slope is like embroidery. Passing through kalpas, dead ash flares again. From who knows where. So many vines and creepers, each one planted by Layman Zhang of Yuzhong by hand upon a shadowless tree, the whole body is exposed. Until prajna without speech makes the gods rain flowers. After a hundred and seventy or eighty years, a patch-robed monk suddenly pierces the nostrils straight through. A precious fragrance never smelled before, in one day water surges and clouds steam, and through eighty- four thousand pores it is everywhere and universal. It can be called profoundly rare, hard to encounter, hard to meet. After that, the layman’s two sons fell ill of the heart. Some said: Because you diligently treasured the scriptures, Senior Kegui burned the blocks; the layman should not have gathered leftover ashes, and so by the light of sun and moon you received such a recompense. The layman doubted this claim and asked me about it. I said: In Yuanwu’s gate there are people upon people, and then there is Senior Kegui. Blue Cliff is blue of itself; how could one speak about Senior Kegui? Seeing the moon, you lose the finger. So he went on to fault even the ancient Buddha, with poisonous flames blazing across the sky, toppling the monastery pole, not letting through a single thread. Those who have never known the moon, who will use a finger to show it to them? Others again said: Senior Kegui burned this book, and the oath to the shrine-ghosts was heavy; the layman’s two sons’ illness is exactly because of this. I said: When Senior Kegui clearly held the torch, he refined the old paper until it was glowing red. How could a hidden room have a draft? Old Qinba’s vital gate and tongue root have their own unbreakable place. One spark bursts and scatters, the bright moon over an empty mountain. Where would Layman Zhang get this news? He took a natural stretch of Western Shu brocade loom and still wove the old patterns of former days. Perhaps it was done by the forest’s ruling spirits in the dark, guarding and protecting it to this day. I suppose it was also the time when this book’s conditions for appearing in the world had come. At the Clear and Cool Pool, needle and mustard seed meet; then the merit of copying, reading, reciting, and expounding it for others should obtain exceptional blessings. How much more so when carved in metal and stone and passed along in turn. The root of the layman’s two sons’ heart illness is not here at all. A hired-hand fellow rashly divined it with feelings and consciousness. The layman, on account of what lay before his eyes, counted up and pulled at blessings and misfortunes, also using feelings and consciousness to divine it. This is following each other into a fire pit. Is it not unjust? In the Record of Hidden Responses: In Pei, the Zhou family had three sons, all mute. One day a visitor came to the gate and said: You should inwardly examine past faults. Suddenly he strongly recalled that in childhood he had seen a swallow’s nest with three chicks, and when their mother went out, he made each swallow a caltrop. In a short while they all died. The mother returned, cried sadly, and flew away. He always reproached himself in regret. The visitor said: Since you know regret and blame yourself, your guilt is now forgiven. The three sons then all could speak. Thus, as for the layman’s two sons, if their illness is wind that makes the mind lost, could it be that there is also something to repent and regret? Those who speak of prajna, if they are to help people despised. Such a person's past-life karmic offenses should have made them fall into an evil path, but because in this life people despise them, their past-life karmic offenses are thereby extinguished. If the layman can gain insight into this, then even the various deeds created since beginningless kalpas should be extinguished right then. Then the heart illness of your two sons should, like the Zhou family's three sons, at the proper time be able to speak; you can have no doubt. The World-Honored One dwelt in the world for forty-nine years; six hundred cases of written words cover and store up the whole realm. If you follow Senior Seat Gao's talk, ten thousand years are one thought; what traces would you still leave for what? In the higher Zen groves, countless venerable elders have two lines; the most incisive say: Let you say mind itself is Buddha; I only say neither mind nor Buddha. From now on, if there are those who slander the Tathagata's true Dharma wheel, you should only answer them: go ahead and say Senior Seat Gao's is right; I only say Teacher Qin's is right. If you do not do so, I fear your face will be scorched, and the four hundred and four illnesses will erupt at once. Then what of the layman's two sons' heart illness? Have you not seen the ancients say: only when raising children do you know the kindness of parents. The layman, studying Buddha, knows gratitude, and repents in old age. Another day, as a seasoned bellows and furnace, you will leap out of the sixteen-foot golden body. I do not know whether you will still see Teacher Qin truly raise his brows and lift his whisk or not. If you can realize even one sentence, you may say: Buddhas and patriarchs have a vow; offenses will not be punished too harshly. Do not let it bring calamity upon that family's children and grandchildren. Even so, for now it has nothing to do with it. On the Zhongyuan day of the Ding-si year of Yanyou, the old man Haisu, Feng Zizhen, inscribed this.

text_zh: 華園玉桃菴主萬寧玄彙序
text_en: Preface by Wannian Xuanhui, Abbot of the Jade Peach Hermitage in Huayuan. The Blue Cliff Collection circulating in the world exists in several editions, with many volumes and cases; for advanced students

text_zh: 碧巖集行于世者數版。卷套多多。到上學徒 盛笈非便也。故予欲成小字縮行省紙冊。有 年所矣。安政丁巳秋。篤信檀士戮力捨財。喜 資上木。即命剞劂氏。事既竣焉。喜捨刊梓製 本賤價。固予初志也。若夫碧巖曲節。先哲序 跋善美盡盡。予何言乎。簡省刻成。故書詹言 於筴端。爾安政六年歲在己未秋七月初吉 勅住華園玉桃菴主萬寧玄彙敬識。
text_en: carrying it in book satchels is not convenient. Therefore I wished to make a small-character edition with shortened lines to save paper and binding; it has I. been some years now. In the autumn of the Ding-si year of Ansei, devout donors exerted themselves and gave funds; happily the capital was put to the blocks, and I at once ordered the engravers. When the work was completed, I gladly gave to have it printed and bound, and sold the copies at a low price; this was indeed my original intent. As for the detailed sections of Blue Cliff, and the excellent prefaces and postscripts of the former worthies, all is perfectly fine; what more can be said? Since this abridged engraving is completed, I therefore write these I. words at the end of the tablets. In the sixth year of Ansei, the year ji-wei, on the first auspicious day of the seventh month of autumn, respectfully recorded by Wannian Xuanhui, appointed resident abbot of the Jade Peach Hermitage in Huayuan.
